Two beds and one planter produced shoots before the usual rain. The other rows followed the dates in the older calendar. The early growth is real for those containers; it is not evidence that all Greenwake soil changed at once. The saved seed came from different lots, and the two beds sit closer to the root wall. Those differences matter before comparing dates.

Mara suspects the seed lots may have been selected from a warmer row. Owen suspects warmth in the masonry moved through the soil. Both explanations fit the small set of observations. A third possibility is that the first rain was recorded late. The weather ledger has missing hours after a storm, so the calendar cannot settle the question by itself.

The next trial separates seed lots, uses the same amount of water and places each group at measured distances from the wall. A caretaker records the planting day and the first visible shoot, not the day someone remembered seeing it. If a planter dries out, the card notes that as a failure rather than excluding it from the comparison.

An early shoot gives a family food sooner. It may also make a keeper overconfident about next month’s harvest. The card therefore includes a space for what the trial does not show. No one should announce that the garden is safe because three seedlings appeared before the rain.

entries.title: A Warm Stone Does Not Name Its Source
entries.body:
The western edge of the stone tray remained warmer than the water collected above it. Dark roots pressed into the same section of masonry. The comparison used one cup with a chipped rim, so the height marks are only approximate. A second reading with a replaced vessel is needed before the difference can be used in a rate calculation.

Warmth might travel from the roots into the stone. The wall could also retain heat from daylight longer than the water does. A small buried channel might carry warmer water past the tray. None of these explanations has been tested against the others. The observation locates the area where a new sample should be taken; it does not identify a machine or a living source below the garden.

If the roots draw heat from a deeper layer, the surrounding soil may cool when the connection is interrupted. Testing that idea requires a controlled comparison and a way to stop the test without harming a bed. The present site cannot provide that test safely. Owen recommends monitoring temperature on both sides of the masonry and leaving the root network intact.

The word “extraction” appears in an older margin, but the handwriting is not dated and the term is not defined. It could describe water being pulled through soil rather than energy being taken from the world. Keep the note as a quotation with its source uncertainty; do not repeat it as a measured result.

entries.title: Work Offered Is Not Work Owed
entries.body:
The Greenwake rota assigns watering shifts by bed. Three residents exchanged one shift, two slots remain unfilled, and a note gives the next review date. The schedule states that declining a shift does not remove a person’s water share. That rule was adopted after a family became ill during a previous dry period and could not tend its row. Their seed was moved to a neighbor’s bed while they recovered.

Signatures on the back correspond to the dates of work completed. They show that someone accepted a particular task, not that they accepted a permanent duty. A person who signed the rota did not consent to the Crown, a levy, or a future transfer of their share. Keeping the opt-out rule beside the names prevents a copyist from preserving only the obligation-shaped part of the record.

Mara wants the rota reviewed every two weeks while the water source is unstable. The review asks which beds can be combined, whether a caretaker needs another person and whether a seed lot should be moved. It does not ask who deserves to eat. That question has no answer in this schedule, and the residents do not want a ledger of hunger to become a test of loyalty.

The rota is useful because it can change. Its blank slots are invitations for volunteers, not missing names. Any later archive should preserve those blanks and the rule beside them.

entries.title: The First Warden’s Trial Rules
entries.body:
The grove trial measures whether Rowan can recognize an attack warning, move clear of a threatened path and stop when the ground line is crossed. It does not test whether he accepts the Crown’s account of the world. The First Warden has no authority to decide that question for the caretakers or for Rowan. Mara Bell and Owen Reed attend as witnesses to the conditions, not as judges of his oath.

A pale line across the soil marks the retreat path. Raising a hand or stepping past it ends the trial. If Rowan falls, the Warden does not strike him again. The roots around the arena are left uncut; neither side may use them to pin the other in place. A bout ends when one combatant yields, withdraws or can no longer stand.

These rules matter because the Champion offer and a combat test are separate acts. Success can show that Rowan can survive an immediate danger. It cannot prove that the cycle is necessary, that the Crown should choose future keepers or that everyone affected gave consent. Failure would not revoke anyone’s right to question the World Will.

The procedure should be read before the gate opens. If the lines are obscured or the retreat path is blocked, the trial is postponed. Readiness is not obedience, and no result at this arena can make a second person inherit the choice Rowan has made.

entries.title: The Second Plate Reading
entries.body:
The Message Plate was read again after the Veilshard Drake encounter. A blank section appears before the final pulse. It is wider than the interval marked on the earlier copy. The eastern brace shifted during the fight, and the plate may have moved with it. The marks can be measured on the surface; the recorder does not preserve the direction from which the pulse arrived.

Two explanations remain open. A source could have emitted an irregular sequence, or the receiver could have dropped part of a longer trace. The plate’s position changed, and its threshold setting is not written on the face. Replacing the first record with a clean drawing would remove the evidence of that damage. Both readings therefore remain in the archive with their dates, instrument positions and uncertainty notes.

A third reading should be made with a fixed brace and a calibrated threshold. The observer should note any strike, wind movement or reset before reading the marks. If a section is missing, the copy should show a gap rather than interpolate a pulse.

Nothing on the plate identifies a speaker, a language or an intention. Its surviving record supports only the narrower claim that the instrument registered changes in received energy at two times. A receiver trace is not yet a conversation.

entries.title: Two Clocks on a Moving Mast
entries.body:
The Outer-Wake wind mast clock and the indoor reference clock disagree by one division. Jace locked the mast pointer before the Veilshard Drake attack. The brace held the pointer in place under ordinary wind, but the mast flexed when the creature hit its eastern support. The indoor clock was not exposed to the impact. Its reading appears in the margin of the same log.

The mismatch cannot be fixed by taking an average until the time at which drift began is known. If the mast stopped during the fight and restarted later, its error would grow differently from a clock that moved briefly and returned. The original entries remain legible, so no one should rewrite them to match a preferred sequence.

For the next observation, the mast must be checked for movement and the indoor clock copied independently. Both entries should include the observer and the time the comparison was made. The field form has separate columns for the instrument reading and the reference reading. A calculated offset belongs in a third column with the method used.

This disagreement changes the precision of the signal timing. It does not show that the pulse came from outside Asterra, and it does not make the rest of the record false. It narrows which conclusions can safely depend on exact intervals.

entries.title: Waterline and Receiver Are Separate Events
entries.body:
The Celestial Pool gauge rose after the wind mast clock shifted. The log contains no water reading for the hour between them. A Farwake Carp reached the shallow edge before the next mark was recorded. The order of these observations is known; their relationship is not.

Water level could change with a leak, an inlet opening, evaporation or movement through the underground channel. The receiver may have captured a separate event at the same time. Without synchronized clocks, simultaneous marks cannot be established. No instrument in this record measures a force passing between the pool and the message plate.

A repeat observation should begin with the water gauge and continue through the full receiver window. The observer writes both clock readings without converting them, notes whether the transmitter is disabled and records visible fish movement as a separate item. If the gauge changes without a signal, that result remains useful. If a signal occurs with a stable waterline, it also remains useful.

The fish is a practical sign that the shallow edge remained accessible during one observation. It is not a sensor calibrated to the Veil, a predictor of future signal or proof that the pool is connected to the outside. Keeping these events in separate columns protects the record from a story that is more certain than its measurements.

entries.title: Jace’s Correction Beside His First Note
entries.body:
Jace wrote “possible reply” in the margin before the receiver registered its next pulse. He says he hoped the plate would answer. In the following shift, he described weaker marks as a return, although the marks were less clear than the first reading. He has asked that both the first phrase and his later correction remain attached to the log.

The admission does not invalidate the recorded marks. It adds information about the conditions under which they were heard and interpreted. A person who expects a sound can notice it sooner; a person who expects silence can also ignore it. Both effects can shape when a human observer chooses to press a button or copy a trace.

Future shifts should use two observers when practical. One person logs the clock and instrument settings without being told the expected sequence. A second person listens and writes what they hear before comparing notes. Disagreements stay in the record rather than being settled by seniority. If the receiver is silent, the report should distinguish silence at the plate from silence in the room and from an instrument that was not powered.

Jace’s correction makes the log more complete, not more conclusive. The plate still lacks enough information to identify a sender. The archive should preserve the expectation because it can affect interpretation, while leaving the measured marks available for independent review.

entries.title: A Recorder That Does Not Transmit
entries.body:
The passive recorder opens during a set interval and stores received changes without powering the transmitter. Its clock is not synchronized with the wind mast, so the recorded start and end times carry a known offset. The latest window contains two pulses separated by a long blank. The receiver threshold and wire condition were not written on the same page.

A blank interval has more than one possible cause. The source may have sent nothing; a weak signal may have stayed below the threshold; a damaged lead may have dropped part of the trace; or the clock may have placed the window incorrectly. The record cannot choose among these possibilities without a calibration page and a repeat sample.

Passive mode reduces one source of confusion: the archive did not intentionally broadcast during the observed window. That lowers the chance that a locally sent pulse is mistaken for an outside response. It does not make the recording complete, remove the observer’s expectations or prove that any pulse came from beyond the Veil.

The next calibration should record the threshold, circuit state, clock offset and room noise. A second recorder should run in parallel. Both raw files remain attached to the report, even if one appears cleaner. A safe instrument protocol can prevent some errors; it cannot turn uncertainty into a speaker’s name.

entries.title: The Silent Console Check
entries.body:
The receiver console completed its check with the transmitter circuit closed. Its lamp stayed dark while the passive recorder continued to count time. This confirms that the silent-mode check did not intentionally send a pulse during that interval. It does not identify the earlier trace or show who might have received it.

The test was made after the eastern brace moved. The console’s local clock was compared with the indoor reference, but the correction was not applied to the raw time. Both values remain in the log. The operator wrote down the switch position before touching the controls and confirmed it again afterward. A second person watched the transmitter lamp and recorded the passive trace independently.

If the console is used again, the transmitter should remain physically disconnected while the receiving circuit is tested. A sealed cover can reduce accidental contact, but it cannot certify the cable path without inspection. No one should repeat the earlier signal simply to see whether someone answers; the sender and potential recipient are unknown, and the site has not established the consequences of a reply.

The full report to Evelyn includes the two plate readings, the wind-clock offset, the tide gap, Jace’s observer note and this silent check. Together they describe a repeatable method with visible limits. They support preservation of the evidence, not a conclusion about language, intention or the existence of a community beyond Asterra.

entries.title: The Diver’s Three-Note Mark
entries.body:
Mara Voss carries a wax slate used by her mother, a diver who worked along the western pipe route. Its three short taps once called a crew back when a lamp could not be seen through disturbed water. The slate records a family practice and the reason this pattern matters to Mara. It does not establish the source of another recording found in the Choir archive.

The newly discovered sample contains three similar taps, but its operator, microphone position and original audience are missing. The northern wall delays part of the sound, while a Whisper Koi can produce a similar interval when water passes through a narrow stone gap. Each fact changes how the sample should be read; none names a speaker.

The register therefore labels it an unidentified three-note sequence. Mara may keep her family memory in her own words without lending her mother’s name to a public recording. If a relative later chooses to identify the voice, that decision will receive a date, a scope and a new version rather than being silently inserted into the old record.

entries.title: Who Held the Wax Slate?
entries.body:
The wax slate has a water-stained edge and a smudged time mark. A surviving symbol resembles the southern receiver stamp, but there is no name beside it. The entry records the visible mark, the uncertain reading and the position where Mara found the slate. It does not turn a family object into proof about a separate archive sample.

Each copied mark is attributed to the person who made the copy. Lyra keeps the photographed original beside the transcription, including the blank where the final character could not be read. A later reader can compare versions and challenge the interpretation without losing the first observer’s description.

Custody has two questions: who possessed an object, and who had authority to disclose what it contains. Possession alone answers neither. The Choir now logs both the physical handoff and each permission granted for listening or copying.

entries.title: Where the Editor Entered the Recording
entries.body:
Lyra once joined several short sound bands into a sentence so new archivists could follow the material. Her index became easier to read, but the joins hid the point where water erased a syllable and the point where an editor chose a likely word. The original samples survived; the distinction between recording and commentary did not.

The revised catalogue stores the unfiltered sound, each processing pass and the written interpretation as related but separate records. An edit must name its author, date and reason. When Lyra cannot reconstruct an earlier decision, she marks that gap instead of claiming to remember it.

This correction does not make the old reading useless. It lets a listener evaluate what it can support. A polished transcript may be a helpful guide, but it cannot be cited as a person’s testimony until its editor’s contribution is visible.

entries.title: Whisper Koi Is a Control, Not a Witness
entries.body:
A Whisper Koi’s fin rhythm produced three short vibrations at the narrow southern channel. The pattern resembled the archive sample after the water delayed its final interval. No diver was speaking during this control recording. This demonstrates one nonhuman way the lake can make a similar trace; it does not prove the old sample came from a fish.

The sample records water depth, receiver position, time and the Koi’s movement. Lyra keeps the raw trace beside the adjusted one. The comparison is useful only if another reader can reproduce the conditions and see what changed when the interval was corrected.

A control narrows the conclusions we can safely draw. It cannot identify a speaker by resemblance, and it cannot erase the possibility that a person made the archive recording. The register leaves both origin and identity unresolved.

entries.title: The Nine-Nine Register and Its Missing Names
entries.body:
Across ninety-nine cycles, the Choir’s register counts many three-note sequences. Some belong to work signals, some are echoes, and some have no surviving operator note. Earlier cataloguers grouped similar intervals together because repetition seemed to promise a stable source. The surviving ledger never contained enough detail to support that assumption.

The First Warden now stores the counts with their uncertainty labels and the criteria used to group samples. A sequence is not a witness simply because it recurs. Separate people may use the same practical signal; one sound may also be copied by water, stone or a living creature.

The old totals remain in the archive so later readers can study how classification changed. New observations do not overwrite a prior count. They attach a dated note describing the evidence that caused the category to be revised.

entries.title: Half a Beat at the North Wall
entries.body:
The northern receiver sits close to a curved stone wall. A test signal returns half a beat later than the same signal recorded on the open platform. That delay can make one three-note rhythm sound like another when two recordings are aligned by their first tap alone.

Rowan saves both waveforms and marks the receiver position on the map. The corrected trace is not a replacement for the raw one; it is a second view with a stated adjustment. Anyone repeating the measurement should record water level and distance from the wall, since both affect the return.

The delay explains one difference between the wax slate and archive sample. It cannot demonstrate that they were made by the same person, at the same time or for the same audience. The register keeps those questions outside the measurement column.

entries.title: Two Timelines in Mara’s Interview
entries.body:
Mara’s memory of her mother’s return signal began during family diving trips. The archive recording was discovered decades later by another survey team. These events are related in Mara’s account, but they are not the same event and neither should be made to impersonate the other.

The interview form records when Mara remembered the signal, when she first heard the archive sample and which parts of her description are recollection rather than instrument data. She may review or correct her own interview. Her permission to discuss a memory does not grant permission to replay the unidentified sample.

Keeping two timelines visible gives future family members room to add another memory or disagree. The archive does not require them to prove Mara wrong before they can ask that a name remain private.

entries.title: A Listening Agreement Written by the Listeners
entries.body:
Anyone present may stop playback without explaining why. A person contributing a recording chooses whether it may be stored, transcribed, excerpted or shared. Permission for one action does not automatically include the others, and a public measurement sheet can omit personal audio entirely.

Copies carry the scope and date of the permission under which they were made. A contributor can revise that scope or request a copy be removed. The archive logs the request, the person responsible for carrying it out and the date it took effect; it does not publish the contributor’s reason.

The agreement applies to residents, visiting researchers and archive keepers. The person with the keys must follow the same stop rule as everyone else. Silence, a missed reply or a closed door is never recorded as permission.

entries.title: Three Different Permissions for One Sample
entries.body:
The consultation table distinguishes three permissions: to measure a signal, to keep a copy and to play the personal segment for other listeners. Mara is willing to let the Choir publish the measurement method. Her family has not yet agreed about the personal recording, and the record states that distinction plainly.

A consent-limited transcript shares the receiver position, timing and water delay while leaving the private segment out. A sealed case keeps that segment inaccessible until a relative opts in under a listening agreement. Either route preserves the method and the unresolved identity; neither route turns a family resemblance into proof.

The choice is recorded as a storage procedure, not as a judgment about what Mara should feel. The archive stores who made the decision and what the permission covers. A later change creates a new dated version with a visible link to the earlier one.

entries.title: A Transcript With Its Edges Left Visible
entries.body:
This public copy contains the receiver location, the measured interval, water conditions and Lyra’s processing notes. It omits the private audio segment and leaves the source-person field blank. A reader can follow how the waveform was compared without hearing material the family has not chosen to share.

The transcript keeps disagreements side by side. Mara’s remembered work signal remains a family recollection; the archive sample remains unidentified. The copy records the scope she approved and provides a route to request correction or withdrawal. Publishing a method does not authorize anyone to infer a name from its conclusion.

If permission changes, the archive issues a replacement with a new date and notes which copies must stop circulating. The earlier version stays in a restricted change log so the history of the decision remains accountable without re-exposing the withheld audio.

entries.title: A Sealed Segment Waiting for a Decision
entries.body:
The personal segment is held in a sealed case. Lyra keeps the key, and Mara or a family member may request a private listening session with the right to pause it. There is no automatic date on which the case opens. A lack of response does not become consent through the passage of time.

The exterior summary contains a sample code, duration and custody history, but not a description of the words or voice. Authorized listeners must agree to the stop procedure before playback begins. The access log records each opening and any pause request so the archive can show whether the rules were followed.

Sealing the segment is a privacy measure. It does not mean the family has rejected the archive, nor does it establish who produced the sound. The public register names only the process and the evidence still missing.

entries.title: A Label That Can Be Revised
entries.body:
The current label reads: “Unidentified three-note sequence; source not confirmed.” Mara reviewed this wording because it does not assign her mother’s name to the archive sample. Her family can ask for a new review later, but nobody has promised that a review will identify the voice.

Every change creates a dated version. The earlier label remains linked so a correction is visible instead of quietly replacing the record. A relative may add a statement, request narrower access or decline to participate; the archive records the scope without asking for a public explanation.

Mara keeps her memory as her own account. The Choir keeps its measurement as a separate account. Both may matter to people who visit the lake, even while their connection remains unresolved.

entries.title: The Playback Log Includes the Stop
entries.body:
The Choir playback log records who opened a sample, when it was played, which version was used and whether anyone invoked the stop rule. One listener ended the third session when the final interval recalled a work siren. Playback stopped at once; the archive did not ask the listener to justify the request.

Names are optional for observers who do not contribute testimony. The custodian records their own access because keeping a key does not make an action invisible. If a copy is made, its permission scope and destination are attached to the same log entry.

The log is not a transcript of private reactions. It documents the conditions of access and the steps taken after a request. This allows the archive to demonstrate how it handled a recording without turning a listener’s distress into new public content.

entries.title: Lyra’s Afterword: The Archive Does Not Own a Voice
entries.body:
Lyra’s revised index links the raw waveform, the filtered sample and each interpretation without merging them. The register names who edited each layer, when it happened and how a resident can ask for a change. A later keeper can now see where Lyra once joined uncertain sounds into a readable phrase.

Mara has not identified the archive voice as her mother. The entry says so in the same place as the measured beats, rather than burying the uncertainty in a distant footnote. If a family member later consents to a new listening session, that session will receive its own record and scope.

The procedure cannot recover a voice that was never recorded clearly. It can keep the archive from claiming more than it knows, and it can give people affected by a recording a way to shape how it is stored. The Choir’s duty is custody with limits, not ownership.

entries.title: The Households Behind the Return Desk
entries.body:
Two households brought questions about the same bundle of returned mail. One asked for a private receipt; another asked that home addresses never appear on the public board. Their requests are not interchangeable, even though the papers sat in the same box.

The barracks register tracks unit, departure date and assigned destination. Family contact details serve a different purpose and belong to the people who supplied them. The archive stores the delivery marks needed to inspect the handoff without attaching a household list to the roster.

No visitor ledger was made for the private review. A family could read its own copy, ask to stop or leave without being counted. Presence is not permission to publish a reaction.

Supplemental family archive note — two requests at one desk

The two households arrived with questions about the same bundle, but each began by asking what the other could see. One wanted a receipt proving that a private copy had been handed over. The other wanted its address removed from the wall index before anyone discussed the envelopes. Neither request answered the question of where the mail had gone. Nia wrote them on separate slips so a clerk could not later read their presence at one meeting as shared permission.

The return desk used to keep one visitor book for every matter. Nia now sees how a convenient book can create a new list of families connected to a missing cadet. She leaves the visitor page unused and gives each household its own code. The codes describe custody of a paper, not the people who brought it. If a family returns, it can bring its receipt without having to prove that it once stood in this room.

entries.title: Five Envelopes, Five Physical Histories
entries.body:
The inventory describes five envelopes by paper, seal and visible wear. Three have torn glue along the left edge; two remain closed. A gray smudge appears on each, similar to dust near the east desk, but the sample is too small to establish where any letter traveled.

Each envelope received a neutral code and a photograph of its exterior. The sealed envelopes were not opened for inspection. A date stamp may show that a clerk handled an item; it does not demonstrate that the intended recipient read it.

The family may request its own envelope for review. The code allows a custodian to find the matching object without placing a name or address on the public index.

Supplemental family archive note — paper is not a travel diary

Nia lays the five envelopes beside the inspection card and turns each one only by its edges. The three torn seals have different folds; the two closed ones are not opened to compare what is inside. A gray smudge occurs on all five, but the east desk is dusty and the mail pouch was stored near a stone stair. The mark can be described without pretending it names a route.

One visitor recognizes the twine around an envelope but cannot say whether the bundle was carried home or brought back unopened. Nia records the observation in the private review copy, not the public catalogue. The distinction matters because memory can help identify an object while still leaving its journey uncertain. A photograph of an exterior can show a crease, a seal or a stain. It cannot tell the archive who read the words inside.

entries.title: The Badges Without Their Straps
entries.body:
Three cadet badges were left in a cloth pouch after the transfer ledger closed. Two serials remain legible. The third has lost its face number and has a different hook from the others. No surviving strap or uniform connects any badge to a named cadet.

The inventory records the readable serials and labels the damaged one as unreadable. It does not assign the badges to the returned envelopes or the missing cadets. Similar location is not a chain of custody.

Badges are stored apart from the morning roll so a future clerk cannot accidentally pair a serial with a roster line. Anyone proposing a match must supply evidence beyond proximity.

Supplemental family archive note — a badge is a tool, not a body

The pouch containing three cadet badges was found after the morning roll had closed. Two serials can still be read. The third has a broken hook and a face worn nearly smooth. Nia remembers cadets trading straps and lending cloak pins before drill; a serial belonged to an issued object, not always to the person who carried it on a particular day.

One damaged badge sits close to an envelope with a similar gray mark. Their proximity is the only link between them. Nia asks that they remain in separate containers so a future clerk will not slide the badge under the nearest roster line. She knows the temptation: the pouch appears in the same drawer as papers about Ellis, and a matching number would feel like a clue. A feeling of fit is not a chain of custody. The inventory therefore marks the badge as unassigned until someone brings evidence that can be checked.

entries.title: Keep the Roster Separate from the Doorstep
entries.body:
The roster requires a cadet’s unit, departure date and assigned destination. It does not require a parent’s address. Household correspondence is catalogued only under the scope its sender approves.

Pinning roster and family mail to one public board would let a reader travel from a name to a home. Nia separates the transit marks from contact details and keeps each family copy within its own envelope.

A household can ask to view or correct its own record. No family may grant permission for another. A request to omit an address is not evidence about where a cadet went.

Supplemental family archive note — a name should not open a front door

The public roster needs to show which unit was sent to which destination and on what date. A home address answers a different question. Nia removes it from the wall copy after a relative points out that the board faces the road where carts stop. The address had been added years earlier to help return lost property; no one had reviewed whether that purpose still justified leaving it visible.

The family keeps its own correspondence and can correct its own contact details. Another household cannot authorize publication on its behalf, even if both families have asked about the same mail sack. Nia records the redaction as a change to the copy's scope and preserves the old version in restricted custody. She does not erase the fact that an address once appeared; she stops the public page from making that information available to every passerby.

entries.title: The Hours Between Two Watch Shifts
entries.body:
The east desk opened during the third hour of the watch. The next clerk began at the fifth hour, leaving a gap in the shift book. Two envelopes carry marks from that interval but no receipt signature.

The marks may have been applied by a guard at the door or before a clerk completed the handoff. The surviving papers cannot distinguish those possibilities. The register shows the open interval as a blank band instead of inventing a continuous chain.

A schedule tells us when staff were expected to be present. It does not tell us who handled a specific envelope without a signed record.

Supplemental family archive note — the hours nobody signed for

The third watch ended before the fifth began, leaving an interval where the return desk had no named clerk. Two envelopes bear marks from that interval. Nia compares the ink with the guard's gate stamp; the colors are close, but the paper absorbed them differently. No one can say whether a guard began the handoff or a clerk finished it after the shift changed.

She used to treat a blank schedule as an invitation to write “routine transfer.” A routine can explain what staff expected to happen, not what happened to a particular piece of mail. The new form shows the gap as a band and asks the next clerk to add a signature only when they can identify their own action. The missing mark remains visible. It does not accuse the guard or clear the desk; it gives the family a more honest limit than an invented continuous timeline.

entries.title: A Delivery Note Ends at the East Door
entries.body:
A courier wrote that a mail pouch was placed beside the east door. The reverse carries a desk stamp from the same day, but its bag code differs from the courier note. The two papers may concern separate pouches.

The archive keeps the note and stamp as separate objects with their own dates. It marks the route between them as unresolved. Someone may have moved the pouch after delivery, but no witness or signed receipt survives.

This distinction matters to the households asking about their letters. A stamp proves an action at the desk, not arrival at the home written on an envelope.

Supplemental family archive note — placed beside the door

The courier note says a pouch was left beside the east door. A desk stamp from later that day carries another bag code. Nia cannot tell whether the second stamp belongs to the pouch, a replacement bag or a separate delivery. The written note never says a clerk signed for the first one, and the pouch itself is not among the returned objects.

The courier is willing to repeat what they remember but asks not to be quoted beyond the delivery wording. Nia copies the statement as a dated note, keeps the speaker's permission beside it and does not add a name to the public index. The account narrows one step of the journey: someone recalls placing a pouch near the door. It does not bridge the distance between the doorstep, the return desk and a household. A later page must not use the word “delivered” to smooth over that missing distance.

entries.title: A Private Review Without an Attendance Sheet
entries.body:
The review room had no attendance ledger. A relative could read a private copy, mark an error or end the meeting. The keeper recorded only which version was made available and whether a copy changed hands.

Families could decline to give their names to the public catalogue. They could also request that a paper be closed before anyone read the next page. The same rule applied to officers and archive staff.

These procedures do not authenticate the letters. They limit who may see them and preserve a path for correction without creating a new list of people associated with a missing cadet.

Supplemental family archive note — a meeting that can stop

The first private review lasted less than a watch. One relative read the outside of an envelope, closed the copy and asked for the rest to be held. Another wanted time alone with a version that contained only their own household's papers. Nia records which version was offered and whether it left the room. She writes no attendance tally and does not ask what the visitors felt when they read.

The keeper's role is to explain the copy, point out what is missing and stop when asked. Rank does not change that rule. Nia has to follow it too; she is not entitled to keep reading because she works at the desk or because the papers concern her brother. A request to pause is entered as a procedural event, not as a reaction or a refusal to cooperate. The family can return later, request another version or decide not to read further.

entries.title: A Count of Mail Is Not a Count of Readers
entries.body:
The consultation offered two storage procedures. An aggregate sheet could publish the number of envelopes inspected and the hours without a clerk’s signature. Alternatively, the table could remain sealed while the households reviewed their private copies.

Neither choice established whether a letter was delivered or read. The aggregate route therefore placed its uncertainty note beside the count. The sealed route described its status as pending review rather than implying that a family had refused publication.

The chosen procedure is stored as a scope flag and can be revised later. It concerns access to this table, not the truth of any story about Ellis Porter.

Supplemental family archive note — what a public count cannot say

The aggregate option would let anyone check how many envelopes were inspected, when the desk was staffed and which seals looked similar. It would not show which household had received a letter. The sealed option would let each family review a private copy before deciding whether any summary could be shared. It would take longer, and an unanswered invitation could leave the public without a count.

Nia asks the player to choose a procedure for this bundle, not a theory about Ellis. A number of inspected envelopes cannot tell whether one person waited at a gate or received a message somewhere else. A sealed packet cannot prove that the archive has been complete. She marks the choice with its limitations on the same page. If the households later ask to change the scope, the record can be reopened without rewriting their earlier request as agreement.

entries.title: The Aggregate Sheet and Its Missing Signatures
entries.body:
The public sheet lists five inspected envelopes, two unsigned time windows and three comparable seal marks. It contains no names or home addresses. The number describes objects found in the barracks bundle, not households that received a letter.

A warning symbol points to the note that a desk stamp confirms handling at the desk only. The original inventory remains available for review by authorized custodians, while the public copy can be challenged through a correction request.

The version number, date and reviewer are printed at the foot of the sheet. If a later inspection changes the count, it will be added as a new version with the reason recorded.

Supplemental family archive note — five objects on the public page

The aggregate sheet lists five inspected envelopes, two unsigned time windows and three seals with similar wear. The number five describes the items found in one barracks bundle. It is not a count of families, letters sent, letters delivered or cadets who received news. Nia prints that warning beside the total in the same type size so it cannot be separated from the number when the page is copied.

An officer asks whether the unsigned marks should be excluded to make the table simpler. Nia leaves them in and labels them “unassigned time,” because hiding an awkward part would make the total look more certain than the papers allow. The public copy can be corrected by anyone who can point to a specific version and field. Private source pages remain available only under their access rules. A transparent count is useful only while readers can see exactly what was counted.

entries.title: Private Packets Waiting for Their Owners
entries.body:
Each family copy is held in a separate packet marked with a code, not a household name. A custodian opens it only when the requester accepts the pause rule for the review session. There is no automatic date when an unanswered request becomes permission.

The exterior index states the packet’s version and who keeps the key. It does not describe its contents or say whether a family has read it. A requester can ask for a copy to be withdrawn using the receipt code.

Keeping a packet closed is a privacy procedure. It does not mean that a household rejected the archive, and it supplies no evidence about a cadet’s destination.

Supplemental family archive note — a packet remains pending

Each sealed packet has a code on the outside and a version number beneath the fold. The outer index names the custodian who holds the key, but it does not list the contents or say that a household has read them. An invitation with no reply stays pending. Nia rejects a proposed deadline that would convert silence into approval once the watch changed.

The keyholder has to log every opening, including a session stopped midway. A family can use the receipt code to request a copy, narrow the permitted audience or withdraw it from the review table. The procedure may delay a public summary, but it protects a choice the family has not made yet. Keeping the packet closed neither confirms nor denies where a letter went. It simply describes what the archive is authorized to show today.

entries.title: A Label That Names the Permission
entries.body:
The label states who may use a copy and for what purpose. Each household’s permission applies to its own papers; it cannot authorize the archive to reveal another family’s address or letter.

When no one has answered, the register uses “awaiting review.” It does not record the silence as consent, refusal or confirmation that an envelope reached its intended recipient.

The label sits next to the version number so a reader can see when the scope was last checked. A custodian who handles the record must add an access entry rather than relying on rank or memory.

Supplemental family archive note — permission in words a clerk can follow

Nia rewrites the scope label after a new clerk mistakes “family copy” for permission to show the packet to every relative. The revised label names the allowed readers, the version they may see, the reason the copy can be used and the route for changing that permission. It says who supplied the scope and when it was last checked. No field asks the family to defend a narrower request.

The label is short enough to travel with the copy but specific enough to stop a custodian from guessing. If the author of a letter is unknown, permission from its recipient does not automatically speak for the sender. If the sender cannot be found, the register says so rather than making the nearest available person the owner of every question. A clerk can follow the label without deciding whose privacy matters more.

entries.title: The Keyholder Is Part of the Record
entries.body:
The access log records each opening of the mail drawer, the stated purpose, the version consulted and the keyholder. It includes the session stopped at a visitor’s request; it does not record the visitor’s reason.

A custodian is not exempt from the log. Their access is visible so a later review can distinguish an authorized copy from an undocumented handling. Failed attempts to open the drawer remain listed rather than disappearing from the page.

The log is separate from the correspondence. It allows an audit of access without describing a family’s private response.

Supplemental family archive note — the drawer records its keepers

The access log begins with the shift supervisor who opened the drawer to check its lock. It records the stated purpose, the page version viewed and the time the key was returned. The next line records Nia's own access while she copied the public summary. She includes herself because an audit that lists everyone except its author would be decoration.

One failed attempt to open the drawer remains in the log. The key did not turn, and no paper was removed. Nia keeps the entry so a future review can distinguish an unsuccessful attempt from an unrecorded visit. The log contains no family responses or letter contents. It makes the custody process visible without making the people who request privacy easier to identify. The keyholder is part of the history of a record, not an invisible space outside it.

entries.title: How to Correct a Record Without Signing Your Name
entries.body:
A correction request can identify a page code and line without naming its sender. The archive asks what should change and which copies the change applies to; it does not ask for a public reason.

Nia compares the request with the stored version and records the date received. If the requested scope is unclear, she keeps the earlier copy unchanged until the sender can clarify. A note can correct a public address without altering a private family copy.

The old version remains linked in the restricted change log so custodians can explain which copies need replacement. The public index shows only that a correction was issued, not who requested it.

Supplemental family archive note — the address changed on one copy

The correction slip identifies the public page, line and address field without naming its sender. Nia compares the request with the restricted contact card, updates the public copy and leaves a reason code rather than a family name. The private packet keeps its own version unless the requester asks for it to change as well. A correction to one copy does not silently rewrite every document in the archive.

At first, Nia worries that an unsigned request will be dismissed as unreliable. The page can be corrected without authenticating the sender's identity because the error is visible on the public copy itself. If the request concerns private information, the custodian can ask for a receipt code through a private channel. The public change log shows only that an edit occurred and which version was replaced. It does not expose who asked for the door to be hidden.

entries.title: What a Copy Receipt Actually Confirms
entries.body:
Receipt B-04 confirms that one person received a copy on a stated date. It does not confirm that the person read it, agreed with it or verified the events described inside.

The receipt carries the version code and a route for requesting correction or withdrawal. A household may keep it without adding an address to the public board. If the archive later replaces the copy, the new receipt links to the earlier issue.

The difference between delivery and reading is explicit because both ideas were once collapsed into one checkmark. The corrected form leaves separate spaces for separate actions.

Supplemental family archive note — receipt B-04

Receipt B-04 confirms that a copy was handed to one person on a stated date. It does not say that the person read it, believed it, approved the archive or confirmed the events described inside. Nia separates those boxes on the new form. The old sheet used one checkmark beside “received” and let later clerks infer the rest.

The new receipt records the version number and explains how to request a correction or withdraw that copy. A household can keep the receipt without placing its address on the public board. If a replacement is issued, its version refers back to the earlier copy so the archive can tell which page may still be circulating. Delivery, reading and agreement remain separate actions. A small set of boxes cannot explain a whole family's response, but it can stop the desk from claiming more than it observed.

entries.title: A Roster with a Place for Revision
entries.body:
Nia added a review date and an access field for the next custodian. Families can change the scope of a private copy by using its receipt code. The procedure does not require them to prove why they want a narrower record.

The aggregate sheet cannot say who caused the watch gap or where a courier left a pouch after the east door. It makes those missing steps visible so the next clerk can avoid treating a stamped page as a complete journey.

Nia still does not know where Ellis is. She keeps that question separate from the desk marks and badge pouch. The new register cannot answer it, but it prevents the archive from presenting its paperwork as an answer it never contained.

Supplemental family archive note — the margin stays open

Nia leaves one margin wide enough for a later custodian to write what changed and which copies must be reviewed again. The board has a public correction mark; the restricted packet has a separate access note; neither asks a family to repeat its private reason in front of the barracks. The register can be narrowed or reopened using the receipt code, even after Nia is no longer assigned to the desk.

She still does not know where Ellis is. The bundle of returned mail, the badges and the unsigned watch interval do not combine into proof that he died or proof that he reached home. Nia resists making her own fear into a conclusion, even when the blank space belongs to someone she loves. The desk can serve the families who need a record and protect those who do not want their names posted. It cannot answer the question she carries beyond the end of this route.

entries.title: A Seed Ledger with a Right of Appeal
entries.body:
Greenwake opens its seed vault before each planting season. The public copy lists aggregate seed totals, measurement dates, missing observations and later corrections. It does not publish a household’s name or private reason for a short harvest. A blank row stays blank until someone brings evidence; no keeper may fill it with a guess.

Each household can review its own record. A resident may correct an entry, limit access, withdraw a copy or decline to participate. Where a resident has moved away, the archive marks the record as awaiting contact. Time alone does not turn silence into permission.

The two custody keys are held by people chosen by the community. Their names and the date of each handoff are posted beside the appeal procedure. A person may submit a correction through a messenger station; the response date and delivery status are logged without copying the private explanation into the public ledger. If a copy is withdrawn, the aggregate notes that its totals changed while keeping a dated link to the earlier version.

These rules do not settle who deserves water in a hard season. They make the decisions visible, leave room to challenge them and prevent a closed vault from becoming the only witness. A seed count can estimate a harvest. It cannot speak for the people whose beds were never counted.

entries.title: Alden's Call Sheet: Dates Before Names
entries.body:
Alden tìm thấy trang này ở đáy hộp lệnh hành quân, được gấp theo đường đã mòn đúng chỗ đóng dấu. Trang không ghi tên người nhận. Nó ghi giờ phát lệnh cho người đưa thư, ngày mở cuộc họp của các đại diện và một ô cuối cùng dành cho “ứng viên được xác nhận”. Ô ấy đã được in sẵn. Chữ ký đi sau tất cả các mốc thời gian kia.

Không có dòng nào ghi ai đã chọn mẫu giấy, cũng không có biên bản của cuộc họp đầu tiên. Alden không thể kết luận rằng mọi chữ ký đều bị ép buộc; ông chỉ có thể khẳng định hồ sơ được sắp xếp để một người nhận lời mời sau khi cộng đồng đã biết mình được gọi tên. Một chữ ký trong hoàn cảnh đó vẫn là chữ ký, nhưng không thể tự nó trả lời câu hỏi về áp lực, trách nhiệm hay khả năng từ chối.

Ở lề, một viên thư lại đã viết: “Bản này giúp người kế nhiệm đến đúng lúc.” Câu chữ nghe như một sự thuận tiện. Nó cũng cho thấy quy trình đã dự kiến một người kế nhiệm trước khi người ấy có cơ hội hỏi vì sao mình được chọn. Alden giữ lại dòng ghi chú thay vì cạo nó đi.

Trang này không xóa công lao của những người đã ký, cũng không tuyên bố họ không có lựa chọn. Nó buộc người đọc phân biệt bốn việc thường bị gộp thành một: phát thư, nhận thư, ký tên và hiểu cái giá. Chỉ hai việc cuối có dấu tay rõ ràng; những việc còn lại cần được đối chiếu với lời khai của người sống sót.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — send the question before the meeting

Rowan asks Alden whether a person who received the call sheet could answer before the council met. Alden searches the box for a reply slip and finds none. There may have been verbal answers that never entered the file, so he does not mark every recipient as silent. He adds a new blank receipt card to the copy room, with separate spaces for delivery, reading and answer. A person can return it privately or leave the answer field empty. The current archive cannot repair the sequence used in an earlier cycle. It can make the next call arrive with room for a response before the decision has already been scheduled.

entries.title: Dấu Sáp và Ngày Gửi
entries.body:
Bản chỉ thị có ba lớp mực. Lớp đầu ghi lịch mở các cổng tiếp tế; lớp thứ hai ghi ngày gửi thông báo tới những người được cân nhắc; lớp cuối để trống chỗ ký. Con dấu sáp che một phần tên người nhận nhưng vẫn để lộ rằng nó được đóng trước cuộc họp xác nhận.

Ngày tháng không chứng minh một cá nhân đã cưỡng ép người khác. Chúng chứng minh một hệ thống đã chuyển động trước khi có hồ sơ đồng thuận hoàn chỉnh. Người có quyền điều hành biết chiến dịch sắp bắt đầu. Người nhận thư có thể đã phải lựa chọn giữa ký vào một mệnh lệnh gần như không thể dừng và mang trách nhiệm cho mọi người đang chờ lương thực.

Alden yêu cầu Rowan không gọi tất cả chữ ký là giả. Một số người hiểu tình thế và thật sự chấp nhận hy sinh. Cũng không được gọi tất cả họ là tình nguyện chỉ vì văn phòng đóng dấu như vậy. Cả hai cách gọi đều bỏ qua câu hỏi quan trọng nhất: người ấy đã biết điều gì, vào thời điểm nào, và có thể từ chối mà không đẩy người khác vào nguy hiểm tức thì hay không.

Rowan chép ngày tháng ở cột riêng, còn câu giải thích nằm ở cột khác. Nếu phát hiện thêm một lá thư hoặc lời khai trái chiều, bản ghi vẫn có thể sửa mà không xóa dấu vết cũ. Cách lưu này chậm hơn một kết luận duy nhất, nhưng giữ được đường đi của bằng chứng.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — the courier's route is not an answer

The courier's route map shows that the sealed notices reached the east gate before the council session. It does not show which person carried each envelope after the gate, or whether the intended reader opened it. Rowan copies the delivery marks onto a separate sheet and keeps the recipient field unresolved where the seal obscures it. Alden recognizes a stamp from the old dispatch office but cannot identify the clerk who used it. The dates help reconstruct the order of events; they do not reveal what a recipient understood. A future letter may fill one gap without filling every one. The archive holds the map beside the call sheet, not in place of it.

entries.title: The First Warden’s Unanswered Question
entries.body:
The First Warden remembers the first champion arriving at the edge of the old council chamber with mud on his boots and a map folded inside his coat. The champion had been told that the World Will needed a vessel. He asked whether the council could keep the people alive without choosing one person to carry the Crown.

The Warden does not remember the exact reply. He remembers moving the map aside to make room for a schedule of supply convoys. The convoy list was useful, urgent and measurable. The question was difficult to answer, so it was left beneath the list. Later copies describe the champion as having accepted the call after a full briefing. None record whether anyone returned to the question about refusal.

A memory repeated for a century can become cleaner than the event it describes. The Warden has heard later generations say that the first hero chose freely. He has also heard others say the council forced him. Neither claim is supported by a surviving transcript. The Warden will not borrow certainty from either side simply because the final decision now depends on it.

His testimony is narrow: the question was asked; the answer is missing; and a paper trail continued as though the omission did not matter. Rowan records that limit beside the recollection. The Warden asks that his regret be preserved as a reason to ask better questions, not as proof that the first champion would have chosen a different path.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — remember the question before the legend

The Warden returns to the council chamber with Rowan and stops beside the stone lip where the champion once set his folded map. The map is gone; a shallow dust line remains beneath the later supply ledger. He can still point to where the champion asked if the people might live without selecting a vessel. He cannot supply the answer the council gave. Rowan asks whether the Warden could have insisted that the question be copied into the record. The Warden says he remembers making room for the convoy list instead. His regret belongs to this witness. It does not tell Rowan what the first champion would choose today.

entries.title: Emberroot: Crownfall Plot Trial
entries.body:
The Crownfall plot has shallow soil, an ash crust and a narrow seam where rainwater can collect. Rowan planted Emberroot in three pockets: one beside the warmed stone, one near the old channel and one on the higher gravel. Only the first two produced roots worth weighing. The harvest is enough for a small medicinal test and no more.

Mira's earlier note warned that the plant's first green leaves can hide a weak root system. Rowan follows that instruction: he weighs the roots after cleaning away the ash, records how much seed was used and leaves one sample uncut. The result is a record of a single plot under known conditions, not proof that the crop can replace an entire food supply.

The old cycle ledger counts the kingdom as if every field could recover on command. This small trial cannot disprove every projection. It does show that living resources respond to local water, seed choice and care, which means a world-scale estimate must say where its samples came from. A number without its method cannot tell a village whether it can safely plant another season.

Rowan leaves part of the Emberroot in the soil rather than taking the whole crop. If the plot fails later, the failure belongs in the record too. The test offers no promise that refusing the Crown will be easy. It shows one narrow alternative to burning every reserve at once: preserve enough life to test, learn and revise the next decision.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — leave the planting note with the seed

Mara asks Rowan to return the unused Emberroot seed to the keeper who loaned it, rather than seal it inside the public trial file. The keeper agrees to let one seed remain in the archive packet until the next review, with a note that it is borrowed and may be reclaimed. Rowan writes the germination conditions on a separate card so the sample can be replanted without treating its current owner as a permanent supplier. The harvest supplies one narrow trial. The seed could fail in another patch, and a future grower may decline to lend more. Evidence of a possible crop is not permission to requisition it.

entries.title: Starlit Minnow: Field Sample from the Reach
entries.body:
The minnow turns toward the same faint interval that Evelyn marked on the Outer-Wake receiver. Its movement repeats only a few times before it returns to the shadow beneath the stone lip. Rowan records the water temperature, the time of day and the position of the catch before placing the fish in a covered bowl for observation.

Evelyn cautions that a living creature can react to a current, a vibration, a change in light or a sound too soft for a person to hear. The receiver and the fish respond within the same interval, but the sample does not establish that the signal caused the movement. The minnow has not spoken, and its behavior cannot be treated as a message from an unknown shore.

The sample is returned to the pool after the observation. No one has measured whether every Minnow would react the same way or whether this individual followed a different rhythm before the test. Rowan keeps the observation alongside the uncertainty rather than writing “proof of life beyond the Veil” in the margin.

A route can be worth investigating without being called safe. The fish offers a concrete point for comparison in later seasons: if the signal changes, another observer can repeat the same test under recorded conditions. That is smaller than a guarantee and more useful than a promise.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — the pool has no duty to answer twice

Evelyn checks the observation card against the passive receiver's time marks. The clock drift leaves a window rather than an exact moment, and the minnow's return to the shadow overlaps that window only within the margin of error. She asks Rowan to retain both timings and to avoid drawing a line from the fish to the signal. The animal was returned to the pool; no one has permission to capture it repeatedly just to make the chart look convincing. A future observation can use another method or another day. The current result is worth keeping because it shows what the team saw and where the timing remains uncertain.

entries.title: Two Marks, Two Kinds of Record
entries.body:
The stone roster names those who returned, those who fell and those whose final location was never recorded. Its three carving styles are not interchangeable. A missing location is not proof of death; a return mark does not describe what its owner believed about the war; a signature on Alden's sword records that an order was carried.

The sword mark sits below the binding where it would not be visible in a public ceremony. Alden says he scratched it there after receiving his command. He intended the mark to remind him that the order had a person attached to it. The inscription does not identify which soldiers agreed with the campaign or whether they could leave after it began.

Rowan places a tracing of the mark beside a copy of the roster but keeps the originals untouched. Anyone reviewing the file can compare the angle of the cut, the date of the command and the names associated with each return entry. If the tracing is wrong, the error can be corrected without altering the stone or the blade.

Neither object speaks for every person listed. Together they make a more precise record of what can be known: Alden carried the order; several people did not return; and the archive lacks a complete account of each person's understanding. The missing statements remain missing even when the rest of the evidence is compelling.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — a mark can authenticate a handoff

Tomas checks the sword tracing beside an ordinary work-order signature. The cuts on the blade were made with a narrow tool at different depths; the ink signature follows a separate pressure pattern. He can compare the physical marks, but he cannot infer how many people agreed with the order from the way Alden signed his name. Nia labels the sheet as a comparison of objects, not of consent. Rowan keeps the roster's return marks on another page so a reader will not mistake a weapon for a list of witnesses. Each source proves a different act. Neither completes the record of the people who never returned.

entries.title: Draft Protocol for the Consent Archive
entries.body:
The draft separates a person's name from the claim made about that person. A public page may carry a name only beside its source, the date of the source and a note describing any gap in the testimony. A sealed page must still carry an index number and a verifiable count, or privacy becomes a convenient way for officials to make a person disappear a second time.

A family may ask to see the material connected to its own record. The draft does not let a relative rewrite another person's words, but it allows them to correct a date, point to a missing letter or request that a private name remain closed while a public method stays available. The custodian must keep a written receipt for every change and retain the earlier version.

Alden asks who should hold the seal. Rowan proposes that the key be kept by two people from separate groups, with the opening condition recorded before either group knows which name will be revealed. If the rule is written after a dispute begins, those in power may shape it around the outcome they already want.

The protocol does not repair the old choices. It describes one way to prevent a future archive from claiming consent merely because no one can find the person who objected. The final copy will note its own limits. It will not say that every one of the ninety-nine champions would have chosen the same protection.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — review the key rule before a name is requested

The two custodians read the draft procedure aloud before any family asks to open a sealed page. They notice that the first version says who may request access but not who must answer if both custodians are away. Nia adds an alternate contact outside the office that stores the packet and writes a maximum response date beside the appeal route. A late answer will be logged as late, not treated as permission to publish. Alden asks to sign the cover as commander; the reviewers tell him his role does not give him authority over another person's record. He signs only the receipt showing the procedure was reviewed.

entries.title: Public Copy: Names with Their Evidence
entries.body:
The public copy keeps the names visible, but it does not print them as a list of willing heroes. Each entry sits beside the date of the first notice, the date of the recorded answer and the source that supports each claim. Where one of those dates is missing, the page says “not recorded” rather than filling the space with an assumption.

Families can challenge a transcription without erasing the historical copy. Rowan's draft gives every correction a time, a source and a custodian. If the request is disputed, both versions remain visible with a note about who reviewed them. The purpose is not to make the archive immune from disagreement; it is to make disagreement traceable.

Some readers argue that a public list is necessary because secrecy allowed earlier leaders to repeat the same choice. Others point out that publication can turn a private person into evidence for a political argument they never endorsed. The record preserves that disagreement instead of pretending one rule settles every case.

The consent flag means only that this group chose to publish the names under the stated limits. It does not establish what each hero wanted, and it does not decide whether Rowan will accept the Crown. The ending remains a separate choice with its own cost. This document controls how the past is handled, not who owns the future.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — publication does not end the correction period

A person named in the public copy returns with a different spelling on a letter written by their own hand. The page has already been read aloud at Crownfall, so Nia cannot make the first copy disappear. She adds a correction slip that preserves the earlier version and asks the person which spelling should appear in the next printing. The contributor chooses the corrected spelling and asks that the old one remain visible only in the revision history. The request changes that record alone. It does not authorize the archive to rename other people or describe every champion as willing. The public edition remains open to correction after release.

entries.title: Sealed Copy: A Key with Conditions
entries.body:
The sealed copy replaces public names with durable reference numbers. It leaves the chronology, the evidence types and the unanswered questions visible, so later readers can test the method without learning a family's identity before that family is ready to review it.

The seal is not a blank page. Two custodians from different groups must sign when the packet is closed. Either family may request a private reading of its own record, receive an exact copy of the evidence attached to it and submit a correction for the public index. Every opening is logged. A custodian cannot destroy the request merely because the proposed correction is not accepted.

There is a danger in postponement. Leaders may call a file temporary for so long that the person inside it is never remembered by name. To limit that risk, the protocol requires a review date and an appeal route outside the office that holds the key. If either is missing, the seal fails its own condition and the archive must publish that failure.

This choice protects names from immediate circulation; it does not assert that every family would prefer silence. Rowan records who supported the seal and when it should be reviewed. The public method remains open to inspection. Privacy can protect a person, but only when the person or their family has a real way to speak later.

Supplemental Last Oath archive note —Supplemental Last Oath archive note — inspect the seal without opening it

The seal arrives with one edge softened by damp. The custodians photograph the packet from four sides, compare the cord with the closure mark and log the condition before deciding whether it must be opened for preservation. The family receives the condition report and can choose whether to attend a supervised inspection. The packet stays closed while they decide. Nia adds a line for the reason if the seal is broken, so a necessary repair cannot be mistaken for unauthorized access. A locked file still requires care, review and a route to challenge the custodian. Privacy lasts only while those duties are visible.

entries.title: A Tag Is Not a Name
entries.body:
The Lockhouse tally does not identify the workshop that pressed the letters E.P. It records the width of a die, the direction of a shallow slip and the salt that settled in the groove. A similar mark can narrow a search only when comparison pieces come from dated, independent sources. This tag has no date.

The edge is bent inward. That may have happened in a cart, under a boot or in the chain where it was found. The oil sits over the salt crust, so the crust predates the coating. These details describe the object after it was made. They do not describe the person who carried it.

Nella recognized the initials because she is looking for her brother. That recognition belongs in the record as her testimony, with her permission. It cannot replace a maker's mark, a route receipt or a second witness. The archive keeps the tag in a numbered sleeve and leaves the name field empty.

If another tag appears, both objects must be photographed beside a scale and examined under the same light. A match would suggest a shared tool, not a shared owner. Every step should remain reproducible by someone who does not already know which answer the family hopes to find.

entries.title: Three Bearings, No Arrival
entries.body:
I fired the red signal toward the north ridge after the toll bell changed its spacing. My notebook gives the firing point, wind direction and ridge where the shaft landed. It does not list everyone who could see the arrow. Fog covered the lower road, and I had no second lookout on the lockhouse side.

The signal meant the upper pass was unsafe. It was an instruction to change course, not a report that a group reached a shelter. A map can show the direct route from the firing point to the Lockhouse gate, but directness is not evidence of use.

The dispatch sheets contradict each other about whether the bell rang before or after the arrow was released. Their clocks were not synchronized. The timing margin stays visible instead of being solved by choosing the account that makes one witness look more careful.

This copy includes three bearings and a shaded uncertainty band. It includes no estimated passenger count. The original arrows remain sealed in the hunter ledger so a later examiner can check the description against the physical marks.

entries.title: Where the Wheel Marks End
entries.body:
The paired scrapes on the return road are separated by a distance consistent with several kinds of cart axle. The surviving section bends toward the lower trail. It disappears where water crossed the road and carried away the loose salt crust.

A wheel mark can reveal direction only if its edges remain clear. A dragged branch, a later cart or a repaired road may produce another groove on top of the first. We photographed each visible segment before measuring it and marked the camera position beside every reading.

No continuous line connects this trace to the Lockhouse gate. The ground between them has been rebuilt twice. Old residents remember a footpath, but their recollections disagree on which season it closed. Their statements are useful leads; they are not a substitute for the missing track.

Nella asked for a map she can inspect without being told what it means. The working copy uses broken lines and dates. The break is intentional. Joining it by guesswork would hide the gap that a future witness may be able to fill.

entries.title: Ruth Calder's Unclaimed Tag Order
entries.body:
The order to separate unclaimed tags was written during the week the tollhouse ledger disappeared. I feared that anyone holding a brass token would be charged for a missing crate or forced to name someone who might not have traveled with the caravan. The order tells the clerk to store each token in a sleeve and record who touched it.

It does not tell the clerk to mark a person dead, escaped or delivered. Those columns were added later by a toll collector who had no authority to invent certainty for a family's search. I did not find the collector's complete list, and I cannot say whether the missing pages were destroyed or carried away.

I should have written why I was separating the tags. Without that explanation, the order looks like concealment. That is a fair question to ask. It still does not make the initials on this tag belong to Ellis Porter.

If Nella chooses to see the measurements, she should also receive the wording of the order, its date and the name of its custodian. She may challenge my memory or ask for a new examination. No public summary should turn my statement into a finding about her brother.

entries.title: The Unnumbered Chime, First Reading
entries.body:
The brass rubbing beside the towing chime preserves two short marks separated by a longer gap. The metal carries no cycle number, name or date. Lyra Moss measured the marks twice with the same gauge, but no surviving ledger tells us whether an earlier keeper used another scale.

Sound in the Choir travels through water, stone and the old towing cable. A note heard at one end may arrive late at another. The rubbing is a record of pressure against metal; it does not preserve a voice. Calling it an echo of a missing traveler would go beyond the evidence.

The first reading was taken before a control sample was available. Low vibration from the lake may have been counted as part of the second mark. The measured intervals and the estimated error are written beside each other. The first result remains in the archive even if a later result changes our interpretation.

This chime may help reconstruct when a signal could have crossed the waterway. It cannot tell us who heard it, whether they followed it or what happened after the sound ended. The archive will not fill those fields with a character's name.

entries.title: A Living Control Sample
entries.body:
A Whisper Koi is not a recording device. Its swim path responds to current, light and disturbance. A live fish brought from the pool can help identify the low vibration in the room while a chime is measured, but it cannot reproduce a signal from a century ago.

The sample log records the pool location, water temperature and time of capture. Rowan released the koi after the control reading. We kept no scale and took no tissue. Its presence helped us distinguish the chime's paired pulse from a slow tremor traveling through the floor.

The fish shifted toward the eastern side of the basin during the second reading. That movement could be ordinary feeding behavior or a response to current. It is written as an observation, not a translation. Lyra declines to call it agreement, warning or memory.

Controls answer a narrow question: what else was vibrating while the instrument was active? They do not validate the whole story that brought someone to the instrument. We keep the first reading, the control reading and the second reading separate so another examiner can repeat the method.

entries.title: Two Measurements and Their Error
entries.body:
The second reading was taken after the live control identified a floor vibration the first pass had included. Once that background was removed, the chime retained two short pulses and a pause. Their spacing fell within the instrument's margin of error in both examinations.

Repeated timing is evidence that the metal can produce a stable pattern under present conditions. It is not evidence that a person set the pattern deliberately. The towing bell may have been struck by a cable under tension, by a keeper testing the mechanism or by a later repair crew.

The water temperature changed between sessions, and the lake current did not move at the same speed. Those differences are part of the record. A reader should not see two matching intervals and imagine that every other condition also matched.

No words emerged from the chime. The report contains no voice transcript because we heard no voice. It gives Nella a route possibility, a measurement she can repeat and a clear statement of what remains unknown. Grief cannot be used as a shortcut around missing evidence.
