The number may be accurate within the shipping ledger while failing to represent actual need. Evelyn had treated the source's precision as proof that it measured the correct thing. The review now names the ledger's original purpose and warns later readers against substituting a precise shipment count for a measure of hunger or population.

entries.title: Greenwake Seed Exchange Rules
entries.body: The Greenwake exchange separates three entries: seed retained for planting, fruit distributed for eating and stock held for an agreed trial. The totals change after a poor season, but the ledger does not list household names beside public counts. Mara says families may correct their own entries or withdraw a sample from the trial. The record therefore describes a process rather than a universal yield. A carrying-capacity model that treats all seed as immediate food would erase the reserve that makes the next season possible.

entries.title: Seed Reserves Are Not Surplus
entries.body: The public Greenwake sheet reports the fruit distributed during one harvest. A narrow margin lists seed retained for the following planting, but that amount is absent from the chart reproduced at Outer-Wake. The margin does not prove that the reserve was sufficient; it shows that it was reserved for a different purpose. Counting it as current food would make the public supply appear larger and leave the next cycle unaccounted for. The correct report must show both quantities and say who is allowed to revise them.

entries.title: Glassplum Trial: One Bed
entries.body: The trial began with one grafted seed in the Greenwake bed. The crop matured after the configured interval and produced two fruit in this run. No second bed was planted, and the graft has not been tested through winter. These observations are useful for repeating the same trial, not for promising a valley-wide yield. Mara keeps the seed source, planting date and harvest together so another gardener can compare conditions. The model must distinguish a measured plot from an assumed regional rate.

entries.title: Greenwake Well Marks
entries.body: Two marks remain on the Greenwake well wall. The upper mark was noted after rain; the lower scratch predates the storm and may belong to an older gauge. The notes give no controlled reading of water entering or leaving the well. Joining the marks into a single trend would conceal their different conditions. Rowan records both heights and leaves room for a later measurement made with the same reference point. This evidence describes the wall, not the total groundwater reserve of Greenwake.

entries.title: Listening without Naming
entries.body: Lyra's Choir ledger separates the measured interval from any voice heard during it. A participant may agree to a timing test without granting permission to preserve or publish a recording. The model needs the interval and the conditions of measurement; it does not need a private name to calculate that interval. Lyra's practice records consent scope beside each sample and permits withdrawal before the report is issued. A count that omits those limits may be mathematically tidy while taking more from a participant than the test required.

entries.title: Whisper Koi: Local Sample
entries.body: One Whisper Koi was caught at the Choir pool for this review. The entry records the pool, time and physical condition of the specimen. The fish's faint vibration is an observation made by the keeper, not a decoded message or evidence of population size. Other species and uncaught fish were not surveyed. Lyra files the sample separately from the listening test so that a memorable catch cannot be used to explain an unrelated sound without further evidence.

entries.title: Cultivated and Wild Echo Kelp
entries.body: The Choir bed produced cultivated Echo Kelp after one measured growth interval. The earlier field samples were collected from deeper water under unknown seasonal conditions. Both entries share a species label, but their growing environments differ. Lyra keeps the cultivation result out of the wild abundance column. This prevents a garden harvest from being mistaken for a naturally replenishing lake stock. A later study could compare the two environments, provided it records the location, season and number of samples.

entries.title: Echo Balm and Observer Fatigue
entries.body: The Echo Balm was prepared from one cultivated kelp harvest and two choir motes using the Archive Loom. It eased fatigue during the review, but it did not alter the receiver's recorded interval. The original worksheet mixed the observer's late shift with the signal strength measurement; Rowan separates them. Human fatigue may affect when a keeper notices a sound, so the condition belongs in the procedure notes. A remedy can support the observer without serving as proof that the measurement itself is correct.

entries.title: A Pause Is Part of the Record
entries.body: The Choir score includes a measured pause that was initially removed from the aggregate interval. Lyra restored it after the singers approved using timing data, while leaving their names out of the public copy. The pause changes the total, but its inclusion is not a license to preserve every voice. The record distinguishes consent to a timing measurement from consent to audio publication. Future comparisons should use the same inclusion rule and document when the rule changes.

entries.title: A Wick Is Not a Water Survey
entries.body: Talia uses a prepared wick to compare salt concentration between individual Cinderwell samples. Its color cannot estimate reservoir volume, identify a contamination source or describe all water delivered to households. The wick is a small test with a narrow purpose. Talia separates sample location and time from the allocation ledger so an indicator result cannot be used to assign responsibility for a shortage. The carrying-capacity report should identify the test's scope and make clear which larger questions remain unanswered.

entries.title: Salt Saffron: Yield and Inputs
entries.body: One Salt Saffron bed grew from a saved seed and required the configured watering interval. The harvest produced two blooms in this run. The crop sheet had listed the blooms without the seed retained for another planting or the water used during growth. Talia adds those inputs beside the output. This does not decide whether Salt Saffron is an efficient crop; it supplies the information needed for someone else to compare it with alternatives under a stated set of conditions.

entries.title: Brine Wick Preparation Card
entries.body: The Brine Wick uses one Salt Saffron bloom and a Dryglass shard. Talia prepares it at the assay bench and labels the sample cup before the color test. The wick responds to salt concentration in that cup; it does not report a water level, household access or the source of the salt. Rowan records the recipe so another worker can reproduce the tool. The prepared wick is an instrument with a limited range, not a shortcut around a basin-wide survey.

entries.title: Two Samples, Unequal Conditions
entries.body: The first cup was collected before rain at the upper channel; the second came from the lower bend after a storm. Their wick colors differ, but both the location and timing changed. Without a matched collection schedule, the difference cannot be assigned to distance along the channel or to household use. Talia retains the separate readings and adds the weather note. The result motivates a controlled repeat; it does not prove that one district received worse water than another.

entries.title: Deliveries Are Not Needs
entries.body: Nia's gate ledger records sacks delivered, the person who signed and the hour of arrival. It does not record how food was shared after the gate or which household members were absent. A shipment total can help plan transport, but it cannot serve as a direct measure of hunger or demand. Nia allows a household to correct its own receipt and keeps neighboring names private. Rowan copies the ledger's scope into the final report so readers do not mistake a precise count of deliveries for a complete census of need.

entries.title: Blackreed Trout and Waterline
entries.body: One Blackreed Trout was caught below the Dawnkeep weir during this review. The note includes the location and same-day waterline, but no repeated catch survey or flow reading. Fish presence and a visible mark do not establish the volume available to homes, gardens or downstream species. Rowan keeps the catch log beside, not inside, the distribution ledger. The two records can be compared later when collection dates and methods align, but neither can replace a measurement it was not designed to make.

entries.title: Waterline without Gate State
entries.body: The stone mark was measured to the lower step, but the observer did not record whether the weir gate was open. A separate schedule lists a release that afternoon; its clock was not checked against the observer's watch. The two documents may refer to the same event, but their connection has not been verified. Nia keeps the original note and appends a cross-reference rather than merging them. The waterline remains a valid observation with an incomplete operating context.

entries.title: A Packet of Non-Equivalent Measures
entries.body: The review packet contains crop yields, fish catches, listening intervals, sample colors, shipment totals and waterline marks. Each entry has a different unit and collection method. Combining them into one score would require assumptions that have not been tested. Evelyn drafts a report that keeps the measures in separate sections and identifies the observer, date and known limits. The evidence can challenge an overconfident projection without pretending to solve the world's resource crisis or determine what every community should choose.

entries.title: Revised Projection: Open Uncertainty
entries.body: The revised chart keeps seed reserved for future planting, notes water used during crop trials and shows receiver clock uncertainty. It places consent limits next to Choir timing data and labels Nia's figures as deliveries rather than needs. The resulting range is wider and less decisive than the original curve. That change is not evidence that the world has escaped collapse. It means the available measurements support fewer precise claims than the earlier presentation suggested. A future review can narrow the range only by collecting comparable evidence under disclosed rules.

entries.title: Publication Policy Decision
entries.body: The report is ready for a decision about publication, not a decision about whose life matters. One route releases bounded ranges, assumptions and an explicit review date while keeping personal records private. The other releases the calculation method immediately and delays regional totals until local stewards have checked whether the source records can be compared. Both routes preserve corrections and identify missing evidence. Neither route proves the World Will's forecast correct or false; the choice concerns how uncertainty and accountability are presented to readers.

entries.title: Public Range and Review Date
entries.body: The public sheet shows the projection range, the rainfall and harvest scenarios, the seed-reserve adjustment and the receiver's timing uncertainty. It names no household and includes no private recording. A review date is printed at the bottom, along with a route for submitting corrections. This version offers more immediate public scrutiny, though readers may still mistake a bounded estimate for a promise. Evelyn adds a note that the range describes current records and must not be used as an eligibility rule for aid.

entries.title: Method Released, Totals Under Review
entries.body: The review receipt confirms that the calculation method has been released while regional totals remain under review. Local stewards may correct dates, definitions and source references before publication. This protects communities from having unmatched delivery and harvest records presented as comparable measures, but it delays public comparison. The receipt includes a review date and a way to challenge the delay. The sealed case does not make evidence private forever; it sets a short accountability window before the totals must be reconsidered.

entries.title: Afterword: Review Before Judgment
entries.body: Evelyn files the selected report with its method, scope and review date. The team has not settled whether the world can endure without the recurring sacrifice. It has established that resource projections must be open to correction and that a measurement cannot consent on behalf of the people it counts. The next hearing will compare repeated crop, water and delivery records under shared definitions. The archive preserves both the earlier chart and the revision so later readers can see why the estimate changed rather than inheriting a claim without its history.

entries.title: Ruth's Admission
entries.body: Ruth confirms that she hid a dispatch during the Salt Road retreat. She does not claim the hidden page explains every decision or every loss. The route begins with the sealed axle note, then compares it with Nella Pike's pass card and Silas Vane's signal sketch. The aim is to recover what the paper actually says, identify where each witness was standing and record what remains absent. Ruth accepts that concealment was her choice; the archive will not convert that admission into a verdict about the whole convoy.

entries.title: Dispatch Fold and Grease Mark
entries.body: The dispatch was wrapped around the inner axle strap. A crease crosses the date line, while a dark grease mark covers part of the lower edge. The fold shows that the paper was carried inside the cart; it does not show who opened it later. Ruth recognizes the cord but cannot say whether another hand retied it. Rowan records the physical condition separately from her recollection. The date and destination remain partly legible, and neither has been compared with the other two witness records yet.

entries.title: Nella's Position at the Lower Marker
entries.body: Nella places herself at the lower checkpoint when the caravan changed direction. Her pass card confirms her own passage and records a bell count in the margin. It does not list every traveler who remained on the road or prove what Ruth could see from the weigh station. Nella agrees to let Rowan copy the card's location and time while keeping her missing sister's name out of the public copy. Her testimony defines a boundary around what she witnessed rather than filling the blank for other people.

entries.title: Two Notches, No Shared Clock
entries.body: Nella's card bears two shallow notches beside the checkpoint stamp. Their spacing resembles two quick bell strikes, but the card was trimmed and the toll clock was repaired decades later. No clock appears in the pass record. Rowan can compare the relative spacing with a known mark, not align it to an absolute time. The note preserves a useful local observation while refusing to turn an approximate rhythm into a precise sequence of events across the entire road.

entries.title: Saltspool Scale for Directional Rubbing
entries.body: A Saltspool Skate scale leaves a faint oily sheen when drawn across dry paper. Silas uses the sheen to compare stroke direction on a practice strip, not to make invisible writing appear. The scale cannot identify a writer, set a date or establish what the dispatch meant. Rowan records the pool and catch date so the sample is not confused with a scale kept from another trip. The test will be used only after a split-light plate has been prepared and checked on scrap material.

entries.title: Repair Marks inside the Toll Bell
entries.body: The toll bell's inner shell contains two rows of hammer marks. A replacement bracket covers part of the lower row, and rust crosses both groups. The marks show that the bell was repaired at least once; they do not establish the repair date or which strike could be heard from Nella's checkpoint. Rowan photographs the relative positions in the field log. The bell remains an object with a maintenance history, not a reliable clock shared by all three witnesses.

entries.title: Roadglass Sentinel at the Cart Cut
entries.body: The Roadglass Sentinel patrols the narrow cut below the toll station. Its marked rush follows the rut and can be evaded sideways when the warning line appears. A glass filament is lodged in its casing after the encounter. The material has a practical use in the assay lens, but the creature's presence does not explain why the old cart route was selected. Rowan keeps the combat note and the dispatch investigation as separate records.

entries.title: Roadglass Filament Receipt
entries.body: The recovered Roadglass filament has a clean break that fits a fracture on the practice frame. This confirms that it was caught there recently. It cannot date the older dispatch or show whether a glass tool was used to scrape the original ink. Talia's assay recipe uses a measured filament strand as part of the split-light plate. The receipt records where the material came from and prevents a new sample from being mistaken for a century-old trace.

entries.title: Windglass Fiber and the Test Frame
entries.body: One Windglass Reed was grown for the split-light plate's frame. The crop was harvested at the local Salt Road plot after its configured growth interval. A single reed can brace the test frame; it does not estimate how much material the ridge could supply to a caravan. Rowan records the seed, location and harvest together. Talia will compare this fiber with the Roadglass filament and the Saltspool scale before any part of the tool touches the dispatch.

entries.title: Split-Light Plate: Bench Test
entries.body: Talia prepared the Split-Light Plate at the Cinderwell assay bench from one Windglass Reed, one Saltspool Skate and one Roadglass filament. Its two beams reveal small differences in raised ink when the paper is held at a fixed angle. A test on scrap shows that the plate works; it does not authenticate a writer or guarantee that every mark on an old page is original. The work order lists the ingredients and station so later reviewers can reproduce the same setup.

entries.title: Sister June's Copy Rule
entries.body: Sister June recommends that a correction identify the person who changed the record while retaining the original page and its uncertainty. She will witness the transfer of copies but will not sign for events she did not see on the Salt Road. Her rule distinguishes custodianship from testimony. A corrected manifest can clarify the dispatch without claiming that every traveler was counted or that one signature explains why the caravan turned back.

entries.title: Exposure without Scraping
entries.body: The Split-Light Plate reveals a raised line beside the route instruction when mounted at the Lockhouse light box. The final line ends at a tear. No scraping or chemical wash was used, so the page remains available for another reading. Ruth recognizes the fold but does not claim to know when the raised mark was added. The exposure identifies a surviving physical feature; it does not determine who wrote the line, who read it or which witnesses saw the instruction before the retreat.

entries.title: Reverse Text and Missing Initials
entries.body: The reverse of the dispatch contains a destination code and a return instruction tied to the third bell. A tear removes the initials and the sentence explaining why the cart was to return. The toll receipt carries a matching code but no person or hour. The documents support a connection between the dispatch and the checkpoint; they do not show who authorized the instruction or whether it was issued before every traveler had arrived. Rowan records the strengthened link and the unresolved gap on the same page.

entries.title: Silas's Revised Position
entries.body: Silas places himself inside the weigh station when he fired the first signal. His earlier statement put him on the ridge. He explains that the first account felt easier to survive, but his present admission does not fill the views blocked by the station wall and road bend. Rowan keeps both statements with their dates. The revised position narrows what Silas could have observed; it does not prove that the signal caused the retreat or that he knew who remained out of sight.

entries.title: Sightline Is Not a Headcount
entries.body: The weigh station wall blocks Silas's view of the lower bend. A signal could travel farther than the person who fired it could see. The sketch marks the obstruction and the approximate gate position, but it is not a surveyed map. Rowan adds a note that the hidden stretch cannot be treated as empty merely because Silas did not see it. This correction limits the testimony without replacing it with an invented count of travelers.

entries.title: Ruth's Responsibility and Its Limit
entries.body: Ruth acknowledges that she removed the dispatch from the common ledger and concealed it. She describes preservation as one reason, but admits that the choice also prevented others from examining the page. Her account does not establish how many travelers were beyond the bend or what each person knew. The archive keeps her responsibility beside its limit: she can answer for hiding the paper, while the missing initials, torn sentence and blocked sightline remain unresolved.

entries.title: Signing Scope Decision
entries.body: The correction needs a signature for Ruth's concealment and a distinct boundary around Nella's checkpoint testimony. One policy places Ruth's acknowledgment first so readers meet the act before its explanation. The other lets Nella countersign only the location and bell interval she witnessed, while Ruth signs a separate statement about hiding the dispatch. Both options preserve the original, identify who changed the record and leave the torn reason and unseen road unresolved.

entries.title: Ruth's Signed Addendum
entries.body: The first line of the addendum records Ruth's choice to hide the dispatch from the shared ledger. A second line states that she cannot verify who was beyond the bend when the order was followed. The page remains attached to the original rather than overwriting it. This arrangement makes responsibility immediately visible, though readers may focus on Ruth before considering the limited evidence about the convoy. The addendum has a dated space for later correction and does not speak for Nella.

entries.title: Joint Copy with Bounded Witnesses
entries.body: Nella's signature appears beside her checkpoint position and remembered bell interval. Ruth's signature appears beside her admission that she hid the page. The copy does not merge their testimony or imply that either witnessed the entire road. This format protects the difference between the two accounts, but readers may miss Ruth's responsibility if they skim the second section. Both sections point to the original dispatch and retain a date for review.

entries.title: Afterword: The Road Remains Open
entries.body: The filed correction preserves Ruth's admission, Nella's bounded witness account and Silas's revised signal position. The papers now describe more than before, but they do not identify every traveler or settle the outcome of the retreat. Ellis Porter's name remains absent from the manifest; that absence cannot establish whether he reached the road by another route. Ruth keeps the ledger open for another witness and dates the next review. The two signing policies remain distinct in the codex so later readers can see who accepted responsibility and who described a place.

entries.title: Nella Opens a Family Search
entries.body:
Nella carries the pass card of a younger sibling who did not return from the Salt Road crossing. She asks Rowan to preserve the card and the gap between its stamped passage and the missing person's later route. No name is added to the public count, and no destination is inferred from the card. The family may request, correct or withdraw a copy. The investigation records where each mark was found and who could see it, leaving the search open for evidence that can still be checked.

Supplemental family search note — a file belongs to those it describes

Nella asks Rowan to place the pass card on a clean board while the family decides which parts may be copied. One relative wants the stamp drawn; another asks that the cord hole remain unphotographed because a household token once hung there. The two requests can coexist. Rowan records them on different slips so neither is treated as permission on behalf of the other.

The first catalogue entry names the objects and the current access rule. It does not ask the family to explain its worry or prove its connection before asking for privacy. Nella says the search can remain open while the copies stay limited. No public list is needed for the archive to remember where to look next.

entries.title: Pass Card: A Bounded Record
entries.body:
The pass card establishes that one person crossed a named checkpoint and that two notches were scratched beside its stamp. A trimmed corner and an empty cord hole show the card was handled, but not by whom or at what later time. Rowan makes a line drawing rather than writing a presumed destination. The card is not a list of the travelers who followed it, and a matching route mark cannot stand in for the missing person's own account. Nella approves a family copy with space for correction.

Supplemental family search note — measure the paper before reading the route

Rowan measures the trimmed edge from three corners and notes the spread between readings. The card bends near its cord hole; he supports the fold with a flat weight rather than forcing it level. A second drawing marks the stamp and notches at larger scale, with the card's outline kept beside them so a future reader can check that the details belong to this object.

Nella recognizes the shape of the punched hole but cannot date when it was made. The record distinguishes her recognition from the measurable crease. A later conservator can inspect the card without turning a family memory into an official date.

entries.title: The Wall Does Not Supply Nine Names
entries.body:
Nine hook positions on the shelter wall are empty. A larger section of plaster has broken away, so the original arrangement is uncertain. Nella remembers seeing several tags here but cannot identify which one belonged to her sibling from this wall alone. The count describes hooks that are empty now; it does not establish how many travelers stayed in the shelter or when the tags disappeared. The wall map preserves the damaged area beside the empty positions and leaves every identity unassigned.

Supplemental family search note — the count depends on the wall's edge

Rowan photographs the plaster from straight on and from a shallow angle. The angled image shows a pale rectangle where a tenth hook may once have been, but there is no attachment left to count. They preserve both images and describe nine visible empty positions in the current frame. The damaged corner stays in the drawing as damage, not as a hidden name.

Nella remembers tags on the wall from several visits, not all at once. Her memory can direct a new search through stored labels, but it does not tell which hook held which tag. The public method card explains how the count was made without implying nine travelers or nine missing people.

entries.title: The Dispatch and the Missing Place
entries.body:
Ruth confirms that the recovered dispatch contains a route instruction but no complete passenger list. Her admission that she hid the page is preserved separately from Nella's account of a missing younger sibling. The document cannot show who was beyond the road bend, and it does not provide a name for the empty place on the shelter wall. Rowan links the dispatch to the investigation as one source among several, without treating the two families' records as a single case or allowing Ruth's responsibility to overwrite Nella's evidence.

Supplemental family search note — Ruth's correction has a separate author

Ruth signs the date on which she disclosed the dispatch and the date on which she corrected its archive location. Those are two actions in the present investigation, not a reconstructed timeline for the old crossing. Nella reviews the reference number but does not countersign Ruth's statement. A family member should not have to certify a witness's account in order to retain control of a separate card.

Rowan adds a reference tab that lets the two documents be found together while keeping their custody histories apart. Ruth's responsibility for hiding the order can be recorded plainly without allowing the order to supply a name or destination it never contained.

entries.title: Transfer Docket: Cargo Is Not a Person
entries.body:
The Lockhouse docket records bundles transferred between shelves and a small number of unlabelled margin marks. Its units refer to containers, not people. One line is overwritten and the surviving tally cannot be reconciled with the total in the dispatch. Rowan copies the entry with the overwritten line visible and marks the mismatch as unresolved. The docket has no sibling name and no destination field. Its value is in showing how records were moved through the Lockhouse, not in turning cargo counts into a count of missing travelers.

Supplemental family search note — an overwritten tally remains visible

The Lockhouse clerk copies the docket on a sheet with a transparent window aligned over the overwritten row. A second copy shows the surrounding shelf numbers so later readers can locate the entry without handling the older ledger. They mark the two tallies as incompatible and preserve each version with its own source label.

Nella asks whether the larger number could include her sibling. No unit in the ledger says person, passenger or cadet; the written headings describe bundles. Rowan declines to convert one unit into another. The mismatch may help locate where a container record changed, but it cannot become an estimate of who passed through the Lockhouse.

entries.title: Rail Mark: Similar Width, Different Claim
entries.body:
A dark mark on the return rail is close in width to the worn edge of Nella's pass card. Salt deposits can widen a stain, and a card can be trimmed after its original use; the comparison therefore does not establish that the two marks came from the same object. A dryglass chip can be recovered from the rail casing for a protective sleeve. Rowan logs the chip as material from the Lockhouse return rail, not as evidence of who handled the pass card.

Supplemental family search note — orientation is part of a trace

The rail chip is placed in a paper cradle so its salt crust is not scraped off by a glass vial. Rowan sketches which side faced the road and which side faced the return desk; Talia adds the height above the floor. A similar width on another surface is only a resemblance until the two objects' histories can be linked.

The pass card is compared in its sleeve and again on the flat board. Its edge has softened since the family first brought it in. The archive adds the new observation without changing the earlier measurement, preserving both dates and the handling conditions that may explain the difference.

entries.title: Saltspool Sample Receipt
entries.body:
One Saltspool Skate was caught at the sheltered Salt Road pool using earthworm bait. Its oily scale film is used on a practice strip to see whether a Windglass fiber can lie flat beside a salt-marked surface. The test is about contact and preservation, not chemical dating or personal identification. Rowan records the catch location, date and bait so that this material cannot be confused with a fish taken during the earlier dispatch investigation. The whole specimen is consumed by the sleeve recipe as a recorded sample.

Supplemental family search note — consumption is written on the receipt

The practice strip receives a small amount of scale film at one end, leaving the other end untouched for comparison. Talia records how much was used, who applied it and when the test was finished. The rest of the catch is not saved as an unexplained souvenir; the recipe consumes it for the preservation trial and records that use.

Nella reads the receipt before the sample is prepared. She can ask for a different method or stop the activity without losing the card from her family's custody. The fish's catch record belongs with the sample test, not with the old crossing, and the index keeps those categories apart.

entries.title: Windglass Fiber for Safe Storage
entries.body:
A Windglass Reed grown at the Salt Road plot provides the soft inner layer for a removable pass-card sleeve. The crop was planted from a seed Nella supplied after the route opened and harvested after the configured growing interval. Its fiber protects the card from abrasion; it does not restore the trimmed corner or reveal what was written there. Rowan records seed, plot and harvest together so a future conservator can replace the liner without claiming that a natural fiber has authenticated the card's owner.

Supplemental family search note — a protective material needs its own label

The fiber is stored with a crop label until Talia prepares the sleeve. Rowan notes the seed source, plot, watering interval and harvest day; a replacement liner should be traceable to its material without being mistaken for part of the original card. The family can request a new sample if the first becomes worn.

Nella touches the practice strip through a clean cloth and approves the softness, not an authentication claim. The fiber cushions an edge and makes the drawing easier to inspect. It does not repair the trimmed corner or reveal whether a mark was added before or after the card left the checkpoint.

entries.title: A Reversible Liner
entries.body:
The harvested fiber holds the practice strip without glue and can be lifted without leaving residue. This small test makes the proposed sleeve reversible: a family member or conservator can inspect the card later, change the liner or withdraw it from display. It is not a test of archival durability over generations. Rowan records the dry conditions and one successful removal, then asks Talia to build the sleeve with a clear inspection edge. No permanent seal should prevent the family from asking questions that the current record cannot answer.

Supplemental family search note — one removal is a small trial

Talia lifts the liner once, checks for residue under angled light and lays it back without pressing the card. Rowan writes “one removal observed” rather than “reversible in all conditions.” Dust, moisture and repeated handling may change how the fiber behaves; the archive does not have years of aging tests to support a stronger claim.

Nella asks for an open edge wide enough to grip with a cloth. She should not need a tool or a clerk's permission to take the card out if the family changes its mind. The construction note explains how to open it and records who may do so under the current policy.

entries.title: Removable Sleeve Bench Record
entries.body:
Talia assembled a narrow dryglass frame with a Windglass fiber liner and recorded the Saltspool surface sample used during the practice test. The recipe produces one removable sleeve with an openable seam. It is designed to prevent rubbing while keeping the pass card visible and accessible; it is not a secure evidence vault or a device for revealing erased marks. Rowan stores the recipe with the object so the family can request a replacement, refuse display or ask for the liner to be removed without losing the original card.

Supplemental family search note — the original is not an ingredient

The bench recipe consumes one Windglass fiber and one practice sample, not the pass card. Talia lays out the parts on a diagram before Rowan begins crafting so the family can see what will be spent. The resulting sleeve is inspected with a blank card first; the original remains on Nella's cloth until the frame is ready.

After assembly, the openable seam is tested by hand and the replacement steps are written beside the ingredient list. A future craftsperson can make another sleeve without using any part of the family's evidence. The copy of the recipe stays public only to the extent that it contains no household identifier.

entries.title: Copy Rule: Method Public, Search by Consent
entries.body:
Sister June proposes two layers of record. A public copy may describe how the checkpoint count and transfer mismatch were measured, with names and household details excluded. A separate copy about Nella's sibling remains under family control and can be corrected, requested or withdrawn. June's rule is a procedure, not proof that every family wants the same privacy. Rowan records who authorizes each copy and dates the request. The two layers should never be joined merely because they use the same road map or shelter-wall diagram.

Supplemental family search note — method and search are different records

June separates the public method card from the family's search sheet by color, category and storage location. She points out that a public explanation of hook counting does not authorize a public image of the pass card. A person can learn how Rowan documented the wall and docket while remaining unable to identify which household has a private file.

The rule applies to this case because Nella requests it. June does not turn the request into a universal practice that overrides another family's choice. The record lists who approved each copy and when that approval can be reviewed again.

entries.title: Review and Withdrawal Rule
entries.body:
The pouch stores no household name on its exterior. Its accompanying request slip states who may ask for the private copy to be opened, how a correction is attached and how the family can withdraw the copy from the archive. The seal protects access only while that rule remains available and understandable. It does not make the material more accurate, and it is not a substitute for a date or custody receipt. Rowan files the opening rule next to the pouch so that a later keeper cannot mistake secrecy for consent.

Supplemental family search note — access instructions must travel with the seal

The outer pouch has a plain face; its numbered receipt is stored in the restricted ledger. The opening rule names the family contact route and explains how to request correction, renewed review or withdrawal. Nella asks Rowan to read the rule aloud before the pouch is sealed so a future holder will not have to guess what the number means.

The seal indicates handling, not truth. If it breaks, the keeper records what happened and contacts the family through the approved route. A damaged mark alone cannot say who opened the pouch or why.

entries.title: The Pass Card in a Reversible Frame
entries.body:
The pass card now sits behind a removable fiber liner in the Lockhouse frame. The clear edge leaves its stamp and two notches visible while keeping the card from rubbing against the glass. The family review seam remains openable and is recorded in the custody receipt. Installation consumes one crafted Tag Sleeve, but does not consume or alter the original pass card. A later inspection can remove the liner, add a dated note or take the card back out of public display.

Supplemental family search note — display can be undone

The frame ledger records the sleeve's item number and the date it was fitted. No adhesive touches the pass card. A visitor can see the checkpoint stamp and notches through the clear edge, while the family can request removal through the same counter where it was installed. The display card says that the drawing shows the present object, not every stage of its journey.

Nella checks that the frame can be opened with gloved fingers. Installation consumes the crafted sleeve, but the original card and the family's permission remain separate from that gameplay object. A later change of policy can return the card to private storage without rewriting the installation record.

entries.title: Unassigned Tags and a Broken Link
entries.body:
Two chain tags in the Lockhouse case have no surviving name, and one link is broken. Salt and pressure have worn the edges; the break may be old, but the file has no dated inspection. Nella recognizes neither tag as her sibling's. Rowan photographs the arrangement, records the empty interval and leaves both objects unassigned. The chain may show that a group of tags was handled together, but it does not prove that all tags belonged to people on one cart or that the broken link marked a departure.

Supplemental family search note — the broken link has no owner

Rowan photographs the chain tags from above and from the side, placing a scale at the same distance in both images. One link has a bright interior under the dark surface, but no conservator can tell whether that came from a recent break or repeated motion. The storage case is recorded as the location where the tags were found, not as proof they traveled together.

Nella declines to choose either tag as her sibling's. The archive uses “unassigned” rather than “unknown traveler,” because even the connection to a traveler is not established. If a later mark can be compared, it receives its own date and source.

entries.title: Signal Reach Is Not Sight
entries.body:
Silas places himself inside the weigh station when he fired his first signal. The wall and bend blocked his view of the lower road, though an audible or visible signal could travel beyond that obstruction. His statement can narrow where he stood; it cannot establish who heard him, how the order was interpreted or how many travelers remained out of sight. Rowan keeps his revised position beside the earlier ridge account, with both dates visible. Neither version identifies Nella's sibling or assigns a tag in the Lockhouse case.

Supplemental family search note — a signal can travel farther than a witness sees

Silas draws the weigh-station wall on his statement and marks his remembered standing position with a distinct symbol. The word “inside” is kept as his present description; it is not converted to a measured coordinate. Rowan places a second mark for the modern survey and labels its date so a reader cannot mistake the two positions for one observation.

Nella does not use the statement to assign the chain tags. Silas's account can establish what he remembers doing and where his view was blocked. It cannot identify who received a signal or which road a missing person took.

entries.title: Sightline and Signal Radius
entries.body:
The sketch separates Silas's line of sight from an estimated signal radius. The lower bend falls outside the visible wedge, while sound or light may have traveled around the wall. The radius is not surveyed and does not prove that any particular person received the signal. Rowan marks the hidden road as uncounted, adds the station wall and gate for orientation, and labels the drawing as a field sketch rather than a measured map. The image can guide another search without turning the unseen section into an assumed empty road.

Supplemental family search note — the shaded area is not an empty area

The sketch uses a hatched wedge for the section blocked from Silas's recorded position. Rowan adds the station wall, gate and two known markers for orientation, then labels the estimated signal radius with a question mark. That line is an untested guide for a future survey, not a circle that contains everyone who might have heard or seen the signal.

The lower bend remains uncounted in this sheet. Nella requests that later copies keep that label even if a new map has more detail. A clearer view can improve the field record; it cannot make the present uncertainty retroactively disappear.

entries.title: Nella's Copy Boundary
entries.body:
Nella consents to public release of the counting method and the locations of the damaged records, with identifying details removed. The pass card, private request slip and family search remain under her household's control unless the family asks for a copy to be opened. She requests that the archive state that no destination is known and that the person remains missing from this record. Her decision is a boundary for this file, not a general rule for every family or a declaration that the search has ended.

Supplemental family search note — consent has a narrow subject

Nella reads the public copy line by line. She approves the method, the damaged-record locations and the statement that no destination is established. She does not approve publication of the card image, the household's request slip or anyone else's account. Rowan records that scope rather than checking a single broad box marked “family consent.”

Her signature confirms the copy boundary on this date. It does not mean that she accepts every interpretation in the archive or that she gives up the right to change the boundary later. Nella can speak for this file and this request only.

entries.title: Archive Access Decision
entries.body:
The archive can publish the counting method and the measured locations while keeping all family details out of the public record. Alternatively, it can keep the pass-card copy behind a family-controlled review rule and publish only the fact that a private file exists. Both policies preserve the missing destination as unknown, retain a correction date and allow the family to withdraw its copy. The choice controls access and disclosure; it cannot determine whether the sibling crossed another route or what happened after the recorded checkpoint.

Supplemental family search note — either policy preserves the same open question

Before Rowan records the choice, he reads both descriptions back to Nella: a public method-only card, or a public notice that a restricted family file exists. Neither option publishes the card or names the sibling. Both retain a correction date, a withdrawal path and the same warning that no destination is known.

The decision changes the audience for records, not the events the records can prove. Nella is allowed to choose without predicting what every other family would want. The selected policy is saved so a later custodian does not quietly substitute the path they find more convenient.

entries.title: Public Method-Only Copy
entries.body:
The public copy describes how Rowan recorded the nine empty hook positions, the transfer-docket mismatch and the wall damage. It contains no name, card image, household route or unverified destination. A note explains that the count applies to hooks and bundles, not people. This policy makes the method easier for other road communities to inspect, but prevents readers from following the family's private search through public documents. The record carries a correction date and a contact rule so that new evidence can amend the method without exposing the household.

Supplemental family search note — the correction date is not a deadline

The public card includes a date for the next archive review. That date prompts Rowan to recheck the method and the contact route; it does not require Nella to report a result by then. The wall count may change if plaster is repaired or a lost tag is found, and such a change can be added without turning the new count into a count of people.

The card uses a blank space for future corrections rather than leaving room for household names. Anyone who finds a new record can send its source and date through the listed channel. The archive can respond without displaying the family's private search.

entries.title: Family-Controlled Review Copy
entries.body:
The private copy holds the pass-card drawing, custody receipt and a request slip authored by Nella's family. Its outer cover contains no household name. The opening rule limits access to a family request and records who handled the copy; the correction slip allows a later statement to be attached without replacing the original. The withdrawal receipt gives the household a way to remove the copy from archive display. This protects privacy at the cost of public access to the card evidence, while leaving the search itself open to the people it concerns.

Supplemental family search note — withdrawal returns the copy, not the evidence

If Nella asks to withdraw the family copy, the archive returns that copy to the named holder and records the handoff. The public method card and the original docket remain in their own custody because they are different objects under different permissions. The withdrawal entry says what was returned, not why the family asked.

The family may later request a new copy under a revised rule. The earlier receipt stays in the ledger so custodians can account for the history without keeping a version the family asked them to return. Privacy is maintained through an explicit procedure rather than a promise that no record of handling exists.

entries.title: Afterword: Leave a Place for a Witness
entries.body:
The completed file preserves the pass card, the unassigned chain tags, the damaged shelter wall and the limits of Silas's view. Nella chose either a public method-only copy or a family-controlled review copy, and the save retains that policy. Neither version names the missing sibling or claims where they went. Ruth's dispatch remains a separate document with its own signed correction. The family search remains open: a future witness can provide a dated account, request a correction or ask for the private copy to be withdrawn without requiring Rowan to rewrite what the current evidence says.

Supplemental family search note — leave room without promising an answer

The file's final index lists where a witness may send an account, how the family may reopen the private copy and how an older statement can be corrected. It does not set a deadline for an answer or a required final status for the search. Nella wants the archive to stay useful if someone remembers a date, a place or a paper mark years later.

Rowan leaves the destination field blank. That blank records the limit of today's file, not a conclusion about the sibling's life. If a future witness arrives, their account will begin with its own source, date and permission, not with a verdict written in advance.

entries.title: June Reopens the Kitchen
entries.body:
Sister June does not describe the meal as payment for work or proof that the displaced people have been accounted for. She wants the kitchen fire lit again because the sluice crew and the remaining households still need to eat. The convoy report has been delivered, but its list does not describe who is hungry at this hour. June keeps one cooking place open and invites each person to take food without giving a reason.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — leave a place without asking why

June sets the ladle on the table before she calls anyone in. The first person to arrive can take a bowl and sit without telling her which crew they belong to. She keeps a separate pot for anyone who needs to leave quickly, but does not mark the bowl against a roster. The kitchen is a place to eat, not another checkpoint on the road.

Rowan asks how June will know whether the meal reached enough people. She says a list might count servings, but it cannot count hunger outside the room. She will ask whether the pot should stay open and what can be cooked next, then let people answer or keep walking.

Second hearing — the door is not a question

On the first morning the kitchen opens, June leaves the door unlatched even while she carries the stock book from the pantry. Rowan asks whether anyone might take supplies. June answers that a latch would make every hungry visitor explain why they came before she could explain what the kitchen can offer. She does not call the choice risk-free; she asks Oren to keep the dry shelf in sight while the pot is unattended.

Two people pass the threshold without sitting. One accepts a cup of water, then leaves it rinsed beside the basin. June does not add their initials to the day sheet. She records only the cup returned and the water used. For Rowan, the small entry becomes a lesson in what the ledger can honestly hold: a kitchen can count its own work without claiming to know the lives that touched it. The door stays open through the next shift, but the stock check remains a shared responsibility rather than a test of whether a visitor deserves to enter.

entries.title: Hearth Inspection
entries.body:
A thin crack runs from the iron pot ring to the hearth's drainage groove. The stone remains level, but the crack could lengthen if the pot is heated unevenly. June chooses the portable brazier until a mason can inspect the full hearth. Rowan records the safe limit as a cooking precaution, not as a claim that the structure has been repaired.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — warmth does not repair stone

June traces the crack with a piece of charcoal and stops where it meets the drainage groove. The line looks unchanged after a small brazier test, but the hearth has not been inspected beneath its ring. She refuses to let Rowan call the mark stable after one short heating. A mason can check the structure when the lower path is safe.

Until then, the portable brazier sits on the dry platform with clear space on every side. The note lists the pot weight and the brief test so another cook can avoid repeating it. Cooking can resume at a smaller scale while the question of a permanent repair stays open.

Second hearing — repair work has a stopping line

The mason arrives after the last bowl is washed and asks June to clear the hearth stones. June gives him the portable brazier card first. He studies the charcoal line and says the trial tells him where heat was used, not what the crack looks like beneath the ring. She appreciates the distinction and refuses to let the tired crew hurry him into a verdict before he has lifted a stone.

Rowan carries the cooking pot to the dry platform. Its iron bottom leaves a dark circle on the boards, exactly where June expected it. The mason marks that circle as a work position, not as proof that the platform can bear a full night of cooking. June asks for a second inspection after the lower stair is dry. The room can make small meals in the meantime, provided each shift checks the legs and clears the walking space. Her relief is visible when the fire is moved; her caution remains on the card. The hearth is still a question with a safer temporary answer.

entries.title: Pantry Muck Cleared
entries.body:
The Cinderwell Muck has left the grain locker, and the access path is open again. June inspects the remaining sack seams herself and separates those that stayed dry from the ones softened by the drain. The creature's presence explains why the door was left shut; it does not explain how the grain was stored before the flood or who last used each sack.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — keep wet sacks away from the meal bed

June spreads the sacks on two shelves: dry seams above, softened seams below on a draining board. She does not open the dry sacks just because the Muck has been cleared; each one is checked when a portion is needed. Rowan draws the shelf positions, and June adds the damp line from the flood wall for the next cook.

Some grain is fit for a small meal and some needs Oren's review before it is moved. The new arrangement protects what is usable without turning the pantry into an official reserve. June writes “inspect before serving” on the work card, not “all clear.”

Second hearing — the sack that was opened too late

Oren finds a softened seam at the back of the lower shelf and asks June if she wants him to discard the whole sack. She cuts only the wet corner away and checks the grain that stayed above the damp line. Some is sound enough for a small test; some has begun to clump. They put the portions on separate cloths and write the inspection time beside each one, so another cook can repeat the check instead of trusting the word usable without context.

June remembers a previous kitchen where throwing out one damaged sack had left the next crew with no supper. She also remembers that serving spoiled food would have harmed the people she wanted to protect. She does not tell Rowan that either memory settles today's decision. They keep the tested grain for the current pot and ask Oren to inspect the remaining stock. The Muck's defeat cleared a route to the shelf. It did not certify everything stored behind it. On the work card, June writes the next checker's name only after asking whether that person has agreed to take the task.

entries.title: Brazier Draft Notes
entries.body:
Talia marks the path between the lower gate, the air gap and the portable brazier. The draft changed while the sluice wheel was moving, so she recommends leaving the gap open and moving the flame uphill. It is a practical arrangement for the current work shift, not a building inspection or a promise that every later fire will draw the same way.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — a safe flame belongs to a shift

Talia and June test the portable brazier once with the sluice wheel idle, then again after a gate worker turns it. The airflow changes when the lower opening is partly covered by a moving cart. They mark the gap and the brazier's uphill position for this shift, with a reminder to check the draft whenever the gate changes.

June asks Rowan not to leave a fixed diagram over the stove as if the room's air never moved. The note is kept near the fire tools where a cook can see it and update it. The meal can be repeated; the exact flame path still depends on who is working nearby.

Second hearing — hear the room when the gate turns

Talia visits during a quiet hour and asks June to repeat the brazier test while the sluice worker turns the lower gate. The flame leans for a moment, then settles. A cart rolls past the opening and changes the draft again. No one is in danger, but the movement is enough to make the old diagram incomplete. June takes it down from the wall and carries it to the tool shelf, where it can be read as a record of one arrangement rather than an instruction carved into the room.

Rowan notices that Talia waits for the worker to finish before asking for another turn of the wheel. June says the cook must be able to see who is changing the air around the flame. A fixed number cannot replace a glance at the door, the cart and the people beside the stove. The new note has three small sketches and room for another. Each cook may add a condition that changes the flame path. The recipe stays repeatable because it says when to stop and look again, not because it pretends the room never changes.

entries.title: Oren's Barley Lot
entries.body:
Oren gives Rowan a small packet of Cinderwell barley from a lot reserved for kitchen trials. He asks June to keep the crop apart from the protected seed store, since the same grain cannot be eaten and replanted. The packet is not a share of the strategic reserve and does not change the basin's official allocation. It gives the kitchen a local ingredient and a chance to save seed if the harvest permits it.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — kitchen grain and seed grain

Oren counts the trial packet into a small bowl and labels it with the kitchen bed, not the basin reserve. June sets one measure aside for cooking and returns the intact seed heads to him after harvest. The two portions cannot do the same job: a cooked kernel cannot be planted, and a planting seed is not a promised meal.

June asks Oren to write the packet's origin on both containers. If the next crop is poor, the kitchen will know what it used and the reserve ledger will still show no change. The trial creates a choice for this meal without pretending to solve the basin's food supply.

Second hearing — a measure can carry two histories

Oren holds the kitchen packet in one hand and the basin reserve card in the other. Both use the same weight mark, yet he says he would never want a clerk to combine them. The first belongs to an experimental row and can be spent on a meal; the second is guarded against a season when the water schedule fails. June writes each source on its own label, then asks Oren to check her spelling of the old bed name.

The shared measure reminds Oren of his mother's tin, but the packet is not taken from it. He says this matters because a familiar size can make two stores look interchangeable. Rowan copies the measure without copying the ownership. In the evening, June uses the trial portion and returns the unground kernels to Oren. No one treats the small cooking decision as permission to draw on the reserve. Oren keeps the kitchen receipt beside his own notes, not inside the tin. The two histories now sit next to one another where they can be compared without being merged.

entries.title: First Barley Harvest
entries.body:
The barley was planted in the kitchen bed and harvested after reaching maturity. The bed's position beside the stone wall kept it warmer than the open basin, although one crop does not establish a dependable yield. June sets aside two measures for cooking and returns any intact seed heads to Oren for review. The kitchen lot remains separate from the reserve crop, so the harvest does not silently alter the basin's seed ledger.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — one harvest teaches one bed

The kitchen bed received morning water from a small can while the outer basin plots waited on the sluice schedule. June records each watering instead of calling the warm wall a reliable advantage. The plants matured, but the crop occupied only one short row and grew under one wall's shade pattern.

After harvest, June and Oren sort the heads on separate cloths. Barley with intact kernels goes back for seed review; cracked grain goes to the meal bowl. Rowan notes the distinction so later cooks do not copy the cooking portion into the garden ledger. The harvest is useful and local, not a forecast for every field in Cinderwell.

Second hearing — the row that could not be hurried

June remembers arriving at the bed before dawn and finding Oren there with his sleeves rolled past his elbows. He wanted to pull one shoot to see whether the roots had taken. She gave him the watering can instead. A crop can look unchanged while it is doing work below the soil; pulling it early would answer a question by destroying the chance to observe the next day.

Oren laughs at himself when Rowan mentions this in the ledger. Later, he measures the same row at noon and finds the wall-side soil drying first. The difference is useful for this bed, in this stretch of weather. June adjusts one small watering, not the whole basin schedule. When harvest comes, they keep the food grain and seed heads separate. Oren takes pride in the few intact heads, but he asks not to have the bed called a success for every grower. His row taught him how to wait and which patch to watch; it did not promise the same result everywhere. June keeps his observation with the date and shade conditions so another gardener can test it again.

entries.title: Cinderwell Warm Run Catch
entries.body:
Rowan caught an Emberscale Perch where warm outlet water meets the basin. The Cinderwell spot has a weighted catch table and uses one unit of Earthworm Bait per cast. A single successful catch gives the kitchen one ingredient; it is not a population survey and does not establish that the outlet is safe for drinking. The fish goes to June for cooking rather than to the water ledger.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — bring the catch to the cook, not the ledger

June meets Rowan at the kitchen door with a clean board and asks where the fish was caught, when and with which bait. She records one Emberscale Perch from the Warm Run and sends the water question to Talia's separate notebook. The kitchen needs a food-handling note, while the sluice team needs observations about the outlet; one page should not claim both.

The fish is cleaned for the meal, and the catch record stays with the recipe ingredients. A single perch does not tell them how many fish remain or whether the water is safe to drink. It gives June one ingredient she can cook today.

Second hearing — a fish has more than one destination

The Warm Run is quiet when Rowan brings the catch back, and June asks him not to lay it beside the seed cloth. She clears a different board and rinses the knife before touching the perch. Talia arrives with a water jar but waits until June has finished the food check. They agree to write two notes: June's records how the fish was handled for the kitchen, while Talia records the outlet and the time of collection for her separate inquiry.

Neither woman wants the other's page to become a broad claim. June cannot use one fish to describe the whole run. Talia cannot infer drinking safety from its condition. Rowan records the bait and the exact spot so a later catch can be compared fairly. The perch is cooked that evening, and its cleaned bones go into a small covered bowl rather than back toward the water. June says a meal and an ecological survey may share an afternoon without becoming the same task. The record gives each purpose enough detail to be useful and leaves the rest open.

entries.title: Kitchen Millstone
entries.body:
The hand mill turns evenly after grit is brushed from the lower lip. The shelf stayed above the last visible water mark, though June will still inspect each measure before cooking. The mill is suited to a small batch; using it for the whole reserve would create a different job and require a separate cleaning and storage plan.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — the small mill has a small batch limit

June catches the ground barley in a shallow tray and checks it for grit with her fingertips. The lower lip is brushed before each use, then the hand mill is wrapped so dust from the pantry cannot fall into it. A single kitchen portion takes only a few turns; a full reserve sack would need more space, time and a different cleaning plan.

Oren asks whether the mill's steady turn means it is ready for a public work line. June says it is ready for this batch. She logs the cleaning and amount used so the kitchen can decide later whether the same tool can serve more people.

Second hearing — one turn belongs to the person at the mill

Oren offers to keep the hand mill turning while June checks the recipe. She lets him begin, but stops him when he starts matching the speed of the sluice wheel outside. The grain shifts under the stone when the handle is rushed. He slows down, feels the resistance and finds a small grit fleck caught under the lip. The cleaned tray catches the rest of the flour before it can mix with the dust left from the pantry shelf.

June tells Rowan she once treated a quiet worker as proof that the mill was easy to use. She now asks each person who wants to grind to try the handle with an empty bowl first. Nobody is assigned the job because they are the strongest or because they already know the kitchen. The card records the batch size and cleaning steps; it does not set a pace. After the test, Oren wraps the handle to keep dust out. He is pleased to have found the grit, though June credits the pause rather than the force he used. The next shift will begin with a clean stone and the chance to learn the turn.

entries.title: Stone-Pot Broth Recipe
entries.body:
The first Cinderwell Stone-Pot Broth uses two measures of local barley and one Emberscale Perch. The kitchen recipe produces two bowls, allowing one serving to be shared while Rowan keeps another for recovery. June records the ingredients and brazier position so that the meal can be repeated. The recipe is a field kitchen dish; it is not a claim about nutrition beyond its in-game restorative effect.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — repeat the pot, adapt the serving

The first pot yields two bowls from two measures of barley and one perch. June writes down when the barley enters the water and how long the pot stays over the brazier, but she leaves the seasoning line blank for whoever cooks next. Rowan keeps one bowl for travel recovery; the other goes to the table or into the road crate according to the choice made in the route.

The recipe describes how to make this batch, not how every person should eat. June asks cooks to offer a smaller serving when requested and to let the person decide whether to take more. The in-game restorative value belongs to Rowan's item; it does not measure the meal's value to the whole kitchen.

Second hearing — the recipe leaves room for a cook

The first batch tastes thinner than June expected. She reaches for salt, then pauses so Rowan can write down the original seasoning before anyone changes it. One worker wants more broth; another prefers the grain firm. June makes a small adjustment in a second bowl instead of rewriting the whole recipe. Both portions come from the same pot, but they do not have to be served as though every person asked for the same texture.

Rowan's restorative meal is set aside before the kitchen table begins. June wants the player's inventory item to have a clear use, while the kitchen recipe has a different question: can the people eating it ask for a change without being treated as a problem? She records two versions and the amounts used. The page is longer, but no version becomes the official taste of Cinderwell. June signs only for the batch she cooked and invites the next cook to make a new note. Her method preserves what can be repeated and keeps preference where it belongs, with the person holding the spoon.

entries.title: First Pot Check
entries.body:
The barley has softened and the perch flakes apart, showing that this batch reached June's current cooking standard. The dish has only been made once, so the timing is a starting point. June asks for feedback from the people eating the meal and leaves room to change the recipe. A clean pot and a repeatable procedure matter, but neither substitutes for asking whether the food is welcome.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — feedback is not a vote tally

June sets three blank slips beside the pot. Anyone can write a note about salt, texture or serving size and leave without signing; the slips are kept apart from the workers' duty board. The first comment asks for a softer barley, while another says the perch should stay in larger pieces. June pins both beside the recipe as suggestions, not as the basin's decision.

Rowan records that one pot was tasted and that its maker was June. A clean bowl and a repeatable method make the next batch easier, but the recipe remains changeable. Nobody needs to praise the meal in exchange for eating it.

Second hearing — leave the blank slips blank

After the first pot, one person returns a slip with three words about salt. Another leaves a smudge where a name could have been. June does not ask whose mark it is. She pins both to the underside of the recipe sleeve, where a cook can see the comments before starting but a visitor cannot read them from the door. Rowan asks whether she will need to count the slips to decide which seasoning wins. June says a handful of anonymous remarks is useful guidance, not a vote that speaks for everyone who never wrote.

Oren reads the note about salt and suggests offering a small portion before the next pot is served. June agrees, then asks him to record the suggestion as his rather than attributing it to the table. He does. The cook may still choose the seasoning according to what ingredients remain, and diners can refuse without explaining themselves. The sample check records how the meal was received by the people who chose to comment. It cannot tell the kitchen how many people came hungry or what they would want tomorrow. The empty slips stay beside the full ones for whoever prefers to write later.

entries.title: First Bowl Decision
entries.body:
June offers the first bowl to either the people remaining at the cistern kitchen or the road crew preparing to leave before dawn. The choice affects who receives the first serving and the token Rowan carries afterward. It does not determine who is more deserving, change the water allocation or settle the convoy's destination. One bowl stays with Rowan and can restore health through the inventory menu.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — choose where the first bowl goes

June gives Rowan the bowl and lets him carry it either to the people still at the cistern table or to the road crew preparing before dawn. She does not rank the two groups. The kitchen shift faces another sluice check; the road crew faces a longer walk with uncertain stops. Both needs are real, and one bowl cannot settle what anyone should receive tomorrow.

The saved choice records the handoff and opens a different keepsake for Rowan. His second bowl stays in inventory as usable food. June leaves the serving dish by the brazier so either group can return if the next pot is ready.

Second hearing — there is no clean arithmetic for a bowl

June does not follow Rowan when he carries the first bowl away. She watches the doorway, then asks Talia how long the next gate inspection can wait. The cistern crew needs someone to write the measurement; the road crew needs food before the walk. June knows what the route choice sent today and what remains on the counter, but she refuses to turn that count into a rule about who should receive tomorrow's first serving.

When Rowan returns, she asks whether the bowl arrived warm. He can answer that much. He cannot know whether it met every need at either destination. June accepts this smaller report and puts the next portion where he can take it if he chooses. The two keepsakes remember different acts of care, not different rankings of people. She asks him to come back after the next shift and listen before the pot is divided again. No story flag can replace the voices of those present at the kitchen table on another day.

entries.title: Common Table Serving
entries.body:
One bowl of Stone-Pot Broth was served at the common table to workers who chose to remain for the meal. June leaves the ladle in reach and does not collect names or signatures. This option gives the staying shift food before the next sluice check. The table record describes a serving event, not the number of people who ate or the amount each person needed.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — keep the ladle within reach

The workers who remain for the meal serve themselves while June checks the next water schedule. She does not collect names or ask for a signature beside each bowl. One late-shift worker leaves half a serving covered for later; another takes a second spoonful after the first table has finished.

The record counts one bowl placed at the table, not the number of people who ate from it. June prefers a simple line that can be checked against the pot rather than a list that might follow people between shifts. The meal is available to the group present; the note does not claim to know everyone's need.

Second hearing — people decide when a meal is enough

The late shift gathers at different times. One worker eats standing by the door because the wheel alarm has not been cleared; another stays to wash cups. June starts to write that three people shared the pot, then crosses out the number when one of them says a traveler took a bowl after she turned to the sink. The pot count is still accurate, but the number of diners is not.

She changes the entry to say how many servings left the pot for the common table. Rowan asks why that difference matters if the food is gone either way. June answers that the count may later be used to plan another meal. A false headcount could make someone believe everyone had eaten or that an extra bowl is always available. She does not need to know who took the serving. She needs the next cook to know what was cooked, what remains and when the shelf should be checked. The table can be open without becoming a roll call, and a small reliable count is kinder than a confident guess.

entries.title: Road Crew Provision
entries.body:
One bowl of Stone-Pot Broth was packed with the road crew's provisions. The cup was left to vent while cooling, then secured inside the crate. June does not assign the food to a named traveler; the crew will decide who carries it. The entry records one packed serving and leaves the road's length, crew size and future food needs outside its claim.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — pack food without packing a person into the tally

The bowl is left uncovered until steam stops rising, then sealed in the crew's crate beside a clean cup. June writes “one serving packed” on the food slip and keeps it separate from the traveler count. A later handoff can change who carries it without changing the amount that left the kitchen.

The road crew decides among themselves where the meal should sit. Rowan does not write a recipient's name on the lid. If the crew shares it, carries it onward or gives it to someone they meet, that choice remains theirs and is not reported back as a completed quest objective.

Second hearing — keep the crate easy to open

The road crew asks to carry the meal in a crate that has a stiff latch. June tries it herself with damp hands and cannot open it. She calls the crew back before they leave and asks them to choose a container that any member can open without asking one person to return the key. They select a basket and wrap the covered bowl inside it. Rowan notes the change as a practical choice made by the people carrying the food.

June's earlier slip said one serving was packed; it said nothing about who had authority to distribute it. She adds no recipient name and no delivery promise. At the gate, a crew member offers to bring the basket back after the next supply run. June declines the promise because their route may change. She only asks that the empty bowl not be left in the rain. Once the group is on the road, the kitchen's responsibility is to keep enough food for its own next service, not to supervise every handoff beyond the wall.

entries.title: Common Table Feedback
entries.body:
The Cinderwell shift asked for more barley and less salt in the next batch. A worker tending the late gate liked the perch's texture. June records both comments as feedback from this meal rather than a vote by the whole basin. The recipe stays adjustable; anyone eating it later can ask for a different serving or decline it without losing access to the kitchen.

Supplemental Cinderwell kitchen note — one comment belongs to one meal

The late-gate worker's request for less salt is written beside the batch number. Another person asks for more barley next time but gives no name, and June leaves the author field blank. The comments can guide the next pot without being described as a survey of the basin or a vote on the recipe.

June keeps the right to adjust the meal and the right to leave it alone if ingredients run short. Anyone may ask for water, a smaller portion or no bowl at all. The kitchen's welcome does not depend on leaving feedback.

Second hearing — feedback belongs beside its circumstances

The request for less salt came from a person who had been working beside the sluice for most of the day. June writes that context beside the comment only after asking whether the person is comfortable being described. They say a role is enough and decline to give a name.
