The board's pocket accepts a public correction card, while the side box accepts a private request addressed to Nella. A person can use either route without announcing a household connection at the notice board. The pocket is checked at the end of each watch by two clerks; both write their initials even when it is empty, so an uncollected silence is distinguishable from a box nobody opened.

The review date marks when the page should be checked, not a deadline for a witness to speak. If nobody responds, the account remains unchanged and is not marked confirmed.

entries.title: After Posting the Account
entries.body:
Silas returns to the board after its first day in public. A passerby has left no name, only a request to keep the line that says the lower road could not be seen. Silas leaves the request attached without treating it as a new testimony. The public route has made his action visible and kept the unknown part open.

Supplemental arrow archive note — an unsigned request is not testimony

The paper left by the passerby asks to preserve the blind-road sentence and contains no description of an event. Silas does not attach it to the evidence column. He logs it as an anonymous request about the notice's wording and keeps the request with the board maintenance record. The public copy remains unchanged except for the note that a wording request was received.

Silas had expected a signed reply to make the account feel complete. Instead, the first response reminds him that people may want the record to stay narrow without adding their names to it. The page now has a visible route for further corrections, but no invented witness.

entries.title: Review Belongs to the Family
entries.body:
Nella requests a private copy for her aunt and sets the limits herself. She does not speak for every household on the road, and the copy does not ask her to validate the arrow's effect. The receipt records who may open the case and how the family can return or correct the page later.

Supplemental arrow archive note — the family sets the table

Nella asks for one copy for her aunt and another for the archive, with different access rules. The aunt's copy includes Silas's admission and the field method; the archive copy keeps the sealed packet's access history. Nella does not request a copy for every household on the road and is not asked to explain that limit.

Before the packet is closed, Rowan reads the return instructions aloud and Nella corrects the contact route. She may ask for another review or return the page without writing a response. The receipt names the permitted holder and the copy number, not the contents of a private conversation.

entries.title: A Seal That Shows Its Own Opening
entries.body:
The case uses a paper hinge and a wax mark split across its flap. A named holder can open it, and the split mark will show whether it was resealed. The design is not a lock against every hand. Its purpose is to make access visible and give the family a way to notice handling, not to claim perfect secrecy.

Supplemental arrow archive note — visible handling has limits

The split wax mark gives the family a way to notice a broken seal. It cannot identify every person who touched the case, and paper can be replaced. Nella asks for a second measure: each transfer is written on the sleeve, with the sender, receiver and date. If a mark is damaged in ordinary handling, the custodian adds an explanation instead of resealing the case in silence.

The archive describes the protection honestly. The case can show that an opening may have occurred and preserve a chain of recorded custody. It cannot guarantee that no one could ever open it.

entries.title: The Interval Travels with the Account
entries.body:
Silas refuses to separate his admission from the limits of his view. The copy carries his full account, the field method and a clear gap for what neither his memory nor the surviving map can establish. The family may read it, return it or keep it private without adding a conclusion.

Supplemental arrow archive note — privacy does not cut away context

The family copy keeps the order reference and Silas's signed account together so his admission cannot be detached from the limit on his view. It also contains the map index, which shows the blind interval without exposing unrelated household records. Nella may return the page with a question attached; she is not required to keep a copy simply because it was offered.

The access card records whether the packet left the desk and returned. It does not report what anyone thought after reading it. The family may keep its response outside the archive, where an official need not turn private grief into a catalog entry.

entries.title: The Source Is Named Separately
entries.body:
Ruth writes the dispatch's archive location and records her own concealment in a separate attachment. The family copy can be checked against the original if they request it. Ruth leaves household names out because the order did not contain a reliable list of who reached the road.

Supplemental arrow archive note — the source can be checked

Ruth includes a location code for the original dispatch and signs a separate account of how she withheld a copy. The family's custodian can ask to compare the packet's reference with the original under supervised access. No household names are written on the request card; the archive needs the code and the permitted holder, not a public explanation for wanting to verify the source.

If the dispatch differs from Ruth's description, the copy can receive a dated correction. The family may choose whether that correction travels with the private account. Ruth's note still does not identify who saw the signal or what happened at the bend.

entries.title: Method Outside, Copy Inside
entries.body:
The public notice shows the line-of-sight procedure, the target positions and the limits of the daylight test. It contains no facsimile of Silas's family copy. A small line explains how relatives may request access through Nella. Public readers get the method; the family retains control over the named account.

Supplemental arrow archive note — two routes can share one method

The public method sheet contains the numbered positions, present-day readings and instructions for requesting another survey. It does not reveal the aunt's name or duplicate her copy. A private holder can compare the method with the account at home, while any craftsperson can repeat the daylight setup in the field.

Nella approves this split because it lets others check the measurement without turning access to Silas's named statement into a public condition. The index explains that the method is independent of the private packet. A public result may be corrected by a new measurement; it cannot be used to infer that the family approved the account.

entries.title: A Private Review with a Narrow Receipt
entries.body:
Nella records that the named holder opened the case and requested the position map. The receipt stores neither her aunt's reaction nor a public summary of it. A later request can add a family-approved correction, but the family is not required to provide one for the archive to accept their review.

Supplemental arrow archive note — the receipt records the handoff

The narrow receipt has four fields: copy number, named holder, handoff date and return option. It contains no box for a family member's reaction. Nella asks to have the inspection witnessed by a clerk from another desk, so a relative does not have to describe the visit to Silas. The clerk confirms the handoff, then leaves before the reading begins.

If the holder wants to correct the account, the receipt points to the return channel. If they want to keep their response private, the empty comment field stays empty. Review is an opportunity, not a demand for testimony.

entries.title: Accountability Does Not Depend on an Audience
entries.body:
Silas signs the family copy before it is sealed. He writes the same admission as in the public route and the same limit on what he could see. Choosing privacy changes who receives the page, not whether he accepts his action.

Supplemental arrow archive note — the same admission under either policy

Silas signs before the copy is placed in the case and asks the custodian to read the page number back to him. He compares it with the public method index to catch a mismatch, then initials the custody line. These small checks establish which page he approved; they do not ask the family to certify the truth of his memory.

He writes one sentence on the inside flap: “My choice is mine; the result is not mine to invent.” Nella leaves it in the packet because it describes the boundary of the account without requiring her to agree with the statement.

entries.title: The First Seal and Its Return Path
entries.body:
The seal record notes the split mark, the family holder and the route back through Nella. It does not call the case inaccessible forever. If the family asks to reopen it, another receipt can record that visit and keep the older seal entry intact.

Supplemental arrow archive note — reopening adds a page

If the family returns the case, the custodian breaks the seal in front of the named holder and records the split mark. A new seal receives a new number; the old entry remains in the ledger. The archive never scrapes wax away and pretends the first opening did not occur. The holder can take the packet again, leave it with the desk or ask for an updated copy.

This route preserves choices over time. A later relative may be granted access only if the family changes the instruction. The first holder's permission does not automatically become permission for every person with the same surname.

entries.title: After the Case Is Filed
entries.body:
Silas checks that the public method notice can be repeated and the family copy remains under Nella's agreed access rule. He admits that he once mistook a signal for a command with a single meaning. The sealed route keeps a family's answer private while still leaving a path for a future witness to correct the record.

Supplemental arrow archive note — a quiet route can still be accountable

The public method notice receives its regular check, and the case sleeve receives a separate custody entry. Silas does not inspect the family's private copy. He asks Nella whether the published method still avoids naming the holder; she confirms only that boundary and gives no report of her aunt's response.

The filing is complete as a procedure, not as an explanation of the old night. Silas accepts that accountability may be read by a small number of people and still be real. The archive will keep the route open if the family later changes who may see the account.

entries.title: Two Daylight Conditions
entries.body:
On a lower-wind morning, Rowan repeats the sightline from the same notch. The far marker stays visible slightly longer, but dust and cloud differ from the first trial. Both entries remain in the record with their conditions. A second measurement narrows a question about present visibility; it does not reconstruct the weather from the old account.

Supplemental arrow archive note — compare conditions before values

The two daylight sheets are laid side by side with their weather cards. Wind speed differs by one ribbon-width, the far marker is damp on the second visit and the observer wore a thicker coat that changed the recorded shoulder height. The team circles these differences before comparing the final visible interval. A larger number would mean little if readers could not see which conditions changed.

Rowan keeps both trials. They show that a present view can vary within a named setup, not that either view recreates an earlier season. A third visit can add a new condition card, never erase the first two.

entries.title: A Doorway for Later Accounts
entries.body:
Nella agrees to a return slip for future witnesses. They may request a private conversation, provide a location or submit an account in their own words. The slip does not name a likely witness and does not presume that anyone will come forward. It simply keeps the archive open to another source.

Supplemental arrow archive note — another account begins on its own terms

The return slip offers three ways to respond: ask for a private meeting, submit a written account or request a new survey. It does not contain a box marked “agree” or “disagree.” A witness can name a place without explaining a family relationship, and can ask for the note to be held while its use is discussed.

Nella chooses the slip's wording but not a likely future witness. She refuses to set a date by which someone must come forward. The archive can remain ready without treating the empty box as evidence that everyone has spoken.

entries.title: Known Variation on the Practice Target
entries.body:
Silas makes a second practice shot under the recorded morning conditions. It lands beside the first, not on top of it. The spread is measured, and neither mark is used to back-calculate the old groove. Known variation makes the current experiment more useful while reminding the team how little a single impact can tell them.

Supplemental arrow archive note — spread is part of the comparison

The second shaft is checked against the bow and target before it is released. It lands beside the first mark, and Rowan measures from the center of each cut rather than from the edge that looks cleanest. Tomas records the difference as a range for this bow and setup. If another craftsperson repeats the exercise, their values will be entered on a new sheet.

The pair of marks shows ordinary variation in a known practice. Neither mark is matched to the old groove, because the old shaft, bow and weather are missing. The experiment helps explain uncertainty; it does not turn uncertainty into a calculable answer.

entries.title: The Second Reed Bundle
entries.body:
The second harvest has a different bend after an overnight salt mist. Rowan records the date, plot and soil dampness before putting it beside, not over, the first bundle. Samples that differ across seasons are useful only if their origin stays attached. The next person can compare the change without mistaking it for a correction to the old measurement.

Supplemental arrow archive note — a second season is not a replacement

The overnight salt mist curls one reed bundle toward the coast. Rowan records moisture in the soil and the time of harvest; Tomas labels the cut height so the next bundle can be taken at a similar point. The two sets are stored in separate paper sleeves with their season tags facing outward.

Silas asks whether the newer bundle is closer to the old shaft he remembers. No surviving material can answer that comparison, so the note declines to rank them. A new sample can teach the team how local plants vary across weather. It cannot become an unmarked substitute for lost evidence.

entries.title: A Correction Can Arrive Without a Verdict
entries.body:
The return slip offers a public correction pocket and a private request through Nella. It accepts observations, locations and account corrections without asking for a verdict. The chosen policy changes who handles a copy, but both versions preserve authorship and dates. The archive can receive new evidence without promising that it will erase the uncertainty.

Supplemental arrow archive note — new evidence gets a date and an owner

The correction form asks for the source, the part of the record it concerns and permission for the requested copy. It does not ask the submitter to decide whether the arrow caused a loss. A location sketch can be shared without a name if the witness chooses that option; a first-person account can stay with its author until they approve a wider copy.

Both the board and the private route keep the earlier page legible. If a new fact changes the interpretation, the archive can explain the change and preserve the older wording. Evidence should alter the record through a visible addition, not an anonymous rewrite.

entries.title: A Record That Does Not Borrow Another Voice
entries.body:
Silas's final entry names his action, the order he received, the limits of his view and the people whose accounts remain their own. One branch posts his statement with a correction pocket; the other keeps the named copy under family review while publishing the method. Both leave the missing interval intact and provide a route for future evidence to arrive without being pre-written.

Supplemental arrow archive note — what Silas can leave for the next reader

Silas adds an inventory of what the archive holds: his dated account, Ruth's dispatch reference, Rowan's present-day surveys and the record of Nella's chosen boundary. It lists no recovered arrow and no statement from a traveler who saw the signal. That absence is not a puzzle the page promises to solve later; it is the limit of this file today.

The next custodian can open a place for new evidence without borrowing Nella's voice, guessing at a household's route or deleting Silas's admission. The folder's last line gives the return address and review procedure. It does not write a verdict for whoever comes next.

entries.title: A Memory Is Not the Whole Beginning
entries.body:
After the report on the ninety-ninth cycle, The First Warden asks to revisit the first oath. He remembers making a promise in a room beneath the lake, but no surviving witness list proves who else heard it. The archive later used his account as a starting point for its chronology. He wants to keep the memory while making its limits visible, so it cannot quietly become a forecast for every generation.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — what a witness can still say

When Lyra asks whether he heard the promise alone, the Warden says he remembers voices around him but cannot separate them now. He will not turn that impression into a witness list. The room beneath the lake has been repaired, flooded and copied into maps across many lifetimes; each change gives memory a new frame to borrow. He can keep the feeling of making a promise while admitting he cannot count who stood nearby.

His request is not to weaken the archive. It is to stop a later reader from treating his survival as proof that he remembers every detail. Lyra writes the limit beside the account, not above it, so the memory remains his own and the missing names remain missing.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the man behind the witness

After the interview, the Warden waits beside the open doorway while Rowan returns the transcript to its sleeve. He asks what Rowan would have written if no one had called him a witness first. Rowan says he probably would have described a tired man refusing to guess. The Warden laughs once, then asks Lyra to preserve that answer as Rowan's impression, not as a new title for him.

He wants visitors to meet him before they decide what his age, memory or office should prove. Lyra adds a small note to the archive index: questions are welcome, but the Warden may end an interview without giving a reason. The invitation belongs to him; the archive cannot make him available on every visit.

entries.title: Wear without a Date
entries.body:
The lowest rim is polished along a narrow arc. The smooth surface may come from repeated handling, vibration or a repair made after the oath. Rowan records its width and position but does not assign the mark to the first night. The bell remains useful as a physical object; the date in the archive stays uncertain until another dated source can be found.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a polished edge holds repeated contact

Tomas checks the bell rim with a cloth and finds no loose scale at the polished arc. He does not scrape the surface to look for an earlier layer. Rowan measures from the same notch on three visits, using the bell's current mounting rather than a drawing whose date is uncertain. The values describe the object now and can be compared if the mounting changes again.

The Warden says the rim was already smooth the last time he remembers the room clearly, but he cannot place that memory before or after the first promise. Lyra records his statement as a recollection, not a date for the metal. The bell's wear and the Warden's memory remain neighboring sources with separate limits.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — a bell does not keep the names of listeners

Lyra taps the bell once with a felt-covered mallet and asks the Warden which part of the sound he remembers. He says he remembers people becoming quiet before the strike, though he cannot tell whether the hush came from this room or from a later telling. Lyra puts the memory in his interview and leaves the bell's present tone on the measurement card.

When Rowan asks whether he wants the mallet placed at the old height, the Warden declines. He would rather hear today's test from where he stands now. The three of them listen without trying to recreate the past. Lyra writes that no person present spoke for the others who may once have gathered around the bell.

entries.title: A First Hand and Many Copies
entries.body:
Lyra finds the Warden's first account beneath three later index sheets. The oldest ink is faded, but its authorship mark remains. A later clerk added a heading that calls the account the beginning of every cycle. That heading is not in the Warden's hand. Lyra proposes preserving both layers with dates, rather than erasing the heading or treating it as a fact from the first night.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the hand beneath the heading

Lyra lays the oldest surviving leaf on a dark support so the faded strokes show without adding chalk. She traces the authorship mark on a transparent overlay, then lifts the three index sheets one at a time. The later heading appears only on the top sheet. Its placement made it look like part of the account when the archive was read from the shelf.

The new catalogue entry describes the physical order of the papers and the order of their copying. It does not claim to know why the clerk chose that heading. Lyra says the title helped later generations remember the promise, but it also gave them a sentence the Warden never wrote. Both consequences belong in the record.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Lyra names the work she inherited

Lyra shows Rowan how many times she has copied the Warden's page. The count is low enough to fit on one strip of paper, yet each copy changed the route by which a reader encountered the story. She used to feel proud when a title helped visitors remember the account. Seeing the attached heading beside the speaker's own sentence makes her wonder which version she taught first.

She does not ask the Warden to absolve her. He says the copies are part of the archive now, including the one she made before she understood the seam. Lyra records her responsibility in her own name. The Warden's memory stays his; the copy history belongs to the people who handled it.

entries.title: One Leaf from the Present Garden
entries.body:
The choir garden grows a new Echo Kelp leaf along its eastern bed. Rowan notes its depth and the date of harvest before bringing it to Lyra. The leaf carries a short vibration while wet and goes quiet as it dries. It is a sample of the present water and plant, not a preserved piece of the first oath.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — living samples change while they teach

The harvested leaf is placed in a shallow tray lined with damp cloth. Lyra records its length, water depth and time before Rowan carries it through the test tone. Its edge curls as it dries, changing how long the vibration seems to linger. A second observer hears the leaf after a short pause and writes a shorter duration.

The sample is returned to the present garden ledger after the trial rather than kept as an imitation of an ancient relic. Its value is that another gardener can grow a leaf and repeat the observation. It cannot retain the first oath's sound, and neither a strong vibration nor a quiet one can confirm which words were spoken in that room.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — tending something that will outlive the visit

Rowan ties a loose Echo Kelp frond back to its support after the tone test. The Warden watches him work and asks whether the garden bed belongs to the Choir or to the people who tend it. Lyra says the bed is maintained by the current gardeners, and its schedule can change when they need it to. She cannot say who first put kelp in the water.

The Warden likes that answer. He has spent too long inside a record that keeps returning to its beginning. A living bed asks for a next day without requiring anyone to repeat an old promise. Rowan leaves the garden card with a blank date for the next gardener to choose.

entries.title: A Whisper Koi and Its Water
entries.body:
Rowan catches a Whisper Koi where the archive's listening channel meets the pool. Lyra records the location, bait and catch time while the sample remains wet. The fish reacts to the current water and nearby activity. Its response cannot identify the source of a sound from the first oath, but it gives the team a repeatable present-day observation.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a catch is also a water record

Rowan writes the pool's depth against the stone step and records the sluice state before wetting the scale. Lyra watches from the channel entrance, where moving water adds a faint sound not heard at the bank. The two notes are kept together because the sample's response depends on the place in which it is observed, not just on the fish.

The Warden remembers a second note after his promise. He does not ask the team to reproduce that memory with a fish or a test tone. A present catch can show how living material responds to today's water and nearby movement. The old phrase remains attached to its speaker and is not presented as a recovered recording.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — a fish gives the crew something ordinary to share

After the sample is filed, Rowan and Lyra cook the catch at the small shore brazier. The Warden sits with them but does not join their discussion of the old phrase. He asks Rowan how the fish was prepared and whether the current had been kind to the line. Rowan explains that the catch took longer than expected because he had to move away from the bell's reflection.

Lyra writes nothing from their meal in the oath folio. It is not evidence, and the Warden asked for an evening without questions. She keeps the conversation in her own memory instead. The record needs room for him to be a guest at a table, not a source being harvested for another answer.

entries.title: A Mote from the Lower Passage
entries.body:
A Choir Merrow has nested beside the lower listening passage and gathered bright fragments into its bed. Rowan clears the path while the Warden waits above. The recovered Choir Mote came from the creature's nest, not from a person or an oath recording. Lyra can use it to compare the hall's current resonance without playing a preserved voice.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the recovered mote came from a nest

After the Choir Merrow leaves the lower passage, Rowan photographs the nest before moving any bright fragments. Tomas collects the Choir Mote from loose material nearest the entrance and labels the exact spot. Lyra confirms that none of the preserved folio leaves were disturbed during the encounter. The Mote is a resource from the creature's present shelter, not an object that came from the first oath.

The team carries it to the anvil in a closed pouch and records when it is used in the resonance rig. The distinction matters because the lower passage contains old stone, current water and newly gathered monster material side by side. Their proximity does not make them parts of one historical event.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the passage was dangerous before it was a page

The Warden sees the pouch holding the Choir Mote and moves his chair farther from it. He does not call the creature a guardian or a punishment. He remembers that the lower passage was unsafe in one of his visits, but cannot tell whether the same nests were there. Rowan asks whether the old account mentioned the threat. The Warden says it mentioned leaving before the lamps failed.

Lyra adds the memory to his interview log, then walks Rowan through the path they cleared. She checks each marked exit and leaves the pouch in the materials chest. They do not carry the Mote into the hearing room. A safe route for today's crew and an account of an earlier journey are separate records.

entries.title: A Weight for a Repeatable Position
entries.body:
Lyra and Tomas shape the Echo Kelp backing around a measured metal weight. A Whisper Koi scale marks the shallow side, and a Choir Mote helps the small edge catch the lamp. The item fixes the rig at a known depth without recording or storing any voice. If the hall's response changes, the same position can be restored and measured again.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the rig has no place to store a voice

Tomas adds a plain stop to the weight so Rowan can lower it to the same marked depth without relying on a spoken count. Lyra tests the rig with an empty backing before the Echo Kelp strip is attached. Its small lamp edge shows where the instrument sits, but the device has no reed, horn or memory plate capable of keeping a voice.

The Warden asks that the inventory say this plainly. He does not want a later keeper to describe the charm as a key to his memory. It is a positioning tool for repeatable measurements. If the hall answers differently next season, the team can compare the current response without playing or extracting any remembered words.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Rowan is allowed to change the instrument

Tomas Reed checks the Listening Weight before the next session. Rowan asks to move its handle so it can be used from the lower step without leaning over the pool. Tomas agrees to draw a second grip and label it as a later alteration. The first version stays in the case rather than being treated as a failed design.

The Warden approves of the change because it lets the next listener choose a safer position. Lyra notes that he did not approve the historical account or the phrase attached to it; he approved a tool for present use. Rowan signs for the modification. The instrument can develop as long as its records show which measurements came from which form.

entries.title: Three Lines, Two Repairs
entries.body:
Three horizontal marks remain on the stone below the bell. Two repairs cross the same surface, and no dated plan shows whether the marks came before or after them. Rowan measures the distance between the grooves and records the repairs as visible interruptions. The spacing may help compare a later diagram, but it does not establish the order in which the first oath or any repair occurred.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — repairs interrupt the pattern

Rowan overlays a transparent grid on the three stone marks and draws the two repairs as bands that cover their edges. The distances between visible grooves can be measured, but the covered portions cannot be reconstructed from symmetry alone. Tomas suggests extending the lines across the repair to make a cleaner diagram; Lyra declines and keeps the break visible.

The Warden recognizes one mark from a later visit but is unsure which repair was present then. His statement is dated to the current interview, not placed into the gap between the marks. The archive can preserve what he recognizes without allowing that recognition to date the stone.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — a broken line can remain readable

Rowan catches himself smoothing the copy where the repair bands interrupt the stone marks. He was trying to make a diagram another cadet could read quickly. Lyra asks him to draw the interruption back in. The cleaner version would save a reader a moment and cost them the chance to see what could not be measured.

The Warden says the first time he saw the marks, he thought they pointed toward an answer. He no longer remembers which mark made him think so. He does remember being pleased when the map was simple. Rowan leaves that admission in the conversation record, separate from the drawing. The archive now shows both the urge to make a clean diagram and the choice to leave its limits visible.

entries.title: A Note from Two Standing Places
entries.body:
From the upper stair, the silent bell's test tone carries past the second landing. From the lower position, the same tone is masked by water moving through a side channel. The present-day difference depends on where Rowan stands. The Warden remembers a note following him down the stairs but cannot date the memory against the repairs. Both positions are recorded.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — an echo changes with the listener

Rowan repeats the test tone from the upper step after Lyra moves the water gate by one notch. The sound carries farther, but the side channel masks its tail from the lower mark. When Rowan trades places with the Warden, both describe a different point at which the note becomes difficult to hear. The group records positions before comparing impressions.

The Warden's memory of following a note down the stairs remains his account, not a measurement made by the present crew. The experiment shows why a remembered echo may feel continuous to one person and interrupted to another. It does not identify the note's source or prove that everyone in the room heard it.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — they trade the place from which they listen

Lyra takes the upper stair while the Warden sits at the doorway. Rowan stands below and speaks the test phrase at a steady volume. The Warden hears it clearly; Lyra hears the water cover the last word. They trade places, and the result changes with the channel gate. No one chooses which listener was correct because each heard the room from a different position.

The Warden smiles when Rowan writes both accounts. For centuries, readers had asked him to describe the chamber as though his location never changed. This time the archive names where each person stood. Lyra asks whether he wants a third reading next season. He says anyone can do it, but he owes no one another demonstration.

entries.title: Two Sentences with Different Authors
entries.body:
The Warden remembers promising to keep the names entrusted to him. The archive heading expands this into a rule for every future generation. He does not remember making that broader promise. Lyra dates the heading to a later copy and keeps it visible as an editorial layer, so readers can see how a private commitment grew into a public doctrine.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the promise had a speaker

The Warden repeats the sentence slowly while Lyra writes down each clause. He remembers promising to keep the names entrusted to him; he does not remember pledging authority over the choices of people not yet born. The later heading joined those ideas by using “every generation” as its subject. The change seems small on a shelf label and large in the rule built around it.

Lyra preserves the two sentences in separate columns. The Warden does not ask her to destroy the expanded heading because generations have acted under it. He asks that readers see how the wording widened, and that his own promise not be used as consent supplied by future people.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the Warden resists becoming a lawgiver

Rowan asks what the Warden meant to protect when he made the first promise. The Warden answers with a person he can still picture carrying a wet cloak out of the bell room. He cannot remember the person's name, and he will not let Lyra place a guessed name beside the image. He says the promise felt narrow then: keep a particular confidence, for a particular person, in a particular room.

The later heading made it sound like he had accepted an office over generations. The Warden does not deny that he served the Choir afterward. He asks the archive to keep those two facts apart. Lyra lets the pause after his answer remain in the transcript, rather than replacing it with a summary of what she thinks he feels.

entries.title: Preserving an Editorial Layer
entries.body:
Lyra proposes a layered folio. The Warden's first-person memory remains in its original position. The later heading is copied on a separate leaf with the clerk's date and an editorial label. A reader can understand why generations used the heading while still seeing that it was added after the first account.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — layers can be read in both directions

Lyra makes a new folio where the oldest account appears first, followed by the later heading and a note about when the pages were joined. A reader can start with the memory and see how it became doctrine, or start with the doctrine and trace the phrase back to the narrower source. Neither path hides the other leaf.

The Warden asks Lyra to leave the editorial label large enough to see without a guide. She worries that the archive will look accusatory toward the copyist. He answers that recording a change is not the same as accusing its maker. The layer describes what the page did across time; motive remains outside the record unless another source supplies it.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Lyra hears her own voice in the copies

Lyra reads three versions of the heading aloud. The first sounds like a clerk giving a shelf instruction; the second sounds like a rule; the newest sounds like a warning. She had once believed the later versions were simply more polished. Now she hears her own careful tone making the sentence firmer every time she repeated it.

The Warden says he understands why people want a short line to remember. He asks Lyra to keep the versions side by side, including the one she prefers. She worries that naming her influence will make the archive look less reliable. Rowan says a reader can judge the work only if the work is visible. She adds her initials to the copy history and leaves the original untouched.

entries.title: Light and Water Height
entries.body:
Rowan fixes the non-vocal rig at the marked depth and tests the low note once with the waterline low and again after the sluice rises. The scale reflects different bands of light. The note remains a present-day test, and the conditions are written beside each reading. The result can help a later observer repeat the setup without borrowing the Warden's memory.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a difference belongs beside its conditions

At the lower waterline, the shallow mark on the scale catches a narrow reflection. After the sluice rises, the same mark appears broader, while the test tone weakens at the deeper rig setting. Rowan leaves the lamp at a fixed angle and writes down the gap between trials. Lyra checks that the second reading was not copied from the first card.

They retain both results even though neither supports a simple rule about the hall. A future listener can repeat the setup at either water height and compare new readings. The Warden's memory is not used as a baseline. This experiment shows how today's space responds to today's water, light and equipment.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — no lamp can illuminate an absent witness

The light test leaves a narrow band along the current waterline. Rowan moves the lamp, and the band follows it. Lyra asks whether the Warden remembers a lamp in the chamber during the promise. He remembers a warm glow but is uncertain whether it came from a lantern, a threshold or the later archive room. He asks that none of those sources be selected for him.

The team files three present-day sketches under their respective lamp positions. The Warden is invited to correct his interview later if a detail returns, but the page does not reserve a line for a confirmation he may never give. Light reveals the shape of the chamber today. It cannot illuminate the choice another person made centuries ago.

entries.title: The Heading Joined Later
entries.body:
The paper seam crosses the lower part of the later heading. The leaf was attached after the older account had already been bound. This establishes a sequence for the pages, not the motive of the copyist. Lyra records the hand and seam beside the words so future readers can tell the addition from the source.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the seam gives an order, not a reason

Lyra inspects the thread holes and finds that the lower heading leaf was stitched into the folio after the older account had already been bound. Rowan sketches the seam and marks the holes that do not line up. The repair dates the physical joining relative to the surviving binding, but the archive has no dated work order for the stitch.

The copyist's choice may have followed a shelf convention, a request from a later keeper or a reason now lost. Lyra records each as a possible question rather than filling the field with a likely answer. Readers can see when the heading entered the folio without being told why the person who added it did so.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the clerk who added a title is still unknown

Rowan asks if finding the clerk's name would settle the disagreement. The Warden says it might explain who joined the pages, but not whether the title helped, harmed or both. Lyra notes the question on a list of possible archive searches. She does not attach it to a suspected person or describe the unknown clerk as an enemy.

The Warden once wanted to know who made the change. Now he is more interested in letting readers see when it happened. He says a name could invite people to stop reading at the person's door. The copy history is a chain of choices, including choices made by later custodians. Rowan files the search request without promising it will find an answer.

entries.title: A Feeling Has No Calendar
entries.body:
The Warden remembers cold stone under his palm. He cannot say whether the season had changed or the water had dropped, and the current archive contains no instrument reading from that day. Rowan records the sensation as a personal memory with no date. It may help explain how the oath felt to him without becoming a measurement of the hall.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a feeling belongs in first person

The Warden remembers pressing his palm against cold stone, then pulling it away when another voice began to speak. He cannot say whether that voice came from the upper stair, the chamber entrance or someone beside him. He is certain the stone felt cold to him; he is not certain what the sensation meant or what season produced it.

Lyra keeps the description in his first-person account and declines to translate it into a water temperature. The room's present measurements cannot travel backward into a night with no instrument record. The memory helps a reader understand how the oath stayed with him without becoming evidence of a dated climate or a complete room plan.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — choosing what not to remember aloud

The Warden declines one of Lyra's questions and looks toward the water instead. She closes her notebook and asks whether he wants the room cleared. He asks her to stay, but not to resume the interview. Rowan waits at the doorway. They sit together until the sluice's next cycle can be heard from the lower passage.

Later, Lyra writes that the interview stopped at the Warden's request. She does not add the subject he declined to discuss. A refusal may be recorded as a boundary without turning the hidden content into another mystery for visitors to solve. When they meet again, he may choose a different question; he is not required to explain this one.

entries.title: Three Sources Kept Apart
entries.body:
The card has separate rows for the Warden's first-person memory, the copyist's later heading and the present-day acoustic test. Each row names its source and limitations. A blank date remains rather than borrowing a date from the next page. The card is now readable without making one kind of evidence stand in for another.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the card joins references, not conclusions

The Warden asks Lyra to read the three rows back in a different order. The present-day test remains intelligible when separated from the copyist's heading, and the memory remains readable when the measurement is covered. Rowan adds a source mark beside every date so the empty calendar field cannot borrow the date of the paper below it.

The card's purpose is to make the archive navigable for someone arriving centuries later. It does not reduce the three sources to a single score. If a new test disagrees with Rowan's readings, the card can accept a fourth row without changing the remembered sentence or the history of its heading.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — three cards, three chances to correct

Lyra lays the measurement card, the interview page and the copy-history leaf on separate cloths. Rowan sees that he had written “first” in the margin of the measurement card, although it was the first test of the day rather than the first test ever made. He circles the word and adds a correction without erasing it.

The Warden asks that every replacement card list which older card it supersedes. He wants future readers to follow the sequence, including false starts. A clean desk can make all three sources look like one account. The new tray keeps them nearby but physically separate, so the next person can compare them without blending authorship.

entries.title: A Policy for the First Account
entries.body:
The First Warden distinguishes ownership of his own memory from the archive's later use of it. A public folio can carry his first-person account, its date limits and the copyist's separate heading. A private folio can keep the memory available only through a review request while the method and copy history remain public. Both choices preserve the layers.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — access belongs to the speaker

The First Warden wants the archive to name its own use of his account. He agrees that the later heading should remain available for study, since it shaped the council's decisions, but he does not agree that his private memory must be public forever. Lyra writes both permissions on the policy card: the heading and copy history may be inspected; the first-person account follows the Warden's selected route.

The choice does not alter which pages came first or which words he remembers. It changes who can read the personal account now and how a future request may be made. The method for testing the hall remains open under either policy.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the Warden asks to be told what the policy changes

Lyra reads the access policy to the Warden before filing it. He pauses at the paragraph explaining who can request a copy. He asks whether the policy also tells a custodian how long a request may sit unanswered. It does not. Rowan adds a response date and a contact point, then reads both lines back to him.

The Warden says he does not need the archive to promise that every request will be granted. He needs it to promise that a request will not disappear into a drawer without a reply. Lyra adds a way to contest a refusal. The policy has a custodian, but it also names the person affected by that custodian's decision.

entries.title: A First-Person Opening
entries.body:
The Warden drafts an opening that names himself as the speaker and labels the cold room as a remembered sensation. He refuses to state a season or a crowd size. The page does not ask readers to accept his account as a universal beginning; it gives them one witness's memory with its edges intact.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — an account can begin without declaring a rule

The Warden removes the phrase “from the beginning” from his opening sentence. It implies that his memory contains a full chronology, when what he remembers most clearly is the promise and the cold surface beneath his hand. He leaves that detail in the first person and marks the date as undetermined.

Lyra asks whether the narrower opening will make readers think the archive is uncertain about everything. The Warden says the archive should be precise about the parts it can check and honest about the part it cannot. The public page gives one witness's account, with enough context to read it and no claim that every listener shared it.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — speaking in public is not the end of a choice

At the courtyard reading, the Warden asks Lyra to leave a clear space beside his statement so listeners can submit questions later. He speaks the account himself and waits through the first silence. One person asks where the copy was stored; another wants to know who may correct the heading. No one asks him to list every voice from the old room.

Lyra files the questions without attributing them until the listeners choose to sign. The Warden can answer a later question privately or decline it. Public access means people can hear him, not that they acquire a claim to all his memories. He leaves before the crowd has fully dispersed, and the archive notes the time without recording a reason.

entries.title: Public Folio Layout
entries.body:
The public folio places the Warden's name above his words, a small label beside the undated memory and a separate note for the later heading. The layout makes the distinction readable without verbal assistance. A correction can be added beneath either layer with a date and author, leaving both earlier pages untouched.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the labels need no interpreter

Rowan moves the copy-history label below the account, where a reader can see that it belongs to another page. The Warden's name appears beside the first-person text; the copyist's field remains open pending a stronger identification. A reader should not need Lyra standing nearby to know which words belong to which layer.

The correction margin is attached to the sheet it concerns. If someone dates the copyist later, the added date will not look like part of the Warden's memory. The folio's layout treats authorship as part of the evidence rather than a detail hidden in a catalogue screen.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — an index can invite a reader without directing them

Lyra removes a decorative arrow from the first public folio layout. It pointed toward the Warden's signature as if his name were the correct ending of every page. She replaces it with an index of sources: his memory, the later heading and the present measurement. A reader can begin with any of them.

Rowan asks whether people will understand the folio without a guide. Lyra says they can ask for one, but a guide must identify when it is explaining and when it is interpreting. She adds a note beside the index asking readers to compare dates before drawing conclusions. The public version is complete enough to navigate and open enough to question.

entries.title: A Method Anyone May Repeat
entries.body:
The public method lists the bell location, weight depth, waterline and distance between two standing marks. It contains no voice sample. A visitor can repeat the low-note test and record a new result without listening to a stored human account. Lyra marks the method as current, so future readers will not mistake it for a first-cycle record.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the low note is a chosen control

Lyra explains that the rig uses a low test tone because it can be produced at the same setting without retaining a human voice. The method card records the bell's position, weight depth, waterline, two listener marks and the length of each interval. Visitors are asked to note any change to the equipment rather than silently copying the prior setting.

The Warden approves the method but asks that no one call it a reconstruction. It is a present-day comparison chosen to protect the private quality of a memory. A repeatable procedure can test whether the hall's current response changes; it cannot recover a lost audience or authenticate a sentence from the first cycle.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — a visitor chooses not to repeat the test

During the demonstration, one visitor reads the method card and decides not to stand on the wet step. Rowan offers a dry position farther back. The visitor chooses to watch instead. Lyra had worried that the public method would be mistaken for an invitation to imitate every setup; she adds an optional observer role to the card.

The Warden appreciates the change. A method should explain how a reading was made, but it should not press a person to expose themselves to risk to prove they understand it. The visitor asks for a copy and leaves without touching the rig. Lyra writes down the request with permission, not the visitor's name. Participation remains available without becoming an obligation.

entries.title: A Review That Can Be Repeated
entries.body:
Lyra reads the folio once from the speaker label and once from the copy-history label. The two passes produce the same separation of sources. She leaves the copyist field open because a later clerk may identify the hand more precisely. Her review confirms legibility, not the truth of the Warden's memory.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a review can test the page's clarity

Lyra reads the public copy once as a visitor who knows the Warden and once as a visitor who has never met him. The headings let both readers distinguish the memory from the later title. She does not certify that the memory is factually complete; there is no independent witness list against which to check it.

Her review card names the sentences that may be quoted and the parts that remain undated. A later keeper can perform the same legibility check after a copy is moved or repaired. The review is repeatable because it asks a narrow question about the page, not because every reader must reach the same opinion.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Lyra lets someone else read the heading first

At the review, Lyra asks Rowan to read the heading before she does. He hears it as an instruction from a past custodian; she hears the sentence she has repeated for years. Their readings are not the same, though both can point to the same ink. The Warden listens and asks them to leave their interpretations signed beneath their names.

Lyra feels relief when Rowan gives a different reading. It means the archive can make room for disagreement without deciding which person has failed to understand. She adds a margin where future readers may describe their own first impression, then keeps the original heading unchanged.

entries.title: An Honest Blank in Public
entries.body:
The public margin holds one blank for a date and another for a second witness. Neither is prefilled from the later heading. The page explains that the Warden's account is undated and that future evidence may be attached. The blank remains usable without being mistaken for an accidental printing gap.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — blank fields need labels too

Rowan adds the words “date not preserved” above the first blank. Without that note, a visitor could assume a clerk forgot to finish the form. The second blank is marked “additional witness, if one is identified”; it does not ask the Warden to name someone from an uncertain memory.

The public sheet says who may attach new evidence and how the addition will be dated. It does not promise that a witness exists or will appear. The Warden asks Lyra to keep the margin visible rather than decorating it with a symbol of completion. An unfinished field is part of the archive's current state.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the empty margin is not a missing witness

The question box stays empty through the first week. Lyra resists the urge to ask people to write something simply so the space will look used. The Warden jokes that he has spent enough of his life being surrounded by empty spaces that acquire meaning without him. Rowan asks if the joke belongs in the account. The Warden says it may stay as his present remark.

Lyra writes “no questions submitted during this period” on the review sheet, not “no objection.” The difference protects a reader who walked past the board or never saw it. A blank margin can record the state of the page without claiming to know the thoughts of everyone who saw it.

entries.title: A Signature with a Boundary
entries.body:
The Warden signs beneath his first-person account and the limits he has stated. He leaves the copyist's heading on its own sheet. The signature authenticates that he gave this memory; it does not certify every interpretation made from it across later centuries.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — signing authenticates the present account

The Warden reads the boundary statement before signing it. He confirms that the page records his memory as he gave it today, including the missing date and unknown audience. Lyra witnesses the act and writes her own name on a separate line to show she handled the folio; her signature does not become a second witness to the first oath.

The later heading stays on its own sheet with its own author field. A reader can trace who signed what without treating the signatures as a vote on the account's meaning. If a correction is requested, it will be attached as a dated page rather than written over either signature.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the Warden reads his signature in his own voice

He traces the signature on the public copy with one finger and tells Lyra which letters he still writes quickly. Rowan notices that his hand is steadier than it was during the first interview. Lyra records the observation only after asking him. The signature dates this copy and identifies its speaker; it does not confirm the later heading above it.

The Warden asks the archivist to stop calling the mark his approval. She agrees and changes the label before the next reading. A signature can authorize one act while leaving surrounding pages open to challenge. The revised caption names the act he chose: he signed the first-person copy for public reading.

entries.title: A Public File with a Correction Path
entries.body:
The posted folio has a pocket for dated corrections and a visible note about its copying history. The original page remains readable if new information arrives. No one is required to provide a correction, and the archive does not announce that one is expected. The Warden's account is public while the space beyond it remains open.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — posting does not summon a response

The notice is placed where a visitor can read it without entering the private stack. It explains how to request a correction and where to repeat the present-day test. No announcement asks former listeners to come forward, and no name appears as a suspected witness. Lyra wants the invitation to remain available without turning it into a demand.

After the first review, the page stays unchanged because no new source has arrived. The archive does not add a mark reading “confirmed by silence.” The Warden accepts that public access can make a memory visible while leaving the room's other voices uncounted.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — a correction box needs someone who checks it

Rowan volunteers to bring the public questions to Lyra each evening. She asks him to keep the sealed letters in a separate tray and to record the time he delivered the others. The Warden points out that a correction path without an assigned receiver is only a box with good intentions.

They add an alternate contact for the days Rowan is away and a note that says when the next review will occur. Lyra will acknowledge a correction even if the archive cannot accept it. The public board can now receive a disagreement without making the person who wrote it argue alone against a locked shelf.

entries.title: After the Public Reading
entries.body:
The Warden reads the folio from the beginning without the later title standing above it. He says his memory now feels smaller, and less heavy. The public route preserves his account and the fact that it was once used as a general rule. It does not require him to approve that old expansion.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a smaller memory can be carried

The Warden reads his account without the later heading printed above it. He pauses at the line about keeping entrusted names and does not add a list. The old title once made the promise feel like a command he had renewed for every person who followed him. Read by itself, it is the promise he remembers making in one room.

He says the page feels lighter, not because he has forgotten the generations shaped by the heading, but because he no longer has to claim they all consented through him. Lyra records this reaction as his current response to the layout, not as a conclusion about what every generation believed.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — The Warden asks what the courtyard took from him

After the courtyard reading, Rowan asks whether the Warden feels exposed. He says he felt watched before the first word and tired by the last. He also heard people discuss the page with one another instead of asking him to settle every disagreement. Both parts matter. Lyra asks whether he wants the reading repeated. He says he will decide after resting.

She records his answer without turning it into a recommendation for future witnesses. A public account can create relief and fatigue at once. The next speaker will need their own terms, and the Warden's experience cannot serve as a template they must follow.

entries.title: A Requestable Private Folio
entries.body:
The Warden chooses a private folio for his first-person memory. A public record will still show that the folio exists, who holds it and how a review request can be made. The route protects access to the memory without hiding the later copy history or pretending the archive never used the heading.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the public record names the boundary

The public index states that a private folio exists, identifies its custodian and gives the route for requesting a review. It does not summarize the Warden's private wording. Lyra asks him to choose a review interval, and he leaves the date open until he wants to revisit it. The procedure permits a request; it does not schedule one on his behalf.

The later heading remains public with its attachment history. This lets readers study the archive's influence while the Warden controls the access to his own memory. The two facts are deliberately held together: privacy for the speaker does not erase the institution's record of what it did with his account.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — privacy is still a relationship with a reader

The Warden asks who can tell him what happens to a private request after it enters the registry. Lyra describes the numbered receipt and the person responsible for replying. He asks whether he can change the custodian if they stop answering. The rule allows a review request, so she shows him where to file one.

He chooses to keep the folio sealed for now. Lyra notes that this decision leaves a relationship in place: a speaker trusts a custodian to respect a boundary, and the custodian owes the speaker a response. The public index explains that relationship without repeating the private words.

entries.title: The Receipt Is Not an Endorsement
entries.body:
The access receipt names the Warden as the memory's speaker and Lyra as the archive holder. It lets the Warden ask for a private reading and records any later opening. It does not say that a reader agrees with his account or that the account stands for the other first-cycle voices.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the receipt names the action

Lyra writes the folio's copy number, the date it enters restricted custody and the person authorized to request an opening. She leaves the reaction field empty because no reading has occurred. When the Warden requests access later, that action receives another line rather than being described as approval of the account.

The receipt distinguishes speaker, holder and reader. Lyra may keep the case secure without becoming the author of its memory; the Warden may be its speaker without controlling the public copy history. Those roles can overlap in the archive but should never be collapsed into a single signature.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the holder brings the receipt to the speaker

Lyra carries the blank receipt to the Warden before she signs as custodian. They read every field together. He asks that the line for a witness remain optional, because requiring someone else to observe his choice would disclose the request itself. She changes the form and gives him a copy to keep.

The receipt is no longer proof only for the shelf. The speaker can use it to ask what happened to his file, while the archive can use its own copy to track custody. Rowan writes the form number, then leaves the witness line empty. No one present treats the missing signature as evidence that the Warden did not consent.

entries.title: The Holder's Duties
entries.body:
Lyra accepts the role of holder with two duties: record each access and honor the speaker's request to close the review path. She will not summarize the private memory into a public index. The archive can publish its method and the copying history while leaving the account itself with its speaker.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a custodian can refuse to paraphrase

Lyra declines to write a short public summary of the restricted account. Even a careful paraphrase could make the Warden's private words appear to speak for the first cycle. The index instead states only the folio's subject, its access rule and the date of the most recent custody check.

She keeps a sealed note explaining how to process a future request. It does not contain the memory itself. If Lyra is no longer the archivist, the next keeper can honor the Warden's rule without inheriting permission to retell his words.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Lyra must be willing to say she cannot tell the story

A visitor asks Lyra what the restricted folio contains. She says she cannot summarize it and explains how the visitor may ask for access if the Warden permits it. The visitor is disappointed and asks whether Lyra could at least tell them the conclusion. She repeats the same boundary without adding a hint.

Afterward, Rowan asks if that felt like protecting the Warden or protecting herself. Lyra admits it was both; she is afraid of becoming the person who decides which parts of his story are useful. She writes the exchange in her custodian journal, not in the public index. A boundary can be kept for the right reason and still be difficult to hold.

entries.title: Public Method, Private Memory
entries.body:
The public method sheet contains the bell's position, the rig depth, current water conditions and the reset steps. It includes no quotation from the Warden's folio. Anyone may repeat the acoustic test while the speaker retains control over the memory. The two records answer different questions and do not need to be published together.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — an open method does not expose a private page

The public method card includes a drawing of the current rig, the waterline mark and a reset instruction for the weight. It contains no quotation from the Warden, no image of the sealed folio and no clue that would let a visitor infer its sentences. A craftsman can repeat the test without requesting access to the memory.

Lyra tests the method using the same blank folio case that carries the equipment, to confirm that no audio is stored by the rig. The check is logged separately from the historical account. Publishing a procedure gives the public a way to inspect present conditions while leaving the speaker's access boundary intact.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Rowan explains the method without offering the memory

Rowan teaches a new keeper to set the Listening Weight and read the waterline. The keeper asks whether the Warden will attend the trial. Rowan says the method works without him and that the Warden decides for himself whether to join. They complete the setup with the chair empty.

The result is easier to compare because no one tries to match it to a particular phrase. Lyra adds the empty-chair condition to the public procedure so future teams do not infer that a private witness must be present. The test can be repeated with ordinary consent and an appropriate safety check; the sealed folio remains closed.

entries.title: A Separate Shelf for the Later Heading
entries.body:
Lyra places the copyist's heading on a public shelf with its attachment date and a note that the source memory remains private. Readers can study how the later title shaped the archive without seeing the Warden's full account. The shelf entry does not paraphrase the private page.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a later title can be studied without the memory

The public shelf holds a copy of the later heading with the paper seam drawn beside it. The label says that the underlying first-person memory is restricted and does not paraphrase its contents. Scholars may compare how the heading was copied across later indexes without seeing the private folio.

The Warden worries that keeping the heading public may preserve its influence. Lyra replies that removing it would hide the way a phrase shaped the archive. They leave the heading in view with its date and editorial status attached, so readers can study the expansion without mistaking it for his original sentence.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the copyist's mark does not unlock the private case

Rowan asks whether the later heading's visible seam should give researchers a path to the sealed folio. Lyra says the seam belongs to the public copying history. It can be studied without opening the Warden's words. She moves the case farther from the display table and puts a separate request form by the index.

The Warden reviews the new arrangement and agrees that visitors may inspect the seam drawing. He does not authorize anyone to read the private copy. The boundary is written on the access card, not left for Lyra to enforce alone in each conversation. A public clue is not permission to open a private page.

entries.title: A Rule Signed by Its Speaker
entries.body:
The Warden signs the access rule as speaker and holder of the memory. He can ask Lyra to open a review or close it again. The public history will retain the date of the change but not a copy of his words. This makes privacy reversible without making the archive's record of its own procedure disappear.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — access can change without erasing the change

The Warden signs the rule as speaker and asks Lyra to write the date in words as well as numbers. If he later closes the review path, the ledger will record the date of closure but will not copy or summarize the private memory. If he reopens it, the new authorization receives its own line.

The rule gives him a continuing choice about access. It does not give him the power to erase the archive's account of how later clerks used the heading. The signed page applies to his own words; the public copy history remains a separate record with its own author and custodian.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the Warden keeps the review date in his own calendar

Lyra offers to remind him when the review window arrives. The Warden says he would rather put the date on his own card, because a reminder from the archive might feel like pressure to reopen the folio. He asks Rowan to note where the request form can be found, then keeps the date card in his pocket.

The registrar records that a review is available and how to request it. The archive will not send an invitation unless the Warden asks for one. A right to reconsider belongs to him even when he does not exercise it on the timetable another person would prefer.

entries.title: A Seal That Records Its Own Change
entries.body:
A split wax mark crosses the paper and case. Lyra records who may request an opening and where the key is kept. The seal is not described as unbreakable. Its purpose is to make handling visible and create a receipt if the folio is opened or resealed.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the seal is an event marker

Lyra divides the wax mark across the folio flap and its case. She records the wax batch, the custodian and the person who may request an opening. If the mark is broken during routine inspection, the case is not resealed quietly; a witness signs a handling receipt and a new mark is given a new number.

The Warden asks that the archive avoid words such as “untouchable.” A seal can show that a particular handling event occurred, but it cannot prove that no one ever approached the case. The procedure makes custody visible without pretending that material controls are perfect.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — a damaged seal starts a conversation, not an accusation

One edge of the wax appears crushed after the case is moved. Lyra stops the inspection, calls Rowan to witness and opens the handling ledger before touching the flap. The Warden waits in the room. They photograph the mark, compare the case number and find no sign the folio itself was opened.

Lyra records the damaged edge and replaces the seal under a new number. She does not write that someone tried to break in; they cannot establish how the wax was crushed. The Warden thanks Rowan for staying, then asks them to finish the inspection. A visible irregularity requires a process everyone can see, not an invented culprit.

entries.title: After the Private Folio Is Filed
entries.body:
The Warden checks that the public method and later-heading history remain available while his account stays closed. The private route changes access, not the archive's claim that his account influenced later records. Lyra leaves the review path ready for a future request, and the Warden keeps the right to decide whether it opens.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the public layers remain available

The Warden checks that the shelf still contains the later heading, its seam drawing and the current test method. His own memory remains closed under the rule he selected. He does not ask Lyra to remove the public pages simply because he chose a private route for the first-person account.

This distinction matters to him: the archive may need to examine its own history even when a witness limits access to personal words. The case remains ready for a request, but Lyra will not announce that an opening is expected. Both the decision to read and the decision to leave the folio closed belong to the speaker.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the Warden spends the afternoon outside the archive

The group finishes reviewing the public index, then Rowan asks whether the Warden wants to remain in the chamber. He asks where the upper garden path leads and walks there with Lyra. They talk about the sound of ordinary rain on the terrace, which does not echo like water inside the Choir.

Lyra does not turn the outing into a test of his memory. The Warden returns before dusk and chooses to leave the folio sealed. His day included both the archive and a place where no one asked him to reconstruct it. She writes no attendance count in the restricted record.

entries.title: Two Present-Day Readings
entries.body:
Rowan repeats the test at a higher rig depth and writes down the new waterline. The low note weakens at a different point than it did at the first depth. Both results belong to the current hall. The Warden's memory remains in its own category whether the player selected a public or private folio.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — a new depth adds a new condition

The higher rig position places the weight nearer the water's surface and changes how quickly the low tone fades. Rowan measures from the marked stair rather than from the railing, which shifts slightly when the sluice fills. Lyra writes that shift beside the result so a future repeat can use the same reference.

The Warden listens from the doorway but does not report whether the new tone resembles his memory. The test card remains valid without his comparison. It records what the hall does now under a named setup, leaving the historical recollection where it belongs: in the account of one witness.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Rowan learns to stop a trial before an answer

The new test begins with the tone drifting after the first reading. Rowan checks the gate and finds that a worker has started the next water cycle. He asks to pause rather than finish the set under a changed condition. Tomas marks the partial result and stores the weight until the chamber settles again.

The Warden says stopping is a choice he wishes he had recognized earlier in life. He does not connect that regret to the exact day of the first oath. Lyra records his words as a present reflection. Rowan waits for the next cycle and starts a fresh card instead of trying to rescue the interrupted sequence.

entries.title: Two Leaves from Different Days
entries.body:
Lyra compares two Echo Kelp leaves gathered on different days. The newer leaf carries the test vibration for less time, perhaps because it is younger or because the water changed. The team records both dates and depths rather than replacing the first sample. The difference belongs to the plants and conditions, not to a human voice.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — two leaves have two growth histories

Lyra lays the samples on separate damp cloths and checks their harvest labels before comparing them. The older leaf came from the eastern bed after a week of still water; the newer one grew near the channel after the sluice was used. The short vibration may reflect age, water movement or a difference in the plant itself.

Rowan does not crush the leaves to force a stronger reading. Both are returned to their own storage sleeves after the observation. A future gardener can repeat the comparison with another pair. The result belongs to current plant growth and cannot establish how Echo Kelp behaved during the first oath.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the garden needs a keeper who can disagree

Lyra finds a new shoot bending toward a patch of light Rowan had not marked. She suggests moving the tray so the two samples receive the same conditions; the gardener says the difference is why they should leave them where they are. They talk through both options and decide to make a second pair rather than disturb the growing plant.

The Warden listens as they disagree without raising their voices. He asks who has the authority to decide where the new kelp goes. Lyra points to the people tending that bed. They add a second planting card and let the gardener choose the placement. The next measurement will depend on a decision openly made today.

entries.title: A Second Fish, a Different Waterline
entries.body:
The second fish comes from a pool whose waterline has risen. Rowan records the bait and level before Lyra places the sample beside the first. The catch helps compare present conditions. It cannot confirm the remembered delay in the first oath's second note, so the old phrase remains attributed to the Warden.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the waterline belongs beside the catch
