The first fish was caught below the lower step; the second was caught after the pool rose to the pale mark. Rowan uses the same bait and the same small tray, but Lyra records that the wind has changed. They compare how long the sample responds without claiming the two catches are identical trials.

The Warden remembers a delay between one note and another. He leaves that wording untouched while the team records the two present catches. A current sample can help the archive describe the pool's variation and improve a later test. It cannot verify that a remembered delay happened in the same way centuries ago.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the sample does not belong to the loudest account

Two fishers return from opposite sides of the pool with different descriptions of the current. One calls it still; the other says it pulled toward the gate. Rowan remembers fishing from the eastern step and admits he may have felt only the surface. Lyra asks them to mark their positions before they discuss the difference.

The Warden says a disagreement can tell the team where to look next, even when nobody is lying. They keep both statements attached to the locations and leave the shared conclusion blank. The sample's journey through the pool matters as much as its name on a page.

entries.title: Access Does Not Change Chronology
entries.body:
Lyra records the selected access policy but keeps the page order unchanged. The public route does not add certainty to the memory, and the private route does not make the later heading earlier. Both policies preserve the same source labels and leave the same date blank.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — an access policy cannot move a page in time

Lyra checks the folio index after the Warden selects his route. The public copy still names the heading's attachment date, and the restricted receipt still names the current holder. She confirms that neither page has been moved to make the memory appear older or newer than the evidence permits.

Her review has two checks: can a reader tell which words are the Warden's, and can a custodian tell who may open the private copy? It does not decide whether the memory is complete. Repeating the review after a policy change can verify the labels again without changing the order of the sources.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Lyra gives the copyist a right of reply

Lyra drafts a review of the later heading and leaves space for the unknown copyist or their family to submit another source. She does not expect a reply and will not send anyone to locate them. Rowan asks whether a right of reply matters when no one knows whom to contact. Lyra says the space also reminds the archive that its account could be incomplete.

The Warden approves the blank but not the review's conclusion. He wants his own response printed beside it, while the copyist's space remains open. The folio now shows two present voices and one unanswered place without claiming they carry equal evidence.

entries.title: A Heading with Consequences
entries.body:
The archive records that the later heading influenced how readers understood the Warden's first promise. The note does not erase that effect, but it keeps the heading's date and author separate from the original memory. A future reader can study both the words and the way they were used.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — consequences need a source too

Lyra interviews a later archivist who remembers being taught the heading as a universal rule. She records the lesson as that archivist's memory, with its own date, rather than using it to claim every generation learned the same thing. The heading's wide use can be documented through surviving copies; its effect on every listener cannot.

The note sits beside the copy history because readers need to understand that an editorial title may shape behavior. It does not blame one unknown copyist for the entire cycle. The Warden agrees that the archive should preserve both the heading's consequences and the limits of evidence about its author.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — people changed the heading for different reasons

Lyra brings a box of later indexes. One writer used the heading to shorten a catalogue; another placed it over a painting of the Warden; a third cited it as an instruction. Rowan notices that readers acted differently while looking at the same line. Lyra adds the uses to a chronology instead of assigning them to one shared motive.

The Warden watches the pages fill the table and asks whether the archive should keep every copy. Lyra says she will preserve the differences that explain how the heading traveled, and note when a copy is too damaged to read. One sentence did not have one effect. Its history is made of separate hands.

entries.title: A Walk Outside the Record
entries.body:
The Warden steps beyond the bell room for a short walk to the garden entrance. He does not call this a new oath or a permanent departure. The action is small and current: the immortal witness chooses to stand somewhere other than the archive. The next visit may find him back at the bell or farther down the passage.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — leaving the room is not leaving the promise

The Warden walks as far as the garden doorway and stops where the damp stone changes to dry tile. Rowan offers to accompany him back, but he asks for a moment alone. No quest log calls the walk a departure and no farewell is written on the folio. The record says only that he chose to stand beyond the bell chamber during this visit.

Lyra does not turn the gesture into a sign of what he will choose at the end of the story. The Warden can question the archive's old use of his promise without withdrawing every act of care that followed. For now, he has taken one short step outside a room that held him for centuries.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the Warden sets the pace of a walk

Rowan starts ahead and then slows when the Warden stops to look at the water reflected under the arch. The Warden asks to walk without a route marker for a while. Lyra folds the map and follows behind. They take a side path that ends at a closed garden gate; no quest opens there and no hidden inscription appears.

The Warden says he wanted to see a place without being expected to remember it for someone else. Rowan leaves his sword sheathed and waits while Lyra asks whether he wants company on the return. He accepts, then chooses the path back himself. The archive records the walk because he asked, not because every movement must become evidence.

entries.title: A Space Not Assigned in Advance
entries.body:
The marker contains no predicted name, title or answer. It has a line for a future listener's date and a blank area for the question they bring. It does not ask each generation to repeat the same test. The archive keeps the space available without suggesting that anyone is expected to use it.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — do not prewrite the listener's question

The marker's lower half has room for a date, the listener's chosen question and the source of any observation. Lyra rejects a preprinted line that said “the next cycle,” because it assumed someone would inherit the same assignment. The blank should be available to a person who chooses to use it, not presented as an appointment already made.

The Warden asks that the marker stay unsealed and replaceable. If a future listener brings a different question, the archive can attach a new card rather than bending the old one to fit. The available space promises no answer and imposes no duty.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — Rowan does not write a question for the next person

Rowan sits beside the blank card and tries several openings before he stops. He had planned to ask the next listener what they would do with the old promise. The Warden points out that the question already carries Rowan's expectations. Rowan turns the card over and leaves both sides blank.

Lyra files the card as an available space, not an unfinished assignment. The next visitor may use it, replace it or leave it untouched. For the first time, Rowan lets the archive end a page without telling another person where to begin.

entries.title: The First Oath Keeps Its Missing Measure
entries.body:
The Warden's first-person memory remains beside, not above, the later copy history and present-day tests. If chosen, it is either publicly readable under his name or held in a requestable private folio. Both routes preserve the undated interval, the right to correct the file and a place for a new listener. The archive records a beginning without dictating how every cycle must end.

Supplemental first-oath archive note — the first page cannot choose the last

Lyra's index closes with the current state of each source: a memory with no reliable date, a later heading with a visible attachment history, and several measurements from the hall as it stands today. The public route exposes the Warden's account under his name; the private route leaves it requestable under his rule. Neither arrangement declares which ending Rowan must choose.

The Warden asks the next reader to begin with the page they are permitted to read and to leave room for another source. His promise to keep entrusted names remains in the archive. The heading that expanded it remains there too. Their difference is now visible, so no one must inherit the same interpretation without seeing how it was made.

Second hearing —
Second hearing — the archive closes for an ordinary reason

At the end of the route, Lyra closes the reading room because the lamps need replacing. No final speech is scheduled. The Warden asks Rowan whether they can meet outside the Choir another day, with no transcript between them. Rowan says yes, then asks Lyra to keep that promise outside the catalogue unless the Warden changes his mind.

The archive records which pages remain available, which folio stays sealed and where a correction can be sent. It does not call the story finished. Lyra returns the key to its hook and leaves the visitor's chair pulled out for whoever chooses to come next.

entries.title: A Case Returned without a Roster
entries.body:
After Evelyn accepted the Outer-Wake report, a sealed instrument case arrived from the receiving desk. Jace recognizes the brass catches and the padded frame, but the index card that should link each sleeve to a surveyor is missing. Four long spaces remain inside. The first copy of his old report called them crew slots; a later copy shortened the phrase to crew. Neither wording proves who carried the instruments, whether the sleeves travelled together or whether every place was occupied during the final departure.

Jace asks Rowan to begin with the object itself. He is careful about the distinction because he has already seen how a plausible summary can become a fact after two or three rounds of copying. The case can be measured. Its hinges can be tested. The missing card can be recorded as missing. None of those observations supplies the absent names.

The case also brings Jace back to a choice he has avoided since writing his first report. He wants another person to check the instruments, but he does not want a new reader to mistake the empty sleeves for proof that their owners died, escaped, or reached a known refuge. He asks Rowan to help him make a record that admits the limit in its first paragraph. If the old expedition remains unresolved at the end, the new page must be allowed to say so plainly.

Supplemental station archive note — the case came back empty of names

Jace recognizes the brass corner guard and the shallow dent beside its latch. He cannot remember which surveyor carried the case on its final trip, and no cargo ledger names a keeper. The archive therefore records the person who returned it now, the desk that accepted it and the older origin as unknown. Jace adds his signature only to the present handoff.

He once thought the case should be displayed as proof that four people had left. Evelyn asks what connects an empty compartment to a person. Jace removes that sentence from the label and keeps the crossed-out draft with the revision slip. The case is evidence of a storage object and a gap in its paperwork; the gap remains open.

entries.title: Four Compartments, No Four Names
entries.body:
The returned case contains four padded sleeves, two sizes of retaining strap and a narrow channel where a paper index card could have been kept. The foam in the first sleeve is darkened at the edge; the third has a newer patch stitched with pale thread. Rowan notes both details and turns the case under the lamp to find a date stamp. The stamp is a maker's mark from a repair shop, not a survey date.

There are no initials in the label windows. One blank has a faint rectangle where a paper tag may once have rested. The rectangle could be the mark of a removed label, but the case has been handled by several archive keepers since it returned. Jace remembers the old report listing four instruments. He does not remember who had each one, and the report copy does not name a keeper beside the list.

The case is evidence of capacity: four tools could be carried in it at once. It is not a census of the people who travelled. The archive entry therefore lists the dimensions of the sleeves, the state of the straps and the repair marks, then leaves the owner column empty. This makes the case useful for a later physical comparison without turning an empty label into a missing-person conclusion.

Supplemental station archive note — measure cavities before assigning cargo

The four hollows differ in depth by a few finger-widths. Jace numbers them from left to right as the case currently rests, then turns it around and confirms that the numbering follows the hinge rather than the room. A small liner shadow appears in the second hollow, but there is no matching piece of packing in the returned inventory.

Rowan records each interior measurement twice. Neither the dimensions nor the count of cavities tells them how many instruments were stored there. The labels stay as “space one” through “space four,” with no names attached. A later conservator can add a packing sample if one is found, without making the sample a roster.

entries.title: A Living Fiber Is Not an Old Packing
entries.body:
A strand caught beneath the case hinge resembles Skyroot fiber, but its color has faded and its surface is flattened. Jace will not call it packing from the old expedition until Rowan has a living sample for comparison. The Outer-Wake bed can grow Skyroot again, so the team records the planting date, seed source and water depth. When the plant reaches harvest, they compare flexibility, split lines and the way each strand holds dust.

The live stem springs back after a shallow bend. The old fiber stays folded. That difference may result from age, dryness, pressure inside the case or a different material. The sample cannot tell the team which explanation is right. It gives them a repeatable comparison under one present-day condition. If a later keeper repeats the test with a different water depth, both outcomes can be kept rather than averaged into a single answer.

Jace admits that he once wrote 'Skyroot packing' in a margin without collecting a second sample. The phrase entered a copied inventory, where it lost the question mark he had pencilled beside it. Rowan records the earlier wording as an unverified label and keeps the new growth separate from the archived strand. The garden has supplied a reference, not a time machine. Nothing in the root identifies a person, proves how long the case travelled or tells the team what happened after the survey stopped.

Supplemental station archive note — new fiber can test a new fit

The Skyroot sample was grown in Greenwake after the case returned. Jace writes the seed source, watering interval, harvest day and drying conditions on the bag before cutting a test strip. The current fiber bends without cracking against the metal lip. That gives Evelyn a safe material for checking the case's present edge; it does not show what the original packing looked like.

The sample is stored in a separate sleeve marked “modern comparison.” If later growth produces a different texture, that result receives a new card. Jace wants future crews to be able to repeat the fit check without mistaking a living plant from this season for an artifact from the missing survey.

entries.title: The Pool's Present Noise
entries.body:
Celestial Pool sits beneath the receiver platform, where the water touches the archive foundation. A Farwake Carp caught there is not a witness to the expedition. It is a living sample from the pool as it exists now. Lyra asks Rowan to record the bait, catch time and visible waterline before moving the fish to the comparison basin. A note that only says 'quiet' cannot be repeated; a note with conditions gives another listener a chance to try the same setup.

The pool carries a low vibration when the wind comes through the west aperture. On the afternoon of the catch, the note grows rougher after a maintenance gate is opened. The fish turns toward the deeper wall, though nobody claims to know whether the sound, shadow or current caused the turn. Lyra keeps the observation beside the measurement instead of choosing one cause.

Jace's old report says the surveyors heard a low interval before the receiver went silent. It does not say that a fish made the sound or that the pool was at the same level. The current catch helps the team isolate one local condition. It cannot verify the old sound or identify the source of any message. The record's narrow claim is enough: a present-day observer can repeat the catch and listen again at a marked waterline.

Supplemental station archive note — the pool had a sound that day

Jace holds the Farwake Carp's scale beside the receiver housing only after Rowan records where and when it was caught. The sample's moisture changes the sound when it taps the case; a dry table gives a sharper knock than the damp bank. Evelyn asks them to log the surface beneath the receiver too, so the fish sample does not become an unexplained “lake frequency.”

The test documents an ordinary environmental variation around the station. It cannot identify a past signal or prove that the carp heard one. Jace adds a line for water level and wind because the same pool may sound different on another visit.

entries.title: The Wind Changed with the Listener
entries.body:
The mast has three sockets where a hand gauge can be fixed: ground level, the observation platform and the upper rail. Rowan reads each one within a minute, using the same instrument and noting the direction of the vane. The upper reading is stronger. A second pass after the sun drops is weaker at all three heights, but the gap between them remains. The instruments were not available to Jace's old team in exactly this arrangement, so the new card is a repeatable test of the archive, not a reconstruction of their night.

One copied report gives a single wind direction. Another gives a direction and the word 'violent.' Their dates are close but not identical, and neither copy says where the gauge was mounted. The three current readings show why height matters. A vane beside a wall can turn differently from one exposed above it; neither has to be false.

Rowan writes the mast position, height, time and instrument ID beside every number. He leaves the old report's column unchanged and adds a note that the mounting height is unknown. Jace wants the discrepancy visible because it affects how a receiver could have shifted, but he does not claim that wind caused the missing signal. The measurements can bound a new test. They cannot identify an old sender, determine who stood at the mast or fill the empty roster.

Supplemental station archive note — height changes the instrument reading

The ribbon is set at three heights beside the north window. It turns at the sill, rests against the middle peg and lifts above the roof edge; Jace repeats the sequence after Rowan moves to the other side of the post. Each observer stands on a chalk mark so the body does not block the airflow in a different way.

The sheet preserves the disagreements rather than averaging them. The wind reading describes this station, this hour and these positions. It does not fill the date column in the old survey ledger. Jace adds the observer's initials beside each height, since a later reader should know whose hands placed the ribbon.

entries.title: Sequence without a Calendar Date
entries.body:
The card holds four vertical marks in a sequence that may represent pauses in a test. A crease crosses the third mark, and darker ink extends the final interval. The marks can be ordered by where the pen overlaps the fold. No calendar date appears on the paper, and the storage envelope has a catalogue number written by a later clerk. The archive cannot infer the hour from the shape of the marks.

Jace used to place the card beside the night the survey receiver stopped sending. He believed the overlap suggested that the interval came from the same test. After reviewing the box, he says the card might belong to another calibration session; its edge was folded to fit a different sleeve. The sequence and the session are separate questions. The first has an answer from the ink and paper. The second remains open.

Rowan draws the marks at scale, photographs the crease in the field record and writes 'undated' where the old inventory left a blank. This is not an attempt to make uncertainty sound precise. The note explains exactly which part can be checked: a reader can compare the line order, fold and ink. A reader cannot use the card to place four people at the receiver, say when it failed or prove that the signal was sent from beyond the Veil.

Supplemental station archive note — order is not a calendar

The recovered notes show that one receiver check came before a change to the case lining, and that a second check came afterward. The page corners are missing, so Jace cannot assign either check to a season. Evelyn draws arrows only where a physical cross-reference supports the order; she leaves the date line blank.

Jace initially writes “winter test” in the margin because he remembers cold air at the station. He replaces it with “temperature not recorded” and attaches the first draft. A memory can suggest a question for the archive. It cannot make a lost date reappear. The sequence remains useful even while its calendar position is unknown.

entries.title: A Silent Receiver Can Still Be Misread
entries.body:
Evelyn opens the service panel and follows the receiver cable by hand. The first switch cuts power to the speaker, not to the signal relay. A second lead continues behind the wall, where a junction box connects the old line to the archive's maintenance network. Rowan disconnects it at the junction and places a dated seal across the open terminal. Only then do they run the passive comparison.

The receiver records three low intervals. The final one may be a vibration from the foundation; the instrument cannot separate it from the pool's movement without another sensor. The team notes the reading and resets the receiver. No outgoing message is prepared or sent. Evelyn asks Jace to write that sentence in the first page, because the word 'passive' can otherwise sound safer or more absolute than the wiring permits.

The survey's original diagram shows a receiver and a separate transmission mark, but the line between them is incomplete. The new test proves how the present archive can isolate one receiver. It does not prove that the old equipment used the same junction, that a signal came from another world or that no one altered the earlier setup. Those are questions for evidence that is not in this case.

Supplemental station archive note — silence has several possible causes

The receiver was disconnected from the archive relay when Rowan found it. During the bench check it produces no signal, but the battery contact is corroded and the antenna joint moves under light pressure. Jace lists those conditions before anyone calls the instrument silent. After Tomas cleans the contact, the unit still records no incoming transmission during the short observation window.

That result is a bounded test, not a proof that no signal ever arrived. The log names the duration, power state and antenna position. Jace asks that another technician repeat it with a calibrated source before comparing the device with an older account.

entries.title: Two Ledgers and One Unfinished Join
entries.body:
Evelyn places the equipment ledger beside the personnel sheet. One contains four fitted sleeves; the other has a blank field where a team list might have been copied. She refuses to write four names, four deaths or four departures into that gap. The ledgers answer different questions, and their matching shelf number may only mean that a clerk stored them together.

She reviews Rowan's three mast readings, the Farwake Carp sample and the receiver test. Each result has conditions that another person can repeat. The old report does not. Evelyn wants to add a method sheet that tells a future observer where to place the gauge, when to read the pool and how to disconnect the outgoing lead. A second reader could then dispute the results without needing to accept Jace's memory.

Jace says the careful procedure feels like a way to make the lost survey less important. Evelyn answers that a method is not a replacement for a person. It can preserve what they were trying to learn while leaving their identities and choices unclaimed. The team decides that the archive will keep the two ledgers side by side but not merge them. A later discovery may connect them; the current record has no authority to do so.

Supplemental station archive note — two ledgers use different clocks

Evelyn sets the field book beside the station clock ledger and circles the places where their readings can be compared. One clock ran slow during a cold night; the other was reset after maintenance without an entry for the correction. A timestamp written in the first book may therefore fall within a range when translated into the second.

Jace confirms which pages he signed, but he does not fill the uncovered intervals from memory. Evelyn adds a join table with source, correction and uncertainty for each conversion. The table makes the records easier to compare without making them one continuous timeline.

entries.title: The Sentence That Went Further than the Case
entries.body:
Jace's draft says, 'The four places were lost with the crew.' The sentence began as a note to himself, then appeared in a typed summary without its crossed-out ending. The case does not establish that the four spaces were occupied during the last test, and the personnel ledger does not show what happened to anyone who travelled. Jace has spent years treating the sentence as a confession that he failed to bring the team home. He now recognizes that the sentence claims more than he knows.

He does not erase the old copy. Rowan makes a correction slip that quotes the original wording, dates the review and identifies Jace as the person withdrawing its factual status. The revised note explains why the statement is unsupported and keeps it available for study as part of the archive's history. The error mattered: readers used it as a summary. Removing every trace would hide the way it changed the record.

Jace asks for a decision about the personal pages in the same box. The pages include his own field impressions and loose writing from an unknown hand. Some passages may be private, and no known author has given permission for publication. The measurement method can be public without those pages. The next choice will decide where each record belongs and who can review it. It will not decide whether the absent surveyors are dead, alive, lost or safely returned.

Supplemental station archive note — the sentence outran the measurements

The draft says the four empty compartments belonged to the people who never returned. Jace wants the sentence to express what he feared when he saw the case, but the case has no roster or baggage tags to support that claim. Evelyn underlines the verb “belonged” and asks him to name the object that proves ownership.

Jace changes the line to say that four spaces remain unassigned in the current inventory. The earlier wording stays on a dated draft page so a later editor can see why it was removed. The correction does not make his fear false as a feeling; it keeps that feeling from being used as evidence about four unknown people.

entries.title: The Policy before the Copy
entries.body:
The box contains a public method sheet, the equipment ledger and loose personal pages. The method describes instruments and settings. The loose pages contain impressions that may belong to Jace, another surveyor or a later keeper. No page states that its author wished to publish it. Jace asks Rowan to choose a storage policy rather than guess the writer's wishes.

One route publishes the measurements, correction history and empty-roster warning, while withholding the loose pages. The public reader can repeat the test and challenge the old summary without seeing words whose author and permission are unresolved. The other route places the personal pages in a requestable folio. The access receipt names Jace as custodian, gives him a correction and withdrawal process, and lets a family request a review without promising access automatically.

Neither policy adds names to the personnel ledger. Neither seals the public method. The choice is about the boundary between an instrument record and personal writing, not about whether the old expedition reached a safe destination. The archive will record who chose the policy and when, so a later custodian can reopen the decision if the missing authorship is established.

Supplemental station archive note — decide who may read before copying

Jace and Evelyn separate the method sheet, the equipment account and any personal recollection before they choose a release policy. The public route gives readers the calibration steps and the conditions needed to repeat them. The folio route carries the named recollections under a request rule. Both copies retain the same empty identity fields and correction path.

The archive records the policy choice after the case inventory is complete. It does not let a desire to publish override the people named in a private account. Jace signs his own section in either route; the choice governs its audience, not whether he accepts his earlier signature.

entries.title: Instructions Anyone May Correct
entries.body:
The public procedure begins with the receiver disconnected from the outgoing relay. It lists the wind mast heights, the time between readings, the visible waterline and the position where a listener stands. A reader can use the same instruments or write down why a replacement was needed. The page includes a correction box with space for date, source and the name of the person making a change.

Jace insists that the limitations be printed in the same type size as the instructions. A low interval in the present hall cannot identify the old signal. A wind reading from one mast cannot reconstruct weather at an unknown date. Four instrument sleeves do not prove four people. The method is still worth sharing because it tells another observer what evidence could improve the record.

Rowan tries to repeat the steps from the page without help. He finds the receiver switch, traces the outgoing lead and writes the same three mast heights. One instruction assumes a tool is stored in the blue drawer; the blue drawer has since been removed. Jace adds a note that the tool's name matters more than the drawer's color. A public procedure stays open to correction, and the first correction comes before the page is posted.

Supplemental station archive note — publish enough to repeat the setup

The open method card includes the window position, three ribbon heights, receiver power state, case measurements and the duration of the listening interval. It omits household messages and the names of anyone who has not agreed to be quoted. A second reader checks the diagram against the station before the card is posted.

At the bottom, an unprinted margin provides room for a corrected value. Anyone repeating the method can add the date and their equipment serial, then request a revision if the instructions are unclear. Jace wants the procedure to outlive his memory without pretending the method explains the old survey's missing roster.

entries.title: A Blank Field Kept in Public View
entries.body:
The public index lists the case, the four sleeves, the receiver test and the date the archive received the box. The personnel field remains blank, with a note explaining that no verified roster was found in the returned materials. The phrase does not imply that the sleeves were empty during the expedition, nor that their users disappeared. It tells the reader only what the archive has not identified.

Lyra attaches Jace's correction slip beside the older summary. She does not remove the sentence he wrote, because its history explains why the archive once treated the equipment count as a crew count. A small index tab directs readers from the old wording to the correction and then to the repeatable method. That arrangement makes the record less clean, but it also makes the process visible.

A visitor can now challenge the way the case was interpreted, submit a new document or request that an error be corrected. The public sheet does not contain personal pages from the box. Jace signs as the keeper of the correction, not as the person who can speak for the unknown writers. The record ends with a question for future evidence rather than a prediction about the absent surveyors.

Supplemental station archive note — a visible blank is a deliberate result

The public index has four ruled fields for former case users. Each remains blank and is labeled “not identified in the returned records.” The phrase is longer than a dash, but Jace prefers it because a dash might look like a printing error or an invitation to guess a name.

The index links to a correction channel that accepts a source document, date and permission to quote. It does not ask a visitor to submit a likely identity. The empty fields can change if checked evidence arrives; until then, the public page makes the limit visible instead of hiding it in a footnote.

entries.title: A Receipt with an Exit Path
entries.body:
Jace lists himself as custodian of the requestable folio. The receipt explains where a future request can be filed, who will review it and how the decision can be appealed. A request does not guarantee access. It begins a conversation about authorship, family interest and the safety of sharing a personal page. If the writer is identified, that person may ask for a correction or withdrawal.

The receipt also records the limits of the archive's authority. Jace cannot consent on behalf of the unknown writer, and Rowan cannot infer consent from the fact that the page was stored with survey equipment. If no author can be found, the method remains public while the personal text stays closed. A dated review may reopen the question when new evidence appears.

The document includes a visible opening mark on the folio, but it does not describe the case as unbreakable. Its purpose is to leave evidence of handling and require the custodian to record a change. Jace signs as a person accepting a duty, not as an owner of the words. The archive will be able to show who held the key, who asked for a review and whether the folio was opened, while continuing to admit that it cannot name every writer.

Supplemental station archive note — a receipt can have an exit path

The folio receipt identifies which copy left the archive, who may request its return and how a correction can be attached. It leaves the comment field empty unless the holder chooses to write something. Jace asks that each handoff record the copy number without repeating private names on the outer wrapper.

If the holder returns the page unread, the receipt records the handoff back, not a judgment about its contents. The family can ask for a replacement under a new rule later. A document can leave the archive without the archive claiming that its reader agreed with the account.

entries.title: What the Seal Protects and What It Cannot
entries.body:
The folio holds the loose personal pages and a copy of the access receipt. It does not hold the public method, equipment measurements or correction history. Evelyn checks the separation before the case is closed. A future reader can reproduce the receiver test without seeing a private sentence, and a family can ask the archive to review access without being promised an answer on someone else's behalf.

The seal is dated and split across the paper edge. If it is opened, the break will be visible and a new receipt must be added. The mark offers accountability, not physical protection from every hand. Jace keeps the key in the archive office and records which two staff members may witness a review. Neither witness can substitute their consent for the writer's.

Evelyn asks Rowan to read the public index once more. It says the folio exists, describes how a request may be made and does not quote its contents. The private route therefore leaves a public trail without exposing the words. The unknown hand stays unknown; the family has a path to ask; the method remains available to everyone. Those boundaries may change if the author is identified, so the seal is requestable rather than permanent.

Supplemental station archive note — the seal does not solve the inventory

The private folio contains Jace's signed recollection and a drawing of the case. It does not contain a roster because no verified roster was found. A restricted holder may inspect the material and request a correction, but access itself does not assign the four hollows to four people.

Evelyn keeps the calibration method outside the folio so the public can repeat a test without seeing personal pages. The folio's cover carries a copy number and review date, not a family name. Its seal protects access under the agreed rule; it cannot authenticate an unsupported sentence or make missing equipment records complete.

entries.title: Four Places Left for a Future Record
entries.body:
The route ends with the same four empty sleeves that opened it. Their shape is now measured, the repair marks are dated where possible, and the unknowns are written beside the claims they limit. Skyroot fiber has a present-day comparison. Farwake Carp has a catch record from Celestial Pool. The receiver has been tested after its outgoing lead was disconnected. None of those steps places a name in the personnel field.

Jace reads the filed version in both forms. If Rowan chose the public index, the method and correction history can be examined directly. If Rowan chose the requestable folio, the public method still stands beside an access receipt that gives personal pages a review path. In either route, Jace no longer asks the archive to turn the four sleeves into a count of people.

He says the correction has not repaired the survey or resolved its ending. It has changed what a reader is allowed to assume. A later letter, instrument log or verified family account could connect one of the sleeves to a person. Until such evidence exists, the archive leaves the spaces unassigned. Jace asks Rowan to keep the empty field visible at the next review. The record can be incomplete and still be more accurate than the finished sentence he once wrote.

Supplemental station archive note — leave the case usable to the next crew

Jace leaves a maintenance card beside the public method and a request route beside the private folio. The card says when to inspect the hinge, how to replace the Skyroot liner and where to enter a new receiver test. It also tells the next crew not to mark a space with a person's name unless a source can be checked and permission is clear.

The four compartments remain four spaces in a returned case. The signal source, the former users and the survey crew's final route are still unassigned. Jace signs the afterword as the person who prepared this index today, leaving future evidence room to arrive under its own date.

entries.title: A Forecast Meets Its First Supper
entries.body:
Ada pins the release forecast beside a list of meals expected at the Crownfall table. The two sheets use the same grain store but different units: one counts sacks issued, the other records bowls offered. At first the totals appear to match. Then Ada points to a blank column where the clerk was meant to note how many people were turned away, asked to return later, or chose not to give a household name. The page records none of these events. Captain Alden says a clean ledger is easier to defend than a complicated one. Ada answers that a clean total can still leave a person hungry. She asks Rowan to follow one serving shift, from the sealed store to the table, without turning a small sample into a promise about the whole settlement.

Supplemental table note — the first tray

The first tray came back with one heel of bread on it. No one could say whether it had been set aside for a late worker, carried from another room, or simply missed when the table was cleared. Ada wrote down where she found it and asked the kitchen to keep returned food separate until its condition could be checked. A surplus was not automatically safe to serve again.

The supper was quieter than the forecast meeting. People asked where the beans came from, whether the portion would change tomorrow, and who had decided that the table closed at dusk. No answer belonged in the grain estimate. Rowan records those questions beside the serving sheet because a meal can be counted without its recipients becoming a survey. The first shift establishes that the proposed table can open. It says nothing yet about who could reach it, who chose not to, or whether the same amount would remain available after a harder day.

entries.title: The Bowls at the Crownfall Table
entries.body:
The table keeps two bowls for measuring a portion. One is wider and shallow; the other is narrower, with a chip under its base. Three scratched marks may indicate a serving size, a repair count, or a child's attempt to keep a place. The kitchen has no key that explains them. Rowan measures the bowls with the same grain scoop used for the store release and photographs the scratches before anyone cleans them. The two vessels are tools in a service routine, not proof of who was fed. Ada asks to list capacity and condition separately from attendance, so a future worker can repeat the comparison without inventing a roster from the marks.

Supplemental table note — a bowl with a name beneath it

The chipped bowl has a name scratched under its foot, too faint to read without turning it in the light. Ada does not rub the mark clean to make a better measurement. The kitchen keeper says the bowl was used by several generations of the same household, then lent to the table when the storehouse lost its plain dishes. Neither account identifies the person who made the capacity marks.

The bowl's history matters to the serving trial only as a limit: a familiar household dish is not neutral equipment, and the person who lends it can ask for it back. Rowan compares its volume with the plain bowl using dry barley, empties both, then records the chip and the order of the pours. The result can help a cook choose a bowl that will not tip. It cannot authorize anyone to take this one, assign it to a family, or infer the size of a serving from its scratches.

entries.title: A Scoop Is Not a Weight
entries.body:
The storehouse scoop has a bent rim and an old notch cut into its handle. Ada's forecast counts each level scoop as a fixed quantity, while the release board calls it a weight. Rowan fills the scoop with the grain currently held for the evening meal, then fills each bowl without packing it down. The amounts differ because the bowls have different shapes and the grain shifts as it settles. A second fill gives a slightly different result. The record therefore names the tool, batch, fill method and date. It does not convert this one comparison into a universal serving size. A later cook may choose a different portion; the ledger should say so rather than silently rewriting the forecast.

Supplemental table note — the cook's hand

The cook fills the scoop differently when the grain is damp. A level rim is still visible, but a small shake settles the kernels and leaves room for more. She has learned this by making bread through several wet seasons, not by using the scoop as a scale. Ada asks her to demonstrate the gesture twice so the record can distinguish a level measure from a packed one.

The cook agrees to describe the method but refuses to have her hand called a standard. Her wrist is sore after long shifts, and another worker may not be able to make the same motion. Rowan writes both facts beside the comparison. A repeatable tool helps a storekeeper close a balance; a repeatable instruction also has to say what happens when the person following it cannot perform the demonstration. The trial keeps the scoop for inventory and lets each kitchen state its serving method in plain language.

entries.title: Why Alden Keeps One Measure
entries.body:
Alden does not defend the forecast as perfect. He remembers two storekeepers arguing over how much had been released after a flood. Their accounts used different scoops and neither had signed the other's page. The accusation spread before the missing grain was found in a dry loft. Alden's fixed issue reduced one kind of dispute: every shift began with the same number of scoops and ended with a lock check. It also made the routine slow to adapt when the queue changed. A family arriving late could be sent away even if grain remained, because the next issue was already assigned to another shift. Alden asks for a replacement rule that can be inspected by the person who inherits it. He fears both waste and favoritism, and he does not accept that good intentions alone protect a shared store.

Supplemental table note — why the accusation stayed

Alden remembers the flood store because its dispute never reached a clean ending. Two keepers brought different totals to a council hearing. One had issued grain before the water reached the lower stair; the other had counted what remained after the sacks were moved. A clerk copied both pages into one column, and the mismatch was treated as proof that someone had taken food. The missing issue slips were found years later in a crate that had been used to brace the door.

He keeps a single measure because it gives the next watch something they can check without trusting his memory. The flood taught him that a bad ledger can injure an honest worker and leave a real loss unexplained. He accepts that one measure cannot tell the kitchen how much a hungry person needs. His request is narrower: record what leaves the store and allow the rule for eating to be discussed in the open.

entries.title: A Shift Rota with One Queue
entries.body:
The rota records who unlocked the store, how many scoops left it and which keeper returned the key. It does not record the time people arrived at the table or whether a serving went to someone outside the hall. Alden says adding names would make the document harder to protect; Ada agrees that a meal should not depend on surrendering a name. Rowan draws two alternative columns: one for a missed or delayed serving, and one for grain returned unused. Neither column identifies a household. The original lock check remains intact. The proposed rota is meant to show where an issue went, not to make the people receiving it easier to monitor.

Supplemental table note — carrying the key

The keeper scheduled to carry the key asks that the rota name the duty, not the household. They are willing to sign for the lock because a missing key affects the whole store; they do not want a public list that turns every late arrival into a question about who they know. Alden checks the returned key in front of Rowan and lets the keeper sign before him.

That order is copied onto the draft. It does not prove that the store was never opened outside the recorded shift. It makes the next handoff visible enough for someone else to ask. The page also notes that a second person can witness the lock without becoming responsible for counting meals. The rota concerns custody of supplies. Attendance remains unrecorded unless a separate, voluntary process is proposed by the people who would be counted.

entries.title: A Root, a Seed, and an Available Meal
entries.body:
Ada asks Rowan to plant Emberroot in the Crownfall bed and write down the seed source before watering. When the crop is ready, they separate a small portion for another planting before weighing the roots offered to the kitchen. The forecast spreadsheet treated all gathered weight as immediately available food. It contained no replacement-seed column and no growing interval, so a repeating harvest looked larger on paper than it was in the bed. The current crop corrects one assumption but cannot estimate the entire region's yield. Some roots are damaged, some are saved, and a later season may fail. Ada puts all three categories beside the date rather than collapsing them into one total. Alden agrees that a reserve exists only if the ledger shows what was actually kept aside.

Supplemental table note — keeping tomorrow's seed

The gardener who lent the Emberroot seed asks Rowan to keep one root from the harvest only if it is still sound enough to replant. The original packet was not a gift to the storehouse; it was a loan for this bed, with the expectation that a good harvest would return seed to its owner. Ada checks the root before separating it and records the packet as returned rather than adding it to the meal total.

The distinction changes the ledger without changing the crop. One portion was eaten, one was held for a possible next planting, and one was returned under the seed agreement. If the root fails to sprout, the bed cannot promise a second harvest. The record keeps the gardener's claim visible so a future keeper will not mistake a reserve for food that belongs to everyone. Shared work still needs clear terms for what is borrowed and what is offered.

entries.title: One Bed Cannot Stand for the Reach
entries.body:
The Crownfall bed is small and close to the stone wall. Its western half stayed damp after the morning watering, while the eastern edge dried sooner. Rowan marks both edges and records the Emberroot harvest separately by row. That split helps a future gardener decide whether to repeat the test, but it does not tell Ada how much food the reach could produce. The bed's shelter, soil depth, water source and tending time are all local conditions. The old forecast used the word 'average' without naming any of them. Ada removes the word from the trial sheet and replaces it with the actual observations. The result is less convenient for a speech, but more useful to a person who will plant here next week.

Supplemental table note — the bed behind the wall

The western shade is not the only difference between the two halves of the bed. A loose stone channels water from the wall into one corner, and the gardener has set a flat shard there to slow the runoff. Rowan records the shard because moving it would change the next trial. He does not recommend the same arrangement for a bed with a different slope.

Two neighbors help turn the soil, but only one can stay for the harvest. Ada lists labor separately from yield and asks whether the absent worker wants their name on the copy. They choose to leave it out. The page therefore keeps the number of hands as an observation and the personal credit line blank. One small bed can teach the Reach how this patch behaves; it cannot predict every plot or decide how much effort each household owes a common table.

entries.title: A Catch Is Not a Nightly Supply
entries.body:
Rowan catches a Starlit Minnow at the lake and writes down the bait, water level and time. The fish goes to the kitchen as a single meal ingredient. The forecast's food column had converted fish from the lake into a dependable nightly supply, though the catch record contained no count of failed casts or days the shore was inaccessible. One successful catch shows that the species was available at this place and time. It does not establish a population, a daily catch rate or an equitable way to distribute food. Ada asks that the meal trial keep the catch attached to its conditions. If the model later uses a fishing estimate, its author will have to explain how many attempts went uncounted.

Supplemental table note — the empty hook

Another fisher tries the same bait after Rowan's catch and brings back an empty hook. A third leaves when the lake begins to cloud near the landing. None of these attempts proves that fish have vanished; each describes a different effort under a different condition. The kitchen accepts the single Starlit Minnow, but does not write it into a nightly ration plan.

The fisher asks that the archive not call a failed attempt waste. Time at the lake was spent watching the water and avoiding the storm edge, even though no food came back. Ada adds a place to record attempts only if later estimates include the hours, weather and bait used. A catch is useful to the meal in front of them. A repeated survey would need permission from the fishers and a method that does not make one successful evening stand in for every night.

entries.title: The Lake Is Not an Open Pantry
entries.body:
A pale line on the landing stone sits above the current water. It may mark a seasonal height, a storm or an earlier measuring point; there is no date beside it. The route from the boat to the Crownfall table is passable today, but the last stretch becomes slippery when the lake falls below the carved step. Ada's projection counted a fish at the lake as available food without including the time it takes to bring a catch to the people waiting. Rowan records the path condition with the catch rather than subtracting a guessed amount from the total. Access can change independently of supply. The note invites a later trial at another water level and does not claim that the old mark belongs to the same season as the forecast.

Supplemental table note — who can cross the landing

When the lake rises, the shortest path to the table crosses the landing stones. A traveler using a cane says the uneven lower step becomes difficult before the water reaches the pale mark. They ask for a second route to remain open along the upper path. The mark records water height; it does not record who can safely approach it.

Rowan walks both paths with the traveler and notes that the upper route takes longer but stays above the wet stone. He does not write the traveler into the public copy. Ada adds the route condition to the serving notice so a cook cannot mistake an empty place at the table for a lack of need. The forecast's water estimate and the meal record remain separate, but access links them in practice: food can be available and still be unreachable.

entries.title: A Memory with a Small Boundary
entries.body:
The First Warden remembers a storekeeper dividing grain into fixed portions at the beginning of a winter. He does not remember whether people could return for more or whether the rule changed when a road closed. His memory was carried through many retellings; he cannot separate every sentence he heard from words added later. The story shows that a reserve was part of the oath's practice, not that every cycle used the same serving rule. Ada keeps it beside the current trial as a question about continuity. Alden listens carefully: he had treated the remembered measure as authority for his own rule. The Warden says he can testify to the measure he saw, but not to every person it served. His limit does not make the memory useless. It keeps it from deciding the meal before anyone at the table speaks.

Supplemental table note — the name he cannot recover

The First Warden pauses after describing the keeper with the tapping scoop. He can picture the motion and the dark sleeve, but not the keeper's face. He recalls a child waiting near the door and a second bowl being filled after the rule was explained. He cannot tell whether the child was allowed another portion or whether someone else spoke for them.

The Warden asks that the missing name remain missing. He has seen later copies attach a familiar official's name to an old store rule because a page looked incomplete without one. Rowan preserves the account as an imperfect memory rather than a witness list. It supports the narrow claim that a keeper used a repeated serving motion during one winter. It cannot tell the table what the child needed, what answer they received, or whether an old practice was fair.

entries.title: The Reserve Needs a Return Date
entries.body:
Two seed jars remain on the shelf. Their seals are unbroken, yet both labels describe the jars as 'for later' without saying which planting they are meant to support. A reserve protects a future meal only if a keeper knows when to release it. Rowan adds a planting window and leaves a second field for the next keeper's mark. He does not assign a permanent guardian; the rotation changes with the watch. Alden admits that his lock schedule was designed to prevent unrecorded withdrawals, not to preserve germination quality. Ada asks for both conditions on the card. Storage and access belong in the model alongside food yield, because one cannot replace the other.

Supplemental table note — the borrowed jar

One jar was placed on the reserve shelf by a seed keeper who expects it back after the next planting. The seal is unbroken, but the cord around its neck is the keeper's own, not the storehouse tie. Ada adds a custody note and a date for the keeper to return. Alden first worries that a separate label will make the shelf harder to count, then agrees that an honest total must distinguish common stock from borrowed stock.

The second jar belongs to the storehouse and can be opened if the first planting fails. Its label needs a germination check before it is treated as a reliable reserve. Rowan records the two jars in different columns. Neither is available for the current supper without a new decision from its owner or custodian. The page makes the next action visible; it does not promise that either jar will produce a meal.

entries.title: Two Ways to Keep the Table Accountable
entries.body:
The trial has shown two risks that cannot be removed by making the page neater. A posted rota makes a serving rule visible and correctable, but names can turn a meal into surveillance. An open table protects privacy, yet a storekeeper still needs to know when the reserved grain must remain untouched. Ada offers two temporary procedures. Rowan may post the portion rule with blank spaces for people who choose not to be counted, then invite corrections before the next shift. Or the team may serve one open meal, record only the amount used and leave household totals out of the book. Alden prefers the first because it gives the watch a handoff. Ada prefers the second because it asks less of the people in the queue. Neither option changes the final allocation or settles the cycle. The choice belongs to this trial and must be reviewed after it is used.

Supplemental table note — what the trial can decide

Ada asks Rowan to describe the choice without calling either procedure a solution. Under the posted rota, a guest can read who holds the key, how much food was released and when the rule will be reviewed. Under the open table, a guest can eat without giving a name, while the storekeeper sees only what was issued and returned. Both procedures leave questions unanswered.

The team does not use attendance as a score for the player's choice. A larger crowd would not prove that one group is more deserving, and a quiet room would not prove that privacy had succeeded for everyone. The decision sets how this particular trial will be run and what its record can show. Ada leaves a space for comments from people who use the table, including a way to decline the survey. The next review may change the procedure.

entries.title: A Posted Rule with a Review Date
entries.body:
The public board gives the trial portion, the amount held for replanting and the time when the next shift may review the rule. Household names are not required. People can add a correction anonymously or ask Ada to read it aloud at the next meeting. Alden checks that the reserve shelf and store key still have separate entries; posting the serving rule does not open the seed jars. A red line marks the page as a one-shift trial, not a standing order. The board gives people a way to challenge the method, though Ada knows some may still avoid a public place. She leaves a covered box beneath it for written comments. The record says what the procedure offers and where its blind spots remain.

Supplemental table note — reading the board aloud

The board is placed where the lower road meets the hall, out of the rain and below the eye line of a seated reader. A volunteer offers to read the rule aloud during the first shift. They ask whether the review date can be repeated at closing, since a notice can be visible and still be missed by someone arriving late or unable to read the lettering.

Ada adds an oral reading to the procedure but does not list who listened. The volunteer's name appears only on the work rota with their permission. A covered box receives notes, and the board explains that a person may speak to Ada instead of writing. These options make the trial easier to approach; they do not guarantee that every concern will reach the archive. Rowan records the placement and the reading time so another group can decide whether the notice was accessible in their own hall.

entries.title: The Queue Arrived after the Page
entries.body:
A correction arrives from the late shift: several people reached the table after dusk because the road gate had been held for a cart crossing. The board had treated dusk as a reliable start time and described anyone arriving later as a late arrival. Alden first wants to keep the old label; he worries that changing the window will make tomorrow's lock check harder. He reads the road log and sees the delay was recorded by the watch, not by the people waiting. Rowan changes the rota wording to 'serving window' and adds the reason for the first delay. No names are added. Alden agrees that a rule can be firm without accusing the person it failed to reach. The correction stays attached to the old version so the next keeper can see why the time changed.

Supplemental table note — the cart at dusk

The road gate was held so a cart could pass while its wheel was steadied. People who had been told the serving window began at dusk arrived after the board was read. The correction names the delay but not the cart driver. There is no reason to make one person answer for a schedule that failed to include traffic on the road.

The kitchen keeper proposes a wider window on days when the gate is in use. Ada asks what would happen if the cart were delayed longer than expected. The group adds a second serving period only when food remains safe to hold, and writes that condition plainly. Rowan attaches the correction to the earlier page. The original time is preserved as the rule that was tried, not as a promise the late group ignored.

entries.title: Correction History beside the Serving Rule
entries.body:
The corrected rota keeps the first serving window, the road delay and the new review time on one page. Ada signs the change as editor; Alden initials the store transfer, not the count of people served. This separation lets a future keeper distinguish a policy edit from a food tally. The trial remains temporary until the next shift reviews it. A person who disagrees may submit another correction without signing for a meal. The board does not show whether everyone felt safe using it, and Ada records that as a question for the review rather than claiming that the new procedure solved it. She asks Rowan to leave the earlier version legible, since a correction without its history could look like an unexplained change to the store's rule.

Supplemental table note — a correction with two signatures

The receipt carries two marks that answer different questions. Ada signs that the public record was edited and gives the reason for the change. Alden initials that the store transfer was checked against the scoop and scale. Neither mark certifies the number of people who ate, since no attendance count was gathered.

A later copyist might compress the signatures into one approval line. Rowan adds a margin key explaining why that would be inaccurate. The page also carries the earlier version number and a note that the serving window was extended after the cart delay. Anyone comparing copies can see that the change was deliberate. The signatures make responsibility traceable; they do not turn a limited trial into a final rule for Crownfall Reach.

entries.title: A Rule Passed Forward with a Question
entries.body:
Alden takes the revised rota and reads the review date aloud before accepting the watch key. He repeats the portion method, the seed reserve and the wider serving window in his own words. If he had missed one, Ada would have corrected the page before the next shift began. The handoff does not prove the rule will work for every person. It gives the next keeper a procedure that can be checked and a time when it must be reconsidered. Alden leaves the correction box at the edge of the table rather than beside the locked store. A person can question the schedule without approaching the key. Rowan notes that the board will remain through one evening and that a longer policy requires another decision.

Supplemental table note — the handoff at closing

At closing, Alden gives the watch key to the next keeper and reads the review date once more. The new keeper asks whether the posted portion applies when the Emberroot reserve is low. Alden answers that the trial only covers the food counted on this sheet. Ada writes the question in the margin so it can be answered before a shortage, not during one.

The board stays up through a single evening. The group agrees to remove it before turning the trial into a standing schedule, then return with observations from the next shift. Rowan records the handoff as a handoff, not a vote by everyone who ate. Accepting a key commits the keeper to a task for that shift. It does not give them authority to speak for the people who were not present.

entries.title: An Open Table with a Store Limit
entries.body:
The open-table notice gives a time, a serving limit and a request that people take only what they can use before the close. It does not ask for names, household size or a reason for arriving. Alden worries that someone may take an extra portion. Ada says the store transfer can still be checked by weighing the returned grain and comparing it with what was issued. Neither method will show exactly who ate. The notice makes privacy part of the trial while keeping the reserve separate. Rowan places it where people can read it before joining the queue, then confirms the storekeeper can close the table at the posted time without taking a name list.

Supplemental table note — the door that stays open

The room has a door, but the notice says it need not be closed. One guest prefers to sit near the exit and leave as soon as they finish. Another asks whether a wrapped portion can be carried outside for someone who cannot come in. The kitchen sets a clear limit on what can be taken, then leaves the path unobstructed.

Alden checks that the store has enough stock to honor the notice before the room opens. Ada keeps the limit in the public copy so privacy does not become an unlimited promise the kitchen cannot meet. Rowan writes down the room layout and the serving time, not the guests' appearance or reason for attending. A quiet table needs boundaries around supplies and space; it does not need a roll call.

entries.title: One Open Meal, No Household Count
entries.body:
Rowan lays out the cooked pottage and a small number of bowls. The seed reserve remains sealed, and the table closes at the time printed on the notice. People can eat in the room or take a wrapped portion for someone who could not come. No clerk asks them to name that person. At closing, Ada and Alden count the food left and compare it with the store transfer. They know how much was offered and how much returned; they do not know how many people ate or whether the serving met every need. Ada resists writing an attendance estimate from the empty bowls. The meal is a test of a privacy-preserving procedure, not a survey of hunger across Crownfall Reach.

Supplemental table note — the covered portion

One guest asks the cook to cover a second bowl and leave it beside the door. They do not give a name. The request can be filled within the trial limit, so the bowl is placed on a clean tray with the meal ingredients listed for anyone who needs to check them. Rowan sees it carried away but does not record who carried it.

Ada asks the kitchen to note that a portion left the table for another person, without treating that as proof that two people were fed. The second person may not receive it, and the guest may have taken it for another reason. The record can safely say that the procedure allowed food to leave the room without an attendance entry. That small privacy choice matters to the trial, even though it cannot measure the meal's final destination.

entries.title: A Return Count Is Not a Refusal Count
entries.body:
The tray holds grain that stayed dry through the serving. Rowan weighs it before the kitchen decides whether it can be stored again. The difference between the amount issued and the amount returned describes what left the tray; it cannot say whether a person refused food, took a wrapped portion or never arrived. Ada writes the returned quantity beside the transfer and refuses to call the difference 'consumed.' The open table kept names out of the ledger, as intended, but it also leaves some questions unanswered. The next trial could ask people for voluntary comments, yet the comment must never become a condition for receiving a meal. Alden accepts the narrower count because it is still enough to close the store safely.

Supplemental table note — the food left on the tray

The returned grain is dry enough to store, but the cook will not reuse a spoonful that touched a wet serving cloth. The amounts are weighed separately. Alden asks whether that means the kitchen wasted food; the cook answers that keeping a store safe is part of serving it, even when a portion must be discarded.

Rowan notes the amount returned, the amount retained and the small quantity that cannot be stored. The totals explain the movement of grain for this shift. They do not show how many people wanted another serving or chose to leave. Ada keeps an anonymous comment box beside the tray but makes clear that a comment is not required to receive a meal. A balance sheet can be complete about its stock while remaining silent about its guests.

entries.title: A Store Check without a People Count
entries.body:
Alden checks the lock, the issued grain and the returned portion. The store balances within the scale's margin. He says that this closes the key check, not the question of how many meals Crownfall needs. In the old rota he would have written a household total beside the transfer and treated the difference as an attendance estimate. The open-table trial gives him no such number. He is uncomfortable with that gap but no longer claims that the grain can fill it. Ada suggests a voluntary conversation at a later meal. Alden agrees only if the serving does not depend on a response. He will keep the store method and retire the assumption that a balanced shelf proves a complete ration.

Supplemental table note — enough for the lock check

The store balances within the scale's margin, and the key is back on its hook. Alden calls this a successful closing procedure. The cook agrees that the stock was handled safely but says nothing about whether the meal was enough. Those statements can both be true because they describe different parts of the evening.

Ada adds a separate line for food safety and keeps the question of portions open for review with the people who use the table. Rowan watches Alden remove the word complete from a draft heading. The page now says the lock check is complete, a distinction the next keeper can verify. A balanced shelf cannot answer a question it was not designed to measure.

entries.title: Three Food Columns, No Demand Guess
entries.body:
The final meal record has three columns: what was harvested, what was kept for the next planting and what was offered at the table. A fourth field names the tools and conditions used to measure each amount. There is no column for 'total need' because no one in the trial measured it. Ada keeps that question open for a later conversation with the people who use the table. The record can support a store check and help a gardener repeat the crop trial. It cannot decide how much food every household requires or whether one serving rule is fair in every season. Alden asks that the sheet stay with the store key. Ada asks that a copy stay by the table. Rowan makes both copies and marks them with the same review date.

Supplemental table note — copies on opposite sides

The store copy is tied to the key ring; the table copy is kept under the board. Neither copy holds the only version. Ada and Alden compare the review date, instrument note and correction number before separating them. If one page is damaged, the surviving copy can show that an earlier version existed, though it cannot restore every detail.

The gardeners ask that the seed return agreement remain with the table copy because that is where the food decision is discussed. Alden asks for the scoop condition to stay with the store copy. The group places a short reference on both sheets pointing to the other. Rowan records who took custody of each page, but the pages remain available for correction. A common meal does not require a single office to own every part of its history.

entries.title: The Measure Did Not End the Argument
entries.body:
The First Warden studies the two copies and recognizes the notch on the store scoop. He remembers a keeper tapping the handle against the stone before every issue. He cannot remember whether that gesture was a measurement check or simply a habit. He will not call the current trial the original rule, nor will he use its successful lock check to settle the ethics of the ration. The meal answered a smaller question: the store can record a transfer without requiring every person to give a name. The Warden says a law kept for a hundred years may still deserve review by the people asked to live under it. Ada writes that sentence in the margin, not as a verdict against Alden but as a warning against confusing endurance with consent.

Supplemental table note — the sound of the handle

The scoop makes a small wooden tap when Alden sets it down. The sound brings back the Warden's image of a keeper at the old store, but the Warden cannot say whether the keeper was tapping to settle the grain or simply to hear that the handle remained firm. The gesture has survived in his memory longer than the reason for it.

Ada leaves the sound out of the measure instructions. It can prompt an inspection of the handle, but it cannot calibrate a portion. The Warden agrees that memory should sit beside the present test rather than govern it. The archive keeps the remembered gesture as a clue about how people worked, not as a command to repeat it. Their disagreement remains attached to the record because both the caution and the uncertainty belong to its history.

entries.title: Alden Accepts a Date for Review
entries.body:
Alden signs a review date rather than a permanent order. He explains that the fixed scoop was his answer to an earlier theft accusation, and that he feared any change would look like favor. The trial did not prove that favoritism has disappeared. It did show that a store transfer can be checked while leaving the meal queue uncounted. Alden is willing to test the procedure again with the next watch. He asks to hear about an empty place, a delay or a damaged measure before someone turns it into a rumor. Ada records that request alongside the date but does not call it a guarantee. A promise can guide the next shift; only the shift can show whether the promise was kept.

Supplemental table note — the mark he chooses to sign

Alden signs the date and key transfer, then leaves the serving recommendation to Ada and the kitchen. He says he once signed a rule that outlived the store conditions that made it useful. A flood had closed one road, grain had come from an emergency cache, and the rule was copied as if it had always applied. He will not make a permanent order from this single shift.

His signature accepts a duty to return for review. It does not certify that every future keeper will arrive or that the rule will remain fair. Ada writes the missed review date as a possible failure state and includes an instruction to suspend the trial if food safety or the reserve is uncertain. The promise has a boundary the next watch can inspect. Alden is still responsible for his part of the rota, but he no longer asks one signature to carry the whole table.

entries.title: The Table beside the Forecast
entries.body:
Ada files the forecast and meal record together without merging their numbers. The forecast estimates what the store may hold under stated conditions. The meal record describes one shift, one crop, one catch and one serving procedure. Alden will carry the store key into the next watch; Ada will return after the posted review date. Neither result decides which ending Rowan should choose or whether the world has enough resources to remain unchanged forever. The trial gives the people at Crownfall a small, revisable rule for tomorrow and leaves them free to change it when the conditions change. Rowan looks at the blank column that began the route. It is no longer mislabeled as zero. It says what the team did not count, and leaves the decision to count it later with the people who would be counted.

Supplemental table note — an empty space left open

The last sheet has room for a question from the next shift. No one fills it in before the archive closes. Ada asks Rowan not to treat the blank as agreement with the trial; it only means that nobody added a question on this copy before it was stored. The board's box remains available at the table for the next evening.

The two routes leave different kinds of record. One lets the public inspect a serving method while keeping household names out of view. The other keeps the meal open without making attendance a condition, while limiting what can be learned about demand. Neither route settles the world's shortage or cancels Rowan's final oath. They give the Reach a small procedure that can be repeated, questioned and stopped. The empty line leaves room for the people who will live with it to answer in their own time.
