The first Emberlily bed fits between the brick lip and the garden wall. Its ash layer is shallow enough for the roots to reach packed earth, and the wall keeps the soil cool after midday. Mira checks the bed at different times rather than treating one morning inspection as a description of the whole day. The plant is small, but the red center can be seen from inside the room when the door stands open.

She asks Rowan to leave the weakest stem alone. The trial is not a contest for the largest harvest. Mira wants to learn whether the bed can renew itself before she relies on it for a recipe. A flower left standing may produce seed, or it may not; the season will decide. The garden card therefore has two boxes, one for the petals used now and one for what remains at the end of the week. The second box is allowed to stay blank.

entries.title: The Dusk Petals
entries.body:
Emberlily opens its bright center late in the day, when the stone around the garden bed has started to cool. The petals release cleanly if they are lifted from the base instead of pulled across the central cup. Mira remembers drying them on cloth away from direct heat. Her mentor used the flower to prepare a simple skin balm, not to cure every injury, and Mira wants to keep that limit with the recipe.

Supplemental room note — a petal left on the cloth

Mira lays the Emberlily petals on cloth and waits until the cup has cooled enough to handle. She does not hurry them toward the mortar. Her mentor used to say that a careful harvest begins when the person collecting it notices what will be left behind. Mira had thought the phrase was about thrift. Now she sees that it is also about not turning a living bed into a shelf of supplies just because a room has reopened.

One petal falls beside the drying cloth and is kept separate. It has a torn edge and is not used in the trial batch. Rowan records the reason instead of writing only the final count. A later healer can tell that the smaller amount was a deliberate choice, not a missing ingredient. The note gives the recipe a place in the garden's history: this first balm came from a cautious harvest, not from stripping every flower the bed could offer.

entries.title: Moonwort for Care
entries.body:
Mira grows Moonwort for a clean wash cloth and reserves one sound leaf for the balm trial. She shows Rowan how to take the outer leaves without pulling up the plant. Her mentor taught this as a way to keep an herb bed alive through repeated small treatments. The crop is used for care and washing here; the harvest does not turn Moonwort into a universal cure or a substitute for clean water.

Supplemental room note — leaves for washing

The Moonwort leaf is set aside for the wash cloth before the balm is made. Mira knows the plant from training, but she does not treat that familiarity as proof that every leaf is clean. Rowan rinses the sound one with water from the covered bowl, and Mira checks it for grit before it touches the cloth. The rest of the plant stays rooted. Its next growth is more useful than one larger harvest that leaves the bed bare.

The wash basin sits beside the cot, so a person resting there can see how it is prepared. Mira wants the work to be visible enough for a guest to ask questions, while keeping the guest's own story private. She writes the plant's name and use on the garden card, not on a patient record. Moonwort helps them prepare this room's materials; it does not make water plentiful or turn a leaf into a substitute for clean water.

entries.title: A Bowl from the Upstream Bend
entries.body:
Rowan caught one Blackreed Trout from the Ashfall brook above the footbridge. Mira wants the fish for a warming bowl for someone who chooses to rest in the treatment room. She does not ask him to use it as medicine or to treat one catch as a count of the fish population. The brook has moved ash since the raid, so the clean bend is chosen by sight and current flow rather than by an old map.

Supplemental room note — the bowl brought from the brook

Mira cooks the Blackreed Trout in the open kitchen rather than at the damaged hearth. The fish is a meal for a person who has chosen to rest, not an ingredient in the balm. The distinction sounds obvious until people start adding every helpful thing to one supply list. A bowl of food belongs in a kitchen record; a medicine jar belongs on a shelf with its ingredients and limits written down.

The upstream bend looks clear today, but the brook carried ash after the raid. Mira will not use one bright stretch of water to certify the whole stream. Rowan marks where he fished and the direction of the current. They have one catch, one meal and one afternoon's observation. Mira tastes the broth before it is offered and asks the guest whether warm food would be welcome. No one is required to eat because the fish was difficult to catch.

entries.title: Mira's Mortar Bowl
entries.body:
The clay mortar has a chip at its base, but the inside remains smooth and unbroken. A folded cloth steadies it on the herb table so Mira can grind petals without cutting them on a rough edge. The bowl belonged to her first training room. She had kept it in the back of a drawer after the room closed, unable to decide whether it was a useful tool or a reminder of a lesson that had ended badly.

Supplemental room note — why the mortar stayed in the drawer

Mira takes the mortar from the drawer and notices that she has been holding its base too tightly. The chipped edge is not the reason she put it away. During training she once rushed a practice mixture, read the mentor's brief instruction as permission to finish alone, and had the batch stopped before anyone used it. No one was harmed, but Mira carried the shame as if the room itself had rejected her. The mortar became easier to hide than the memory of needing correction.

She checks the inner surface with a clean cloth, then lays another folded cloth beneath the bowl so it cannot rock on the table. The repair is ordinary and visible. Mira tells Rowan that a tool can be safe to use while still reminding its owner of a mistake. The room does not ask her to forget the lesson; it gives her a way to use the same tool more carefully and to ask for a second opinion before a batch is offered.

entries.title: Emberlily Balm Recipe
entries.body:
Mira's Emberlily Balm uses one Emberlily petal and one Moonwort leaf per portion. Rowan makes a small pair at the herb table, following the old mortar-and-cloth method rather than heating the mixture over the cracked hearth. Mira describes it as a soothing balm for a small burn or split. It cannot close a deep wound, stop heavy bleeding or replace examination by a healer. The recipe produces two portions so the first service can be shared and still leave Rowan a usable item.

Supplemental room note — the first two portions

Mira keeps the first balm batch deliberately small. She checks the Emberlily petal and Moonwort leaf against the written recipe, grinds them with the cloth beneath the mortar, and refuses Rowan's suggestion to use the cracked hearth to speed the work. The formula is an in-game treatment for a minor burn or split. Its limits are part of the label: it cannot settle a deep wound or replace a healer's examination. The game item restores a small amount of health, but that number is a combat rule, not a claim about every injury.

Two jars come from the batch. Mira asks that the first be offered to a visitor only after they hear what it is and what it is not. The second stays with Rowan so he can use the item during travel if he chooses. Neither jar is treated as proof that the garden can meet every future need. This first preparation shows that the old recipe can be followed in a safer workspace, not that Mira has solved medicine for Ashfall.

entries.title: The Balm Label
entries.body:
Mira writes the balm's intended use and limits on a label facing the patient. The jar sits on an open shelf, not hidden inside a locked drawer. She includes an instruction to ask before applying it and a direction to stop if the skin reacts badly. This label does not make the balm suitable for every injury; it gives the person receiving it a chance to decide after hearing what Mira knows.

Supplemental room note — the label faces outward

The jar's label faces the person who might use it rather than the healer who stored it. Mira adds the batch date, the two plant names and a brief description of the balm's intended use. She leaves enough room to write a correction if the contents change or the jar is set aside. A neat label is not permission to apply something to another person's skin; the jar still has to be offered and explained.

The room's old shelves were arranged so that the healer could reach everything from the work surface. Mira changes that arrangement. Jars are grouped by use, and the label faces outward so the person receiving care can read along. Rowan notices that she has not written the guest's name anywhere. Mira says the recipe needs its own history; the guest does not have to become part of it. If the balm causes discomfort, the offer ends and the jar goes back to the shelf.

entries.title: A Room that Stays or a Kit that Travels
entries.body:
Mira asks Rowan to choose where the treatment room's first dependable supply should go. A fixed clinic keeps its cot, basin and herbs together in Ashfall. A field kit can reach the road and gate, but carries fewer supplies and must return for refills. Both plans leave the patient free to accept or decline treatment. The choice sets the first service arrangement without claiming that one can replace the other forever.

Supplemental room note — choosing where the weight belongs

The fixed clinic places more weight on the room: shelves, a cot, a basin and supplies kept together. The field kit places more weight on Mira: a satchel on her shoulder, a route across broken streets and fewer jars to offer when she arrives. Rowan's choice decides which arrangement is prepared first. Mira does not ask him to choose the one that will always be best; she asks which limitation Ashfall can manage today.

She describes the fixed room as a promise to stay within reach of the village, then immediately adds that staying in one place can leave the road unattended. The kit can travel, but travel spends time and supplies and may separate the healer from the people who know the town. The record keeps both costs on the same page. A policy is useful when it says who carries the weight and where the missing help might be. The patient's ability to accept or decline care applies under either arrangement.

entries.title: The Fixed Room's Window
entries.body:
The old window opens halfway without striking the cracked stone. Morning light can reach the cot while the frame still gives a resting patient some privacy. Mira is drawn to the fixed room because it keeps the mortar, wash cloth and herb shelves together. She asks Rowan to help restore that space as a local place to rest, with the door and window easy to open from inside.

Supplemental room note — morning through a narrow window

The window is narrow, but morning light reaches the cot without landing directly on the shelf of jars. Mira tries it at two different heights before leaving the frame as it is. The room once had heavier curtains; the remaining hooks are uneven, and she does not want to hang cloth that could block the exit path. For now, the window gives a patient a view of the garden and lets the healer see the red Emberlily flower from inside.

Mira keeps the glass partly shaded from the lane. The person resting can see out, while a passerby cannot easily see the cot. She is not trying to hide that the clinic exists. She is making a small distinction between finding help and being displayed while receiving it. Rowan marks the safe opening angle on the frame. If the stone shifts, the window should be checked again before it is used at full width.

entries.title: An Inside-Opening Latch
entries.body:
Rowan and Mira fit the old latch so the room stays closed against a gust but opens from either side. Mira tries it while inside before considering the fixed room ready. Her mentor had insisted that a patient should be able to leave without asking the person who offered care. The new latch keeps the door useful without turning a treatment space into a locked ward.

Supplemental room note — the test from inside

Mira closes the door, sits on the cot and works the latch with one hand. The lever opens without catching her sleeve, and the door swings clear of the basin. She repeats the movement slowly, then asks Rowan to try it from outside without pulling on the frame. Neither test proves that the repair will last through every season, so the hinge is added to the monthly inspection card.

Her mentor's old rule was short: a patient must not need a keeper to leave. Mira had treated it as a principle she already understood, until the first time she found herself standing between a frightened visitor and the door because she wanted to finish explaining. Now she has arranged the room so the latch and exit are visible before anyone sits down. The door can still be closed against a gust. It cannot be used as a lock.

entries.title: The Clinic's Clear Path
entries.body:
The wash basin fits beside the cot, within reach of someone resting. The route to the door remains open, and Mira can refill the bowl without stepping across the warming hearth. She prefers a room where a patient can see the exit from the cot. The fixed clinic plan now has a clean path from door to basin to bed, with enough space for one caregiver and one guest.

Supplemental room note — carrying water without crossing the room

The basin fits beside the cot, but the first placement makes the refill path cross the visitor's feet. Mira moves it closer to the wall and tries carrying a covered bowl from the water station with one hand. There is enough room to pass without brushing the cot. Rowan marks the floor where the basin should stand after the room is cleaned, then wipes the chalk away so it will not become a permanent boundary.

The route is designed for one caregiver and one guest, not a crowd. If a second healer is needed, the stool can move and the door can remain open. Mira likes being able to see the exit from the work surface; the person on the cot can see it too. The placement does not prove that every visitor will find the room comfortable. It makes a few choices visible and leaves enough space to move furniture when the next visitor asks for a different arrangement.

entries.title: Mira Chooses the Fixed Clinic
entries.body:
Mira chooses to reopen the fixed treatment room as a small Ashfall clinic. The room's cot, basin and herb shelf stay together, and its inside-opening latch lets a patient leave on their own. She knows a fixed place cannot reach someone who is already on the road, so she plans to keep a small supply for travelers too. Her choice gives the village one stable point of care without claiming it can answer every need.

Supplemental room note — a fixed place, with a return path

Mira chooses the clinic because the room lets her keep the basin, cot and herb shelf within a few steps of one another. After the raid, she has spent too much time moving supplies from one place to another and too little time hearing what people actually ask for. A stable work surface helps her prepare the balm carefully and rest between visits. It is a choice about how she wants to practice, not an order that every injured traveler must come to her door.

She makes a small traveling pouch for the road even though the fixed room is the main plan. The pouch carries less and has to be restocked from the clinic, but it preserves a way to reach someone who cannot walk to Ashfall. Rowan's help has made a room available; it has not made every road passable. Mira writes the clinic's hours on the sign and leaves one contact bell within reach of the cot. A fixed address can be dependable without pretending to be everywhere.

entries.title: Ashfall Clinic Sign
entries.body:
Mira hangs a red-leaf sign above the treatment room's door. It names the place simply and leaves the latch free to turn from either side. A traveler can recognize the clinic without having to find a particular healer first. The Emberlily leaf recalls the small garden that supplied the first balm. It does not promise that the room is staffed at every hour or that every injury can be treated there.

Supplemental room note — the sign's missing promise

Mira hangs the red-leaf sign high enough to be found from the path, then asks Rowan to stand at the far gate and read it. The words are plain. They name the clinic and state when Mira expects to be present. She declines to add “all care, all hours,” because the room has one healer and a limited supply. A sign that promises more than the clinic can provide could turn a difficult absence into a betrayal.

The leaf mark comes from the plant that supplied the first balm. It lets a traveler find the door without asking someone in the busy square to explain why they came. Mira leaves no list of patients or illnesses on the wall. The clinic can be visible while the person who enters remains private. When the sign is not current, Mira wants the hours crossed out and rewritten rather than left to fade into a statement that used to be true.

entries.title: The Field Satchel's Straps
entries.body:
The field satchel's straps cross behind the shoulder and leave both hands free. Mira used an older bag during her apprenticeship, but its front buckle caught on her sleeve when she tried to lift someone. This design keeps the weight close and lets her carry a lantern or steady a patient. A traveling kit can bring care to a road crew, though its small supply cannot replace a stocked room.

Supplemental room note — the satchel during a long walk

Mira loads the satchel with jars, cloth and a lantern, then walks the lane twice before deciding where the straps should cross. The older bag used to swing forward when she knelt; its buckle caught her sleeve at exactly the moment she needed both hands. This one sits close to her back and opens from the side. Rowan watches her squat, rise and lift the lantern without loosening the straps.

The bag still has a limit. Mira removes one spare jar when the weight presses too hard on her shoulder and writes that choice on the packing card. A traveling healer who carries everything may arrive too tired to help. She does not want the satchel to look like a heroic burden. It is equipment that should be rearranged when the carrier's body says the load is wrong. The person wearing it decides what is comfortable enough to take onto the road.

entries.title: A Dry Roll for the Field Kit
entries.body:
Rowan fits a waxed cloth roll inside the field satchel. It separates the small jars and keeps dust away from their lids. Mira can remove one jar without emptying every pocket onto the road. She marks the roll with the Emberlily leaf so another healer can recognize its purpose. The field kit is easier to carry now, but it holds fewer supplies than a fixed shelf.

Supplemental room note — a pocket for each small thing

The waxed cloth roll has separate folds for jars and clean cloth. Mira ties each pocket with a different knot she can recognize in low light. She leaves one fold empty, not because it is waiting for a particular medicine but because an unexpected request should not require unpacking the whole satchel. Rowan asks whether the empty pocket makes the kit incomplete. Mira says an empty place can be part of a plan if it is labeled honestly.

Dust stays off the lids, and the roll can be removed from the satchel for a quick inventory. Mira writes a short list inside the fold rather than on the outside, where a passerby could read it. The kit identifies a healer's work, not the conditions of the people she has visited. At the end of each journey, the jars return to the herb table and are counted again. No one should discover that a supply is missing only when someone asks for it.

entries.title: A Route Wide Enough for Help
entries.body:
The folded Ashfall map shows two ways from the herb table to the east road. The eastern path is shorter but narrows beside a fallen lintel. The south gate takes longer and leaves enough room for a stretcher. Mira marks the wider route for the field kit. She would rather arrive a little later with space to help than follow the shortest line on the map and discover it cannot serve the person who needs her.

Supplemental room note — the route wide enough for a stretcher

The eastern path is shorter on the map, but a fallen lintel narrows it until two people cannot walk side by side. The southern gate adds several minutes and gives enough width for a stretcher or two helpers carrying a heavy load. Mira circles the wider route, then draws a second line to the east road in case the southern gate is blocked. The map is a working copy, not a guarantee that either path will stay open after rain or debris.

She asks Rowan to walk the route with the satchel and return by the same way. The time is written beside the weather and the condition of the gate. Mira does not want a single travel estimate turned into a rule for everyone; a person who moves more slowly may need another path or a pause. The note helps her prepare. It does not tell the person receiving help how quickly they must be found.

entries.title: Mira Chooses the Field Kit
entries.body:
Mira chooses a field satchel that can reach the east road and the wider south gate. She wants to offer care where a person is already resting rather than make a sick traveler walk back to Ashfall. The kit is deliberately small and each jar will be explained before it is offered. Mira understands that a mobile supply runs out sooner than a stocked room, so she will still return to the herb table between trips.

Supplemental room note — meeting people where they already are

Mira chooses the field kit because some people resting on the road will not be able to cross town to reach the clinic. She remembers how the village square filled after the raid and how a person could be surrounded by help and still have no clear route out. A mobile offer gives her a way to meet someone at a quieter place. It also means every supply has to travel with her and every trip requires a return for refills.

She does not call the kit freedom from the clinic. The satchel depends on the herb table for clean cloth, a work surface and replenishment. She plans to return after each route and leave the bag with Mira's own notes, not with a list of who accepted care. The choice lets her carry help outward while keeping a stable point where materials can be checked. If the road becomes unsafe, she can pause the trip; the choice does not demand that she go everywhere.

entries.title: The Field Satchel Mark
entries.body:
Mira attaches the Emberlily leaf beside the satchel's buckle. A villager can recognize the field kit before it is opened and can return it to the herb table after a journey. She wants the mark to identify a shared tool, not to imply that its carrier owns or controls the people who ask for help. The satchel is ready to travel with a healer who has chosen to carry it.

Supplemental room note — the leaf beside the buckle

The Emberlily mark sits next to the satchel's buckle, where another healer can recognize it without opening the bag. Mira chooses a leaf instead of a name. The satchel belongs to the treatment work and can be returned if its carrier cannot finish a route. It does not belong to the people who ask for help, and no one should read the mark as proof that its owner has authority over them.

The red thread is bright enough to find in a dim room. Mira tests that by turning the satchel over and asking Rowan to point to its opening without touching the straps. He finds it quickly. A clear mark saves time during a handoff, while the blank inside pocket keeps private notes out of view. When the kit returns, the next healer can check the seals and supply card. The plant symbol tells them what tool they found; it does not tell them whose story to ask for.

entries.title: The First Treatment Shift
entries.body:
Mira begins the first shift by asking each person whether they want help and what they are able to do themselves. She does not require a name or a written reason before offering a place to rest. The chosen setup, whether a fixed clinic or a traveling kit, changes how she carries supplies; it does not change the patient's right to hear an offer and decline it. The room is ready for its first visitor.

Supplemental room note — how the first offer begins

Mira begins each conversation with a question rather than a direction. “How would you like me to help?” leaves room for someone to describe a need she had not anticipated, ask only for a place to sit, or say that they want to be left alone. She listens before taking a jar from the shelf. Rowan sees that the room's first shift is not a test of how quickly the healer can use her supplies.

The record counts two people who visited, but does not list their names, injuries or choices. Mira will not turn the shift into proof that the clinic model works for everyone. One visitor used the cot; another only asked where the southern gate led. Both had a reason to enter, and neither has to become a case study. The supply total is written on one page and the visitors' private words stay outside the archive. The next shift begins from the same question.

entries.title: A Button Kept from Training
entries.body:
A small brass button sits in the mortar drawer. It carries a pressed leaf and a smooth edge rubbed by a thumb. Mira's mentor held it during long conversations, turning it slowly while the patient spoke. Mira kept the button after the treatment room closed, though she could not look at it without remembering her unfinished training. She takes it now as a reminder to listen before deciding which tool to reach for.

Supplemental room note — a button turned in the hand

The button from Mira's training years is brass with a small pressed leaf. Its edge is smooth where her mentor's thumb turned it during long pauses. Mira had once mistaken those pauses for uncertainty. Later she learned that her mentor was giving a patient time to find their own words. The button brings back that lesson more clearly than any of the old written instructions in the drawer.

Mira keeps it beside the mortar rather than wearing it as a badge. She is not her mentor, and the button does not certify her skill. Its place at the work surface reminds her to stop before reaching for the next tool. Rowan notices that she turns it once when a visitor declines the balm. She puts it down, listens, and asks whether the person wants anything else. The object has not changed; the way Mira uses the pause has.

entries.title: Mira's First Lesson
entries.body:
Mira's first mentor asked her to let a patient describe pain in their own words before she offered treatment. Mira once thought this was a lesson in politeness that slowed down a busy room. Her mentor explained that the person receiving care knows what they feel, while the healer knows what a remedy can do. A good decision needs both kinds of knowledge. Mira wants to keep the lesson even when the room fills again.

Supplemental room note — knowledge held on both sides

Mira's first mentor asked a student to hear a patient's description before proposing a remedy. At the time, Mira thought the sequence was inefficient. She wanted to show that she had learned the names of plants and could prepare a jar without help. Her mentor pointed out that a healer knows the limits of a remedy, while the person receiving care knows what they feel and what they are willing to try. A sound choice needs both kinds of knowledge.

The lesson had been written on a card, but the card is gone. Mira reconstructs it in her own words and leaves a space for someone to disagree. She says she can still ask the wrong question or misunderstand an answer. What matters is whether she leaves room to correct herself. Rowan watches her rewrite “patient report” as “what the visitor chose to tell us.” The new wording is longer because it admits that the archive does not own the other person's account.

entries.title: A Second Emberlily Packet
entries.body:
Mira supplies three Emberlily seeds from the portion she saved for the garden. She asks Rowan to leave at least one flower standing at harvest, so the bed can renew itself rather than supply every jar at once. The seeds are a small household lot and will not change the region's food or medicine reserve. Mira is beginning to think of the treatment room as a place with another season ahead of it.

Supplemental room note — returning seed to the bed

Mira divides a few Emberlily seeds from the flower left at the first harvest. She keeps one packet for the room and gives another to the neighbor who lent the original seed. The note calls the first seed a loan and the second a return; neither is entered into the village reserve. A small garden can keep its own promise without becoming a strategic store.

The neighbor has not promised to keep growing the plant, and Mira does not ask them to. The seed can be planted, shared again or kept through the winter according to the owner's choice. Rowan labels both packets by source and date, leaving the expected harvest field blank. A new season is possible, not guaranteed. Mira likes that the bed carries something forward, but she refuses to write “future supply” where only a handful of seeds have been counted.

entries.title: Emberlily for a Later Season
entries.body:
The second Emberlily bed produces another small harvest while leaving a mature flower for the next season. Mira prefers a modest yield that keeps the garden alive over stripping every open bloom for immediate use. She has seen medicinal beds disappear when all of their flowers were treated as stock. This patch gives the clinic petals for another balm batch and a visible sign that its medicine depends on care over time.

Supplemental room note — a harvest that leaves a flower

The second bed produces enough petals for another pair of balm portions while one mature flower remains on the plant. Mira chose the harvest line after comparing the stems, not because she expected a fixed yield. If the flower fails to seed, the garden will need another packet. If it succeeds, the next person who tends the bed can decide whether to plant or share. Rowan marks the living flower with a short stake so no one mistakes it for an unharvested accident.

The clinic uses what it needs and leaves the rest outside the jar count. Mira has seen a useful plant disappear when every bloom became inventory. This time the garden continues to belong to the season as well as to the room. She writes down the number of petals used and the number left, then folds the card so rain will not wash either line away.

entries.title: The Emberlily's Noon Shade
entries.body:
At midday, the treatment room's cloth shade covers the open Emberlily flower instead of the bed's hotter edge. Rowan moves it back one brick so the center receives more light. Mira recognizes that her mentor's old garden plan was made for a different wall and will not fit every room unchanged. The new placement lets the flower finish opening without putting the rest of the bed in direct afternoon heat.

Supplemental room note — the cloth shade moves at noon

The shade cloth was hung according to her mentor's old sketch, but the wall now blocks afternoon light differently. At noon, the cloth covers the Emberlily's open center while the eastern edge of the bed grows hot. Mira slides the cloth one brick back. Rowan makes a temporary mark on the wall, then checks the flower again after the shade moves with the sun.

The garden plan is not a rule that can be copied without looking at the site. Mira had once believed that respecting a teacher meant repeating every arrangement exactly. She now thinks it can mean keeping the purpose — protecting a flowering plant from excess heat — while changing the method to suit the room they have. The mark is dated and can be erased. If the wall, season or plant changes, the next gardener should test the shade again rather than follow the old line by habit.

entries.title: The Second Balm Batch
entries.body:
The second batch uses Emberlily from a new flowering and a fresh Moonwort leaf. The petals opened later in the warmer patch, so the balm has a brighter scent than the first pair. Mira covers the bowl with clean cloth while it binds. The recipe remains the same, but the harvest conditions have changed. Each batch contains two portions, allowing one to be offered during the evening round while the other remains available to Rowan.

Supplemental room note — comparing the second batch

The second Emberlily opened in warmer air than the first. Its scent is stronger, but Mira does not change the recipe by guesswork. She prepares the same small batch and writes down the harvest time, the petal condition and the Moonwort leaf used. A different smell may be worth noticing; it is not by itself proof that the balm is stronger or safer.

The bowl remains covered with clean cloth while the mixture binds. Rowan offers to label the jars, and Mira asks him to copy the source plants before writing the intended use. This order keeps the name of a remedy from hiding where it came from. Two portions are made again. One will be offered during the evening service; the other stays available for the player's inventory. The preparation record describes this batch only, so a future healer can compare without treating either one as a universal standard.

entries.title: The Cooling Jar
entries.body:
The second balm jar cools with its lid set aside so steam can escape. Mira closes it only after the rim is dry and marks the preparation day on a removable tag. She does not treat the tag as a guarantee of shelf life; it tells another healer when the jar was made so they can decide whether it is still suitable. The first jar remains open on the clinic shelf for the evening round.

Supplemental room note — when the lid goes on

Mira leaves the second jar uncovered until its rim feels dry. She does not seal warmth and moisture inside just to make the shelf look tidy. The removable tag carries the date, the ingredients and the phrase “check before use.” She deliberately leaves out an expiry claim she cannot support. A later healer can inspect the jar and decide whether it is still suitable, or discard it if anything has changed.

The old cabinet had a permanent label nailed to each shelf. Mira replaces those labels with cards that can be changed when the stock changes. A fixed inscription can make an empty shelf look as if a supply ought to be there. The new cards show the amount actually present and the day it was checked. Rowan copies that practice onto the field kit's packing sheet. The goal is not a perfect archive; it is to make the next decision possible without pretending someone already made it.

entries.title: An Evening Balm Offer
entries.body:
Mira explains the balm's limited use and asks the resting patient whether they want one portion. They accept it and keep the label beside the jar. The treatment uses one of the two portions made from the second harvest. The patient can decide how to apply it and may stop if it irritates the skin. Mira stays nearby to answer questions rather than treating the offer as permission to act without asking again.

Supplemental room note — an offer after the lamps are lit

The evening visitor does not ask for the balm at first. Mira explains what is in the jar, describes the small kind of injury it is meant for and points out the label. She asks whether they want a portion. The visitor accepts, then asks if it can wait until morning. Mira agrees and leaves the jar within reach, unopened. The next choice remains theirs.

One portion is still available from the second batch, and Mira writes that amount on the shelf card. She does not write who took the first offer or what they applied it to. Rowan sees how easily a care record could become a story about the healer's success instead of the visitor's decision. The evening shift closes with supplies counted and no claim that everyone who entered was treated. Mira stays by the door until the visitor has chosen whether to leave now or rest a little longer.

entries.title: The Wash Passage Cleared
entries.body:
An Ash Well Imp had been tipping the wash basin in the passage behind the treatment room. Rowan drove it away before it reached the open cot. Mira dries the floor and moves the basin back within reach of the bed. The imp's presence explains the fresh marks around the drain, but not every disturbance in the old house. The passage is clear for the evening; Mira will keep checking it when the garden draws creatures toward the water.

Supplemental room note — the wash passage after the fight

The Ash Well Imp had been tipping the basin and scattering grit into the passage. Rowan drives it away, but Mira checks the floor before carrying clean water through. The fight left new dust along the drain, while the older cracks remain where they were. She sweeps from the cot toward the doorway so the path stays clear rather than pushing debris back under the bed.

The encounter explains the fresh claw marks; it does not explain why the older stone shifted or whether the drain has a deeper problem. Mira puts a temporary cover over the basin when no one is using it. The room can reopen for the evening because the immediate path is clear, but she adds the passage to each shift's opening check. A healer should not have to spend the first part of every visit discovering that a creature has moved into the same corner again.

entries.title: Scratches around the Drain
entries.body:
The new scratches around the drain begin at the grate and run outward, matching the Ash Well Imp's small claws. Older cracks in the treatment room follow different seams. Rowan clears grit from the rim so Mira can hear if water starts backing up. Separating the fresh marks from old damage helps her repair the right thing, but it does not identify every cause of wear in a room that stood closed for so long.

Supplemental room note — separating new scratches from old seams

The small claws left marks from the drain outward. The older cracks run along the brick seam and do not have the same shape. Rowan sketches each pattern on a separate corner of the inspection card, while Mira keeps grit from falling back into the basin. The sketch helps a mason see what was present after the imp was driven away. It cannot show how the damage began before anyone looked closely.

Mira had once tried to explain the whole room's wear with a single cause because a simple answer seemed easier to repair. Now she prefers to leave two questions open: what did the imp do, and what had the closed room been doing to itself over time? The drain is clear for the moment. The next heavy rain may reveal something different, so the inspection card carries a date and a line for later comparison rather than a final verdict.

entries.title: The Right to Decline
entries.body:
Mira says she will explain what she knows, make room for another choice and stay available if a patient changes their mind. Her mentor taught that care without a way to refuse becomes another kind of pressure. Mira once struggled to hear a refusal as anything but a judgment of her skill. The reopened room gives her a chance to practice listening without treating acceptance as proof that she was right or refusal as a failure.

Supplemental room note — when an offer ends

Mira says that an offer of care has to stop being an offer the moment the other person says no. Her first instinct used to be to list every reason a treatment might help. She thought persistence would show that she cared. Her mentor told her that the patient should not need to win an argument to refuse. Mira still finds the silence after a refusal difficult, especially when she believes she has prepared something useful.

The room's arrangement now supports the boundary: the door opens from inside, the bell can be reached from the cot and the jar is not already in someone's hands. Mira can stay nearby if asked, or step away if that is what the visitor wants. She writes the principle on a small card for herself rather than posting it as a rule over patients. Rowan sees her put the card beside the button from her mentor. It is a reminder to practice, not a claim that she will never get it wrong.

entries.title: A Button on the Curtain
entries.body:
The cloth from Mira's mentor's apron has become too brittle to hold a repair. The brass button's shank remains sound, so Mira attaches it with a new dark thread to the treatment room's curtain. She does not wear it as a badge or claim the old apron as her own uniform. The pressed leaf stays visible beside the door, where it can remind her of her training without standing in for the person who taught her.

Supplemental room note — mending the curtain without keeping the apron

The old apron cloth tears when Mira tries to sew the button back into it. She stops, folds the brittle piece and stores it separately instead of cutting it into strips for the room. The thread of its history matters to her even if the fabric can no longer be used. A new curtain receives the button with dark thread, and the original apron stays in the drawer as something she does not have to turn into equipment.

Mira chooses a place near the doorway where the button can be seen when the curtain is drawn. It marks a pause before entering, not ownership of the person inside. Rowan asks whether the curtain is meant to block every sound. Mira says no: it softens the view while leaving the hand bell and open exit available. The cloth can be moved aside at the visitor's request. A piece of training follows Mira into the room, but it does not get to decide how the room is used.

entries.title: A Quiet Bell beside the Cot
entries.body:
Mira hangs a small hand bell within reach of the cot. One tap can reach the herb table through the open door, but the sound does not carry into the street. A patient can call for help without announcing their name or condition to everyone outside. Mira tests the bell once and leaves it where its user can decide whether to ring. The room becomes easier to use without asking anyone to perform their need in public.

Supplemental room note — a signal small enough to choose

The hand bell sits on a low hook beside the cot. Mira tests it from the stool and hears one clear tap at the herb table. From the street, the sound disappears under the wind. She does not want a patient to have to shout through an open door to get her attention, and she does not want a private need broadcast across the square. The bell offers one small way to call, but no one is required to use it.

The visitor can move the bell closer, leave it alone or ask Mira to take it down. Rowan writes the location on the room plan, not on a record of who rang. If the bell is out of reach for a particular person, the arrangement needs to change. Mira keeps the cord long enough to move and short enough not to tangle around the cot. It is a tool for communication, not a signal that the healer owns the room's next response.

entries.title: A Sign with Room to Choose
entries.body:
The red-leaf marker can be seen from the path into Ashfall without revealing the cot or the person resting there. Whether the village chose a fixed room or a traveling kit, the mark points toward help while leaving the visitor free to decide how close to come. Mira wants the sign to make care easier to find, not to make anyone's need visible to the whole road.

Supplemental room note — a mark visible from the path

The red-leaf sign is tested from the gate at dusk and again in the morning. It can be seen without showing the cot through the window. A passerby can identify where help may be offered without learning who has entered or why. Mira keeps the wording spare. A sign that lists conditions or expected patients would turn the entrance into a public record of private needs.

In the fixed-clinic route, the sign points toward the open room and its posted hours. In the field-kit route, the same mark tells a traveler where Mira can be found between journeys. It is not a promise that she is present at every moment. Rowan makes a small space for Mira to change the time card when her route changes. The sign helps people find her work; it does not decide whether they should come closer.

entries.title: A Stool beside the Work Surface
entries.body:
A small stool fits beside Mira's work surface without blocking the clear path to the door. Someone can sit while they speak with her, rather than being asked to stand over the cot or wait outside. The stool is light enough to move when the room needs more space. Mira likes that the room can hold a conversation without forcing a person to stay in the same place once it has ended.

Supplemental room note — the stool does not belong to the healer

The stool stands beside the work surface, but Mira asks Rowan to carry it to the other side of the room and try the layout again. A visitor may want to sit near the door, look toward the garden or have no seat at all. The stool is light enough to move without turning every preference into a request for permission. When someone is speaking, the healer can sit too; the room does not require one person to stand as the authority.

Mira remembers her mentor working through long shifts without resting. She once copied that posture as if exhaustion were proof of commitment. The empty stool is a quiet correction to that habit. If Mira sits between visitors, she may be more able to listen through the next conversation. Rowan notes where the stool can be placed without blocking the basin path. The mark is a guide, not a fixed position. The room should be rearranged around the people using it.

entries.title: Afterword: Care without a Locked Door
entries.body:
Mira keeps the treatment room open and the field satchel ready under the policy Rowan chose. The first Emberlily harvest supplied balm for an evening patient, while the second flowering began a garden that can renew itself. The Ashfall clinic does not promise a remedy for every wound or a healer at every hour. Mira's former training room has returned as a place where a person can ask for care, accept it, decline it or leave without being trapped by the offer.

Supplemental room note — a practice that can change

At the end of the first run of shifts, Mira reviews the supply card, the door inspection and her own notes. She does not write a total for “people healed.” That column would turn different needs and private choices into one claim she cannot support. She writes what is available, what was offered, what remains to be checked and when she plans to return. The field kit route adds distance and rest stops; the fixed clinic route adds a posted hour and a room to maintain. Each needs a different daily routine.

Mira leaves the clinic sign and satchel mark in place, but neither becomes permanent law. If the room becomes unsafe or the road changes, she can revise the arrangement. The Emberlily garden may renew its seeds, or it may fail in the next season. Rowan's help gave her a place to begin, not a finished answer about care. The afterword leaves a space for the next healer to disagree with Mira and for the next visitor to choose differently.

entries.title: The Slate Was Never a Roster
entries.body:
I reopened the east bed because the slate had been copied into three separate training binders, each with the same blank interval after heavy rain. I thought the empty line meant someone had failed to report. The stone beside the gutter made me doubt that reading: its lower scratch was older than the newer roof hinge, and water could not have followed both marks at once.

Rowan asked why I had not simply corrected the slate years ago. I had no satisfying answer. I preserved the wording because I feared changing a record without understanding it. Then I began treating preservation as if it were the same thing as care. The mint seed in the step crack survived without a schedule, while the garden remained closed because I would not teach an incomplete one.

The bed is not proof that the old rotation worked. It is a place to learn what its writer could not leave in the margin: how the channel behaves now, what a small crop needs, and who wants to tend it. Keep the original slate with this note. Anyone reopening the bed should be allowed to replace our lesson with a better one.

entries.title: The Space Left by the Rain
entries.body:
The slate places the blank interval between an evening watering turn and the next morning's check. Rain is recorded in the margin, but not in the square where a cadet's name would usually go. The stone below the gutter holds a lower waterline, while a second scratch lies closer to the drain frame. They do not line up well enough to be one measurement.

Elara first read the space as a missing person. The tools tell a smaller story: the watering can stayed beneath the awning, the soil did not need another pour, and the runoff channel had filled with grit. Someone may have paused the rota to avoid adding water. We cannot identify who made that decision, or whether one person made it at all.

I have marked the blank with a weather note rather than a name. That does not settle the old record; it only gives the next reader another possibility to compare. The garden's slate should never be copied into the cadet roll as evidence of attendance. A pause in work and a missing cadet are different claims, even when the same empty square tempts us to join them.

entries.title: Years Preserved, No Water Given
entries.body:
I kept the old rotation beside my desk long after the bed closed. When new cadets asked about the blank interval, I repeated the explanation I had inherited: the slate was incomplete, so no one should act on it. That sounded careful. It also meant I never had to find out whether the runoff could be measured again.

The garden remained clean on paper. No one watered a dry plot, no one signed a turn they had not taken, and no one could be blamed for a bad crop. But the mint pushed through a crack at the east step, a stubborn plant outside the record's reach. Rowan brought me one of its leaves, and for the first time I saw that my perfect copy had described a garden no one was tending.

I am not ashamed of keeping the slate. I am ashamed that I let the copy stand in for teaching. The new lesson begins with what we can touch: soil, water, the bent hinge and a seed that may not sprout twice. A cadet can decline a turn. A record can say the bed was idle. Neither statement erases the work of the people who kept the old pages dry.

entries.title: A Hinge That Lets the Channel Breathe
entries.body:
The lower hinge carries two grooves where a clip could rest, one above the gutter and one level with the catch pocket. The lower groove is easy to reach but fills with grit. The upper groove stays cleaner, though a person standing at the bed cannot read a water mark there without leaning over the stones.

Elara asked me to sketch both positions without choosing for the next keeper. We checked the old frame first. It bends when pressed near the channel, so no fitting should be used to brace it or stop its movement. The runoff has to pass through the gutter whether the garden is planted or not. Blocking it would turn an observation tool into a dam.

The useful quality of a marker is not that it never moves. It is that someone can remove it, clean around it and see the channel underneath. I left room in the sketch for a hand to reach the fastener. The frame is still damaged and needs a carpenter's inspection before heavy rain. This note covers placement for a small trial only; it is not a repair order for the roof gutter.

entries.title: Mint from the Step Crack
entries.body:
The first Dawnmeadow Mint did not grow in a prepared row. It appeared in the narrow crack where the step meets the wall, fed by spray from the gutter and warmed by the stone after midday. I saved a seed when the plant flowered, but I did not label it as the last living seed or the strongest one. Several pods were still closed when I gathered this sample.

Rowan planted one seed in the reopened bed. It needed a full crop cycle before we could cut a leaf without pulling the root. The mint smell was strongest after the leaves dried on the table; the fresh ones carried more water than scent. The difference matters to a healer, but we have not tested either batch as medicine. Mira asked us to keep the harvest separate from her remedy stock until she can inspect it.

A seed saved from one crack can restart one small row under these conditions. It does not promise that the plant will take in another bed, nor that the gutter will keep the soil wet. I have placed the remaining seed packets beside this note so a future gardener may compare the two crops. If none are planted next season, record that too. Quiet ground is not a failed lesson.

entries.title: A Trout Scale beside a Ruler
entries.body:
Elara needed a thin mark that would not split in the gutter's damp air. The Blackreed Trout scale was flexible when wet and stiffened as it dried; that gave us a way to set a short edge against the bronze clip. It is an odd ruler, but it was available at the lakeshore and easy to replace with another sample.

I wrote down the catch location and the time before trimming the scale. Its dark rim faded after it dried, and the pale center curled when left near the forge. We adjusted the clip while the scale was still damp, then let the material dry away from the flame. It now marks a height. It does not measure the safety of the lake, the age of the fish or the level of water in every gutter.

The fish returned to the food basket after the scale was taken. No part of the catch was kept as a permanent standard. A later sample may be a different size; whoever makes a new clip should record that difference rather than forcing it to match this piece. Elara wants the garden tool to be replaceable, not rare. The measure belongs to the trial and its conditions, not to a species name.

entries.title: Two Scratches on the Gutter Stone
entries.body:
The pale lower scratch crosses a patch of moss that now grows only on one side of the gutter. The higher mark is sharper, nearer the bent frame. It may be a second waterline, or it may be a tool scrape left when the roof hinge was handled. The stone does not tell us who made either mark.

Nia suggested measuring the distance from each scratch to the fixed corner rather than comparing one to the other. That makes the notes easier to repeat: a reader can find the corner even if the moss grows over the old line. I took two readings after the mint had been watered and a third after the catch pocket was emptied. The lower mark stayed damp; the upper one did not.

These readings are not a history of the storm. They are three present-day observations with different conditions. A future student may find that the moss has moved, the hinge has been repaired or the stones have settled. Keep the measurements beside the date and weather, and start a new column rather than overwriting ours. If no one can tell which mark is which, the correct entry is “uncertain,” not a blended average.

entries.title: Handing over a Turn without a Name
entries.body:
The old handoff slate gives every turn a fixed name before the person has a chance to see the weather or the bed. That works only when the schedule survives the week unchanged. At Dawnkeep, drill times move, rain closes the yard and a cadet may be sent to a different hall. The record then treats a changed duty like a missing one.

Elara asked how I would write a garden turn without handing someone a permanent place in the rota. I suggested recording what needs attention first: inspect the drain, water the mint if the soil is dry, clear grit after rain. A person can choose one task, ask someone else to take it or leave the slate untouched until conditions change. The next keeper writes what actually happened, not what a prior copy expected.

A handoff is useful when the person receiving it can see the state of the work and decline to inherit the schedule. The roster I keep for cadets has its own corrections and missing replies; I will not copy it into a garden list. The bed has no attendance requirement. I left a blank line for whoever volunteers to note a task, and another for a later reader to revise the instructions.

entries.title: Bronze Clip, Mint Fiber, Fish Scale
entries.body:
The clip is made from a narrow bronze strip, a twist of Dawnmeadow Mint fiber and one Blackreed Trout scale. The fiber stops the metal edge from scraping the old frame; the scale provides a short reference mark. None of these parts makes the gutter stronger. Tomas checked the fastener and asked us to leave the cracked hinge visible for a carpenter.

At the forge we bent the bronze over a cold block rather than heating it until the color changed. A hotter strip held its shape, but it also crushed the scale when we fitted the padding. The softer piece can be opened with a hand tool. It is less impressive than a permanent brace and easier to remove after the test.

The clip's mark is readable only when the scale is clean and the bed's edge is not hidden by leaves. Elara will keep spare fiber in a dry envelope. If the scale curls, the fiber loosens or the metal bites into the frame, the clip should come down. The object records a water level during a short trial. It is not a structural part, a roof repair or a guarantee that the channel will stay clear.

entries.title: A Mark That Can Be Taken Down
entries.body:
We placed the clip in the upper groove, where a keeper can read it from the stone path and remove it without reaching into the runoff. The catch pocket remains open. After Rowan fitted the fastener, I ran one cup of water through the gutter to see whether the mark touched the stream. It did not. The test was short and took place in dry weather.

I asked Rowan to leave the clip in place for one observation, then take it down before cleaning the frame. A tool that can be removed invites its owner to inspect what lies behind it. A permanent mark would be easier to copy into a diagram, but it might hide damage or gather grit at the hinge. The old frame still needs a proper repair; the clip does not change that.

We will not ask cadets to climb the roof or handle a fast stream to repeat this check. The garden path is enough for the next reading. If the waterline passes the mark, if metal begins to press against the wood, or if the pocket fills, remove the clip and write the condition beside the date. The lesson is the removable measure and the way to question it, not a claim that the gutter has been made safe.

entries.title: A Map with No Destination
entries.body:
Captain Alden sent me to Dawnkeep with a narrow map folded inside the dispatch. It showed the gate, the eastern yard and three paths down toward Cinderwell. No destination was marked at the end of those paths. I thought the missing label was a clerk's mistake. Elara Wren looked at the fold instead: the paper had been pressed flat so often that the road below the outpost had nearly vanished.

She asked me to speak with her before reporting what the map meant. That was the first order I received here, and the first one whose meaning I could not establish by carrying it out. I can say that Alden sent me, that the map was made for a journey south, and that Elara had been waiting for someone to ask about the old stone. I cannot yet say who traveled that road or why.

I have copied the route without filling the empty destination. A blank on a map might hide a lost village, a discarded plan or a place its maker did not wish to name. I was taught to draw a line until it reached a border. At Dawnkeep, the border is the part we have to investigate.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the fold Elara would not flatten

Elara set the map beneath a pane of glass but left the deep fold untouched. I offered to warm the paper over a lamp so the southern road would lie flat. She moved the lamp away before I could try. The ink had cracked along the crease, and heat might have lifted the faintest line from the page. Instead, she placed a narrow weight at either end and let the curl ease by itself while we copied the visible marks.

She did not tell me where the road ended. She asked which part of the route I could describe without naming its destination. I said there were two lock points, one service road, and a turn where the water narrowed. She added the height of the stone posts and the direction the water ran at that hour. Her map-making is not a habit of filling space. She gives an unknown a border and leaves it room to remain unknown.

By evening the page rested flat enough for a clean copy. We put the original back in its sleeve rather than pinning it beside the yard map. The line is legible now, but it still stops before Cinderwell. Elara says a map can guide an investigation without pretending that the journey has already happened. I had thought an unfinished route was a failed drawing. At Dawnkeep I learned to carry a question without drawing the answer for it.

entries.title: An Impression of the Chiseled List
entries.body:
The east face of the roster stone holds two kinds of marks. Names were cut deep enough to survive the weather; shorter strokes lie between them, where a chisel appears to have passed across the surface. Rowan pressed a sheet over the stone and made a rubbing. The impression keeps the gaps visible, though it flattens every cut into the same dark line.

I recognize the arrangement from an older training copy. It was filed with the yard ledgers, not the muster rolls, and the heading is missing from both. One clerk may have copied the list into another book before anyone scraped it. The rubbing cannot tell us whether a name was removed for correction, privacy or some other reason. It cannot restore the names that no longer catch the paper.

We should keep the rubbing beside a sketch of the stone and note which marks are original. Do not trace the gaps into a new roster as if they were names. An impression preserves the shape of what remains; it does not recreate the person who might once have stood between the cuts.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — pressure from the chisel

The rubbing darkened where I pressed hardest. Elara saw the difference before I did: one of the short strokes looked like a name because the paper caught more graphite there. She asked me to lift the sheet and repeat the pass with a softer block. The second impression was lighter, but it kept the weathered groove and the shallow scrape separate.

We compared the two sheets with the stone in late afternoon light. A cut that seemed to run beneath another mark in the morning ended at its edge when the sun moved. That does not tell us which mark came first; the stone may have been turned, or the surface may have worn unevenly. Elara recorded the angle of the light, the distance of the paper from the eastern seam and which hand held the block. A future copyist can repeat those conditions and judge the impressions for themselves.

The first sheet remains attached to the field sketch. The second is filed as a repeat, not a correction. I wanted the darker sheet to be the better one because it made the roster easier to read. Elara reminded me that clarity can be manufactured by pressure. We can show the marks more plainly without making them say more than the stone does.

entries.title: Two Costs of a Copy
entries.body:
The roster impression can be shown to the patrol or kept while we search the archive. Either course carries a cost. If the patrol sees it now, every empty space will become a question asked in the yard, and the living will have to answer questions the stone cannot settle. If it remains with the archive, those questions may wait while we find a second record. They may also wait because someone prefers the silence.

I put the choice before Rowan as an officer's decision, then asked him to carry it. That is not the same as giving him a clean choice. The copy has already passed through my hands and the Order's rules have shaped what he can do with it. If I hide that, I make his decision look freer than it is.

The patrol deserves to know when an official record is incomplete. It also deserves to know that the marks are uncertain. I have no authority to make the uncertainty disappear for the sake of a simpler report. Whichever version is kept, let the written account name who received it, when it changed hands and which questions remain unanswered.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the runner who carried both copies

I carried the rubbing from Elara's workroom to Captain Alden's table, then carried two sealed instructions back: one for the yard registrar and one for the archive drawer. The envelopes weighed almost nothing. I remember checking each seal twice because I was afraid of delivering the wrong choice to the wrong place.

Elara asked me what I thought should happen. I said the patrol should see the evidence. Alden asked what I would tell a family who read its name beside an empty space. I had no answer. My first response was a wish for speed; his question made me notice the people who would have to live with whatever speed did to the record.

The captain's note did not choose for me, though it shaped the choice by naming consequences I had not considered. I keep both instructions in this archive because a later reader might otherwise imagine that I decided alone. My decision was real, and so were the limits around it: I did not make the rubbing, set its custody rule, or know the missing destination. The branch we followed changed who could read the page first. It did not change what the page proves.

entries.title: The Yard after the Rubbing Was Read
entries.body:
The patrol gathered by the east wall when Rowan read the rubbing aloud. I expected anger first. Instead, the first person to speak asked whether the strokes between the names were old tally marks. Another cadet wanted to know why a training stone had been copied into the archive at all. No one had enough information to answer either question.

I said what I knew: the stone has deep-cut names, shorter marks and a heading that is no longer attached to the record. I also said what I did not know: who made the cuts, whether the list was complete, or whether the people it once described were sent south. Several listeners had family names in the surviving lines. They deserved the plain account, not my confidence in a guess.

The rubbing now hangs beside a slate with room for corrections. Some will write to relatives; others may ask to have their name checked against the remaining rolls. Those requests will take time. Reading the record publicly changed who could question it, not what it proves. I will keep the first copy unmarked so a later correction does not erase what the patrol saw today.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the question after the reading

When the noticeboard reading ended, a cadet stayed behind to ask whether the list had been used to decide who was allowed to leave. Elara answered that the record before us could not settle that. The cadet looked at the surviving names and said that an incomplete answer was still an answer the Order had chosen to give. Elara did not correct them. She wrote the question on a separate card, with the time and the page the cadet had seen.

Nia asked whether the card should carry the cadet's name. The cadet said no. We filed the question without one and added a note that the speaker had requested anonymity. The public copy still shows its source seal, but the question is not evidence that any particular person was transferred. It is evidence that a reader asked how the roster had been used.

Elara read the card back before placing it in the review box. She has started doing this whenever a visitor asks for a correction; a person should be able to hear the words the archive intends to keep. The yard grew quiet after the exchange. We did not count who stayed. We recorded one question we could answer only by finding another source.

entries.title: The Drawer and the Missing Key
entries.body:
Rowan kept the rubbing with the archive while I searched for its heading. I locked it in the shallow drawer beside the yard ledgers. The drawer has room for one copy and no separate compartment for the questions it carries. I have written the inventory on the outside: one rubbing, one sketch of the stone, no restored names, no proof of where the patrol went.

I told the cadets we were checking the record before we spoke about it. Some accepted that explanation. Others asked who had chosen the delay. I said I had helped make it. That answer did not make the lock gentler, but it kept me from presenting privacy as something the archive had decided on its own.

The key stays with the registrar. If a family asks about a surviving name, they may request a supervised reading rather than wait for the entire investigation to finish. We have not found the old heading yet. Until we do, the drawer protects the fragile sheet from careless handling; it also limits who can see it. Put both effects in the catalogue. A locked record can prevent damage and postpone accountability at the same time.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the key's daily route

The shallow drawer key is not kept in the registrar's office overnight. At closing, the registrar signs it over to the watch captain, who carries it while the hall is unlocked. In the morning the captain returns it before reading the access log. Elara discovered the routine when she asked to inspect the rubbing after the clerk had gone home; the ledger named a custodian, but not where the key would be.

She added a location column and a line for an emergency handoff. Alden objected that a lost key could reveal the archive's weakness. Elara replied that a location hidden from the person who needed access was not security; it was uncertainty with a lock around it. They settled on a sealed daily log kept in the watch office, with the public index naming the responsible role but not the room where the key rested.

No one opened the drawer that night. The new procedure did not make its contents public, and the sealed sheet did not identify the family names inside. It made custody easier to question if the key went missing. Elara says that privacy needs a keeper whose actions can be checked, even when the protected page cannot be read by everyone.

entries.title: Beds Put Away for Inspection
entries.body:
The old barracks hold an uneven row of cots. Some frames were dismantled cleanly and stacked against the wall. Others still carry the chalk numbers used to assign sleeping places. Dust covers the lower boards, but a narrow path runs between them, as if someone continued to enter the room after it was closed.

I found a heel mark beside one frame and a pale strip where a blanket may have rested. Neither tells me how long ago a person slept there. A number on wood is an instruction for a place, not a name. The surviving roster has empty spaces, yet I cannot match those spaces to these beds. The room may have housed cadets whose records were kept elsewhere; it may have been used for more than one class.

I drew every cot before moving the ones that blocked the passage. The sketch records which frames were whole, which were split and which chalk numbers remained. We did not find a personal letter, a weapon or anything that would identify an occupant. Until another source connects the room to the roster, the honest description is an empty barracks with numbered beds.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the board beneath the third bed

While we lifted the split cot from the passage, a loose board shifted under its rear leg. There was no paper beneath it, only a line of pale grit and a small copper washer. Elara recognized the washer as the kind used on the barracks window latches. We found one latch with a newer screw and another still bound by a strip of leather. Neither repair could be dated from the metal alone.

The floor marks changed when the cot moved. A dark rectangle that looked like the footprint of a trunk vanished under the dust we had disturbed. I sketched both conditions before sweeping: first the room as we found it, then the exposed board and washer. The first drawing preserves the evidence before our work; the second shows what the inspection uncovered. We marked the cot as moved so nobody will mistake the after-sketch for the original arrangement.

The washer tells us that someone maintained a window latch. It does not identify a sleeper or prove that a particular bed was occupied when the roster changed. I wanted the empty room to yield a name. It yielded a repair detail, which is smaller but still useful: a future inspection can compare the other latches without inventing a person to fit the space.

entries.title: Nia's Correction in the Margin
entries.body:
When I was a cadet, I copied the night assignments into the return ledger. A transfer order arrived with more beds counted than signatures at the gate. I added a mark in the margin and asked the clerk whether to change the total. The clerk said to leave the number as issued because a route order was not proof of arrival. I did. Later copies carried the total but not my question.

I remember this because the question was mine, not because I know which people the number describes. I saw a sealed packet taken south. I did not see its passengers. I heard two versions of why the roster changed, each from someone who had read a different page. Neither version came from a person who could show me the receiving record.

Please file this as testimony about my work on the ledger. Do not use my account to fill the empty cots or restore the erased marks. I can point to the margin where I wrote the question if the old book is found. Until then, someone else's copy of what I remember should remain open to correction by the person who first made the mark.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — Nia's second look at the margin

Nia returned to the ledger with the original question she had written as a cadet. She had remembered a hooked mark at the end of the line. The page we found contains a short diagonal stroke instead. She ran one finger above the ink without touching it, then asked me to read the sentence aloud exactly as it stood. The words were hers; the mark might have been hers, a later correction, or a copyist's shorthand.

She declined to replace her earlier account. Instead she wrote a new note: the remembered shape and the visible shape differ, and she cannot now say when the change occurred. That costs her the confidence of a clean recollection. She said she would rather lose a detail than pretend her memory had not shifted while she spent years retelling the event.

Elara asked whether Nia wanted the two accounts displayed together. Nia chose the archive copy, accessible by request, and asked that the public summary mention the disagreement without printing her old work schedule. She remembers an error in a total and a sealed packet leaving the desk. She still does not know who traveled south. The margin remains a question she can help us examine, not a key to other people's identities.

entries.title: A Dispatch with No Return Column
entries.body:
The transfer ledger places a set of cadet numbers beside an order for the southern road. A clerk has marked that the packet was sealed and issued. The column for a receiving signature is blank. A second page lists stores sent to Cinderwell, but the quantities do not map cleanly to the numbers on the first page. Someone may have joined two records when they copied the ledger.

Nia recognized the margin mark as the one she used when the return count did not match the order. Her mark proves she questioned the total. It does not prove which version was right. I have kept the first and second pages apart in the transcription, noting where the old binding placed them together. A neat table would make their relationship look more certain than it is.

There is no return column at all, only a space where a receiver might have signed. That space cannot tell us whether the party arrived, was redirected or was entered in a different book. The next search should follow the seal number and the supply trail through Cinderwell. Until a receiving document is found, this ledger establishes an order sent south and a record-keeping gap.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — a scale checked against an empty pan

The store quantities in the transfer ledger did not match the weights on the duplicate dispatch. Before we treated that as a discrepancy, Rowan asked the quartermaster to test the scale with an empty pan and a standard stone. The beam returned to its mark. Then we learned that one sheet counted sacks and the other recorded the weight of grain after two torn bags had been repacked.

The totals still differ, but their units differ too. A later clerk had copied the figures into one column and drawn a line between them, making them look like competing counts of the same goods. We made a comparison sheet that keeps sack count, estimated weight and repacked amount separate. The torn-bag note has a different hand from the dispatch signature, so we left authorship blank.

This check narrows the question. The supplies may have continued south in more than one form; the ledger does not yet tell us who accepted them or whether they traveled with the listed cadets. Alden recognized the quartermaster's mark but did not use it to identify a recipient. We can reconcile a measurement without reconciling the journey. The blank return column remains the record we most need to find.

entries.title: The Limit of Naming Names
entries.body:
The ledger gives us a count, a route and several names that survived the scraping. A few families have already asked whether their relatives were on the list. We cannot use the missing return signature to answer them. We can only show which marks remain, which copy they came from and which clerk last handled it.

Publishing the verified names gives families a starting point for their own questions. Sealing the original and sending private copies gives them access without placing every surviving name on a public wall. Neither option tells a family what happened after the dispatch left Dawnkeep. Elara asked Rowan to decide which kind of access he could stand behind while the investigation continued.

I would like to make the choice for him. That would be easier than seeing what the Order's old habits have taught us to call protection. The family copies must not become secret replacements for the public record, and a public list must not be mistaken for a complete roll. Record who can ask for a correction, who can see the source and how a copy can be withdrawn if a family requests it. A name belongs to the person first; the archive only keeps the marks we can justify.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the family that asked for the method
