A family came to the archive carrying no claim about the roster. They asked how we decided which marks were legible and whether they could have the method card without receiving a copy of the names. Elara showed them the graphite rubbing, the stone sketch and the two lighting conditions used in the comparison. They checked the method card and said it was enough for now.

Their request changed the choice we had framed as public names or sealed copies. Access to a method is not the same as access to a person's record. We added an option to request the comparison procedure by itself, and a separate form for families who want a verified copy of the evidence. The new form does not ask why someone needs it. It asks what material they are requesting and where the registrar should send it.

The family did not ask us to withhold or publish any name. We will not describe their visit as support for either branch. Alden said the Order should learn to offer a useful answer before a person has to reveal why they came. Elara added that a method card can still carry errors, so it includes the date and the observer who prepared it. The roster question remains open; our way of asking it has become more precise.

entries.title: A Noticeboard with a Correction Line
entries.body:
We posted the verified copy at the yard noticeboard with the seal still visible and a blank line beneath every uncertain entry. The line is not a request for passersby to guess at the missing names. It lets someone who has a source leave a note about where the registrar can check it. I have put a small box beside the board for letters that should not be read aloud.

Some cadets stopped to look, then left without writing. One asked whether an empty place beside a surviving name meant that a sibling was sent away. I told them the copy does not show that. It shows a name, a cut and the absence of a return signature in the ledger we have. The answer disappointed them. I would rather disappoint someone honestly than offer a story that becomes harder to correct.

The board will stay up for one week before the pages are reviewed for private details. If a family wants a name withheld, the request will be attached to the next copy rather than scraped off the current one without a trace. Public access needs a route for correction and a way to limit harm; otherwise the first posting only gives the loudest reader control of the next version.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — reading the correction line aloud

Nia took the first evening shift beside the noticeboard. A visitor could not see the small print from the walkway, so Nia read the instructions aloud when asked. One person wanted to correct a spelling but had no source with them. Another brought a letter and did not want its contents read in public. Nia gave them an envelope and showed where it would be stored until the registrar could review it.

The board's open line had been intended for references to other records. It looked like an invitation for anyone to write a missing name. Nia covered that line with a short instruction: “Tell us where to check; do not guess here.” She dated the change and kept a copy of the earlier board in the archive. The amendment makes the process clearer without hiding that the first version could mislead.

No one left a correction that night. We recorded the two requests by subject and marked the second as private correspondence. Nia asked me not to call the shift quiet; a lack of written entries cannot tell us how many people read the board or decided not to approach it. She chose to sit there again the next evening, after the amended notice was copied in larger letters.

entries.title: Copies Beneath Family Seals
entries.body:
We placed the original rubbing in the archive drawer and prepared one verified copy for each family who asked to receive one. The copy states how many marks remain legible, which pages were compared and where the receiving signature is missing. I sealed each envelope with the registrar's mark and recorded the recipient privately. A seal can show that the paper was handled through the archive; it cannot prove the contents are complete.

The families may keep their copy, return it or request a fresh one after the next comparison. They do not have to send a reason with a correction. I have also kept an unsealed transcription so that a later registrar can compare the public evidence without opening a family's letter. There are two records of distribution, but only one source rubbing. Neither should be treated as the original.

I used to think a sealed record was a safer record. Now I think it is only safer for as long as people can find its keeper and ask what the seal means. The drawer will be catalogued by subject and date, not by the names whose families received copies. A person looking for a relative should not need to search through someone else's private correspondence.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the envelope returned unopened

One family brought its sealed copy back to the registrar with the wax intact. They had received the packet but had not opened it. The person delivering it asked for a receipt that said only that the envelope had been returned. They did not explain why. Elara checked the seal number, recorded the date, and asked whether the packet should go back into the drawer or be held for pickup.

The family requested that it be kept for one month, then destroyed if nobody returned. That instruction was written on a separate custody card and signed by the person who delivered the envelope. We did not add a reason or a household description. The roster copy itself remains sealed, so the return tells us nothing about whether the family read or accepted its contents.

Elara marked the packet as temporarily held and set a reminder for the named date. She says a copy belongs to its recipient even when it comes back to us; the archive cannot infer that silence means consent to keep it forever. The sealed-copy route now has a clear end point for an unwanted document. The record we retain is limited to the custody request the family chose to make.

entries.title: The Waterway Points South
entries.body:
Elara spread the dispatch across the map of the waterway to Cinderwell. The route follows a service road above the channel, crossing two lock points before it reaches the lower basin. The inked arrow marks where the packet was meant to travel. It does not mark a boat, a camp or a group of cadets. I have written “planned route” beside it so a later reader will not mistake the line for a travel log.

The seals on the dispatch match the format Nia described. One clerk's mark appears beside the stores list, but the receiving space remains empty. At the second lock, the margin carries a note about a gate inspection. No names accompany it. These details give us places to visit and records to request. They do not yet show who passed through either lock.

Cinderwell can tell us whether the supply order was received, whether another ledger survives and whether the seal continued south. It cannot make the missing signature appear in the Dawnkeep book. We leave with better questions than we had when the map was folded: who accepted the packet, which copy they kept and whether the people counted in the roster traveled with it.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the lockkeeper's torn corner

At the first lock below Dawnkeep, the keeper showed us a ledger with a missing lower corner. The remaining paper carried the dispatch seal number and a note that a packet had been passed to the southbound store boat. The entry did not list passengers. Its water stain had spread through the receiving column, so no signature could be recovered from the surviving fibers.

The lockkeeper remembered that the boat stopped again at the lower basin to take on an empty barrel. She could not remember its crew or whether the sealed packet stayed aboard. We recorded her recollection separately from the ledger and asked her to review the wording before it was filed. She corrected “delivered to Cinderwell” to “passed toward the southbound boat.” The distinction is hers, and it keeps our copy from claiming the packet reached its destination.

Rowan traced the torn corner and made a protective sleeve so the page can be handled without losing more fibers. We have a point on the route and a transfer to a boat, not a receiving record. Elara thanked the keeper without asking her to guess who might have carried the dispatch. The next search follows the boat's store account and the barrel's return mark.

entries.title: The Captain's Signature Does Not Answer
entries.body:
My signature appears at the bottom of the transfer order. It authorizes a dispatch of supplies and cadet numbers toward Cinderwell. I remember signing the page. I cannot claim that the memory tells me what happened after the packet left my desk, or why the return column in the surviving ledger was never completed.

I once used the word routine when Rowan asked about the signature. Routine is useful when a hundred orders need to be checked; it is a poor answer to the people whose names no longer appear in the book. The seal is mine to explain, and the gap is mine to help investigate. That does not make me the witness to every journey listed beneath it.

I have requested the original dispatch from the Cinderwell registrar and asked for the clerk's mark to be compared with the copy here. I will not alter the archive entry while we wait. If the comparison shows an error in the count, the correction should preserve this signed page beside the corrected one. My responsibility begins with admitting what I approved. It does not end until another record can show what the Order did with that authority.

Supplemental archive leaf — Supplemental archive leaf — the signature Alden keeps beside the question

Alden returned to the signed dispatch after the lockkeeper's ledger was copied. He placed his signature beside the new transfer note, then asked that we not draw a line connecting them. The documents are related by the seal number and route, but he did not witness the handoff at the lock. A line on a page could make the chain look unbroken when it is not.

He told Rowan that he once signed orders in batches at the end of a watch. The seal had to be checked, the numbers read back and the destination verified; the person who carried each packet was entered elsewhere. Alden recalls the procedure more clearly than this dispatch. That may be because the procedure happened hundreds of times. He will not use repetition as proof that every step was followed here.

Before leaving, he added his own request to the open questions: find the page that records who took the packet from the boat. He did not ask the archive to clear his name or assign blame to the clerk whose mark appears on the copy. His signature remains evidence of authorization. The gap after it is still a gap, and his responsibility is to help trace the authority he gave.

entries.title: Emberroot and Minnow: One Trial Portion
entries.body: Ada asks Rowan to bring one harvested Emberroot and the Starlit Minnow caught for the trial to the field stove. The cookpot yields one portion of pottage. They record the two ingredients, the time spent preparing them and the fact that the seed reserve remains untouched. Neither ingredient is treated as an unlimited supply: the root came from one small bed, and the fish from one baited cast. The prepared portion can test whether the open table serves food without a household roll. It cannot establish how often either ingredient can be gathered or whether the meal meets every need. Ada asks that the recipe remain attached to the trial record so the next watch can repeat the same preparation or explain why it changed.
